Assessment, diagnosis, imaging, classifications and planning
Tooth wear, the failing dentition, interfaces and trauma

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old bruxist has firm, bilateral swellings at the angles of the mandible that bulge on clenching. You suspect masseteric hypertrophy.
Which nerve supplies the affected muscle?
options: Masseteric nerve, from the anterior division of V3, passing through the mandibular notch
questions.why: Masseter is supplied by the masseteric nerve, a motor branch of the anterior division of V3 that passes through the mandibular (sigmoid) notch. Masseteric hypertrophy is a recognised sign of bruxism.
questions.others: The buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the anterior division; the facial nerve supplies muscles of facial expression, not mastication.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old with tension-type headaches and TMD has a muscle tender to palpation above the zygomatic arch, in the temple.
Which muscle is this most likely to be?
questions.why: Temporalis lies in the temporal fossa and is the muscle most often palpably tender in tension-type headache linked to TMD.
questions.others: Masseter is felt over the ramus; the pterygoids cannot be palpated reliably from the temple.

questions.stem:
After a fall, a 22-year-old has a fracture of the left condylar neck. The radiograph shows the condylar head displaced anteromedially.
Which muscle has displaced it?
questions.why: The inferior head inserts into the pterygoid fovea on the condylar neck, so after a neck fracture it pulls the head forwards and medially.
questions.others: Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid act on the ramus and coronoid, below the fracture.

questions.stem:
A patient has lost function of the right nerve to lateral pterygoid after surgery.
On wide opening, how will the mandible move?
questions.why: Each lateral pterygoid pulls its own condyle forward. If the right one fails, the left condyle translates alone and swings the chin towards the paralysed (right) side.
questions.others: Opening still occurs through the left muscle and the depressors, so D is wrong.

questions.stem:
You are explaining to a student which muscles close the mouth during a denture wearer's power stroke.
Which muscles elevate the mandible?
questions.why: Masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid are all elevators. Only the lateral pterygoid opens the mouth.
questions.others: D omits medial pterygoid, which also elevates and protrudes.

questions.stem:
A 41-year-old has 22 mm of pain-free opening, then a click and further opening to 45 mm.
Which movement occurs in the lower (condyle–disc) compartment during the first 20–25 mm?
questions.why: The lower compartment (condyle against disc) allows hinge rotation for the first 20–25 mm; translation then occurs in the upper compartment.
questions.others: Translation is an upper-compartment movement.

questions.stem:
A patient with TMD describes earache with no ear disease on examination.
Which nerve provides the main sensory supply to the TMJ and explains the referral?
questions.why: The auriculotemporal nerve is the main sensory supply of the TMJ (with the masseteric and deep temporal nerves, Hilton's law). It also supplies the ear, which explains referred earache.
questions.others: The chorda tympani carries taste; the great auricular supplies skin over the parotid.

questions.stem:
A patient with disc displacement without reduction has pain on loading the joint.
Which tissue is the main source of the pain?
options: The central part of the disc
questions.why: The disc is avascular and aneural centrally. When it displaces anteriorly, the condyle loads the vascular, innervated bilaminar zone, which is the source of pain.

questions.stem:
You are reviewing TMJ anatomy before examining a patient with a dislocation history.
Which ligament is the true stabiliser of the joint, limiting posterior and inferior movement of the condyle?
questions.why: It is the true stabiliser, limiting posterior and inferior condylar movement.
questions.others: The sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments are accessory and contribute little.

questions.stem:
A dental student asks why the TMJ heals and remodels differently from other synovial joints.
What covers the articular surfaces of the TMJ?
questions.why: The TMJ surfaces are fibrocartilage, reflecting their intramembranous origin. This tissue can remodel under load.
questions.others: Hyaline cartilage covers most other synovial joints.

questions.stem:
A patient gags strongly during upper impressions.
Which nerves form the afferent and efferent limbs of the gag reflex?
questions.why: IX carries the sensation from the posterior tongue and oropharynx; X drives the pharyngeal response.

questions.stem:
A new lower complete denture lifts every time the patient protrudes the tongue. The anterior lingual flange is over-extended.
Which muscle is displacing it, and what is its nerve supply?
options: Geniohyoid; C1 via the hypoglossal nerve
questions.why: Genioglossus and the lingual frenum limit the anterior lingual flange; protrusion tightens them and lifts an over-extended flange.
questions.others: Mylohyoid limits the flange in the molar region, not anteriorly.

questions.stem:
A lower denture rises when the patient swallows. The lingual flange in the molar region extends straight down below the mylohyoid ridge.
Which muscle is responsible?
questions.why: Mylohyoid rises on swallowing. In the molar region the lingual flange should slope towards the tongue rather than run straight down below the ridge.

questions.stem:
A patient reports a sore spot at the distobuccal corner of a lower denture whenever they clench.
Which muscle is pressing on the flange?
questions.why: Masseter contracts on clenching and pushes on the distobuccal flange, forming the masseteric notch.
questions.others: Buccinator lies over the buccal shelf further forward.

questions.stem:
An upper denture is dislodged when the patient opens wide or moves the jaw sideways. The distobuccal flange is very thick.
Which structure is interfering with it?
questions.why: On opening and lateral movement the coronoid moves forward into the space beside the tuberosity, limiting the width of the upper distobuccal flange.

questions.stem:
You are marking the post-dam on a master cast.
Which landmark is a useful guide to its position?
options: Fovea palatini, near the vibrating line
questions.answerText: Fovea palatini, near the vibrating line.
questions.why: The post-dam lies between the anterior and posterior vibrating lines; the foveae sit close to this area and help locate it.

questions.stem:
On the master cast of an edentulous maxilla, you identify the hamular (pterygomaxillary) notches.
What do they mark?
options: The posterior limit of the tuberosity and the lateral extent of the post-dam
The anterior limit of the soft palate
The position of the greater palatine foramen
questions.answerText: Posterior limit of the tuberosity and lateral extent of the post-dam.
questions.why: The post-dam runs from one hamular notch to the other, and the denture must reach into the notches for a complete seal.

questions.stem:
A 76-year-old with a severely resorbed mandible has tingling in the lower lip when chewing with a new denture.
What is the most likely cause?
options: Pressure on the mental nerve where the foramen now lies near the ridge crest
Pressure on the nerve to mylohyoid
An allergy to the denture base
questions.answerText: Mental nerve at a foramen near the crest.
questions.why: In severe resorption the mental foramen comes to lie on or near the ridge crest, so the denture compresses the nerve. Relieve the fitting surface over it.
questions.others: Allergy causes generalised mucosal changes, not lip paraesthesia.

questions.stem:
A patient has a burning pain behind the upper incisors under a new upper denture. The mucosa there is slightly red.
Which area needs relief?
questions.why: The papilla overlies the incisive foramen and the nasopalatine nerve, a standard relief area. Pressure causes burning anterior pain.

questions.stem:
A patient reports swelling of the cheek on eating, with an over-extended upper buccal flange opposite the upper second molar.
Which structure could be compressed?
questions.why: It opens opposite the upper second molar and can be compressed by an over-extended or thick buccal flange.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old has an abscess on a lower second molar, with swelling below the lower border of the mandible.
Which space is involved?
questions.why: By the mylohyoid line rule, lower second and third molar apices lie below the mylohyoid attachment, so infection spreads into the submandibular space.

questions.stem:
A lower first premolar abscess has produced a swelling in the floor of the mouth, above the mylohyoid.
Which space is involved?
questions.why: Teeth from the incisors to the first molar have apices above mylohyoid; infection spreads into the sublingual space.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old presents with bilateral swelling below the mandible and under the chin, a raised floor of the mouth, drooling and a muffled voice.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Incise and drain intraorally in the practice
Extract the cause and send the patient home
questions.why: Bilateral submandibular, sublingual and submental involvement is Ludwig's angina, an airway emergency.
questions.others: Treating in practice, or delaying with antibiotics, risks airway obstruction.
questions.revise: Unit 1 §1.7, companion note 03 (risk and referral) · LO 1.1, 2a.6

questions.stem:
A patient has an upper canine abscess with swelling near the inner corner of the eye.
What is the main danger of this spread?
options: Cavernous sinus thrombosis via the angular and ophthalmic veins
questions.why: Upper canine infection above levator anguli oris enters the canine space. It can spread through the angular and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus.

questions.stem:
You explain to a colleague why infection in the infratemporal region is dangerous.
How does the pterygoid venous plexus communicate with the cavernous sinus?
questions.why: The pterygoid plexus connects to the cavernous sinus through emissary veins, a route for intracranial spread of infection.

questions.stem:
An inferior alveolar nerve block is given.
Into which space is the solution deposited?
questions.why: It contains the inferior alveolar and lingual nerves and vessels and is the target of the block.

questions.stem:
After an infected lower third molar, a patient has marked trismus and swelling over the angle of the mandible.
Which space is most likely involved?
options: Space of the body of the mandible
questions.why: Submasseteric infection, often from a lower third molar, presents with marked trismus and swelling over the angle.

questions.stem:
After a successful inferior alveolar block, the buccal gingiva of 46 is still sensitive during a crown preparation.
Which nerve needs anaesthetising?
options: Long buccal nerve, the sensory branch of the anterior division
questions.why: The buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the anterior division of V3; the inferior alveolar block does not reach it, so the buccal gingiva of lower molars needs a separate injection.

questions.stem:
You are describing the nerve to mylohyoid to a student.
Which muscles does it supply?
options: Mylohyoid and posterior belly of digastric
Mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric
questions.answerText: Mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric.
questions.why: The nerve to mylohyoid leaves the inferior alveolar nerve and supplies both.
questions.others: The posterior belly of digastric is facial nerve; geniohyoid is C1.

questions.stem:
A patient has a lingual nerve injury after surgery, distal to where the chorda tympani joins it.
What does the chorda tympani carry within the lingual nerve?
options: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands
questions.why: The chorda tympani (VII) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and preganglionic secretomotor fibres to the submandibular ganglion.
questions.others: Motor supply to the tongue is the hypoglossal nerve.

questions.stem:
After parotid surgery, a patient sweats and flushes over the cheek when eating.
Which nerve is involved?
questions.why: It carries secretomotor fibres to the parotid. After surgery these fibres can regrow into sweat glands (Frey's syndrome).

questions.stem:
A patient with a skull-base injury is noted to have damaged the artery passing through the foramen spinosum.
Which branch of the maxillary artery is this?
questions.why: A branch of the first part of the maxillary artery, it enters the skull through the foramen spinosum. The auriculotemporal nerve embraces it.

questions.stem:
During palatal surgery, brisk bleeding occurs from the greater palatine foramen.
From which vessel does the greater palatine artery arise?
options: First part of the maxillary artery
Descending palatine artery (third part of the maxillary artery)
questions.why: The third (pterygopalatine) part of the maxillary artery gives the descending palatine artery, which divides into the greater and lesser palatine arteries.

questions.stem:
You are explaining the blood supply to a hypertrophied masseter.
Which part of the maxillary artery gives the masseteric artery?
questions.why: The second part, related to the lower head of lateral pterygoid, gives the deep temporal, pterygoid, masseteric and buccal branches.

questions.stem: Which statement about the nerve to medial pterygoid is correct?
options: It arises from the anterior division of V3
It arises from the posterior division of V3
It is a branch of the facial nerve
It is a branch of the buccal nerve
It arises from the main trunk of V3, before it divides
questions.answerText: It arises from the main trunk of V3.
questions.why: The main trunk gives the nervus spinosus and the nerve to medial pterygoid before dividing. That nerve also passes through the otic ganglion to tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani.

questions.stem:
A patient with a fractured mandibular angle has displacement resisted on both surfaces of the ramus by two muscles.
Which pair forms the sling around the angle of the mandible?
questions.why: Masseter on the lateral surface and medial pterygoid on the medial surface together form the pterygomasseteric sling around the angle.

questions.stem:
A coronoid fracture fragment is pulled upwards towards the temporal fossa.
Which muscle inserts into the coronoid process?
questions.why: Temporalis inserts into the apex and medial surface of the coronoid and the anterior border of the ramus, so it pulls a coronoid fragment upwards.
questions.others: Lateral pterygoid inserts into the pterygoid fovea, disc and capsule, never the coronoid.

questions.stem:
A patient protrudes during a jaw-relation record and the operator guides the mandible back.
Which muscle is the main retractor of the mandible?
questions.why: The near-horizontal posterior fibres are the main retractors; the deep masseter assists.
questions.others: Lateral pterygoid protrudes, the opposite movement.

questions.stem:
You ask a patient to slide the mandible to the left during an excursive check.
Which muscles on which side mainly produce this movement?
questions.why: To move the chin left, the right condyle must move forward and medially; the right pterygoids do this.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old has a reciprocal click in the right TMJ.
Which muscle attaches to the articular disc and is most associated with disc displacement?
questions.why: The superior head attaches to the disc and capsule, so it is the muscle most associated with disc displacement, clicking and locking.

questions.stem:
A patient has weakness of the palatoglossal arch after a brainstem lesion, while tongue protrusion is normal.
Which nerve supplies palatoglossus?
questions.why: Palatoglossus is the only tongue muscle not supplied by the hypoglossal nerve. Normal protrusion shows XII is intact.

questions.stem:
You are explaining soft-palate anatomy before a post-dam is cut.
Which soft palate muscle is not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus?
options: Tensor veli palatini (nerve to medial pterygoid, V3)
questions.why: It is supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3). All other soft palate muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.stem:
After a Bell's palsy, a lower denture wearer finds food collecting in the buccal sulcus and the denture less stable.
Which weakened muscle explains this?
questions.why: Buccinator (facial nerve) keeps food on the occlusal table and grips the buccal polished surface. Weakness lets food pocket and reduces muscular control of the denture.

questions.stem:
You are recording the neutral zone for a patient with an unstable lower denture.
Which structures mainly determine lip support and the labial boundary of the neutral zone?
questions.why: These determine lip support, the neutral zone and the shape of the labial flange.

questions.stem:
A student asks which nerve supplies geniohyoid.
What is the correct answer?
options: C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve
questions.why: Geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibres that travel with XII; it depresses the mandible and pulls the hyoid forward.

questions.stem:
A patient with facial nerve palsy is examined for swallowing problems.
Which hyoid muscle is supplied by the facial nerve?
questions.why: Both are second-arch muscles supplied by the facial nerve. The anterior belly is first-arch, supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid.

questions.stem:
You are checking the posterior extension of a new lower complete denture.
How much of the retromolar pad should the base cover?
options: A narrow strip at its front edge
At least the anterior half to two-thirds
All of it, onto the pterygomandibular raphe
It depends only on the OVD
questions.answerText: At least the anterior half to two-thirds.
questions.why: This gives support and a posterior seal without impinging on the pterygomandibular raphe.

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old has a moderately resorbed mandible.
Which area provides the primary support for the lower complete denture?
questions.why: Between the external oblique ridge and the residual ridge, its cortical bone lies at right angles to occlusal load, making it the primary support area.

questions.stem:
A new upper complete denture is planned for a patient with a large torus palatinus.
Which areas normally need relief on the fitting surface?
questions.why: The incisive papilla, midline raphe and torus palatinus are thin, unyielding or innervated areas, listed as relief areas in the maxilla.

questions.stem:
A new lower denture lifts at the back each time the patient opens wide. The base extends over the whole retromolar pad.
Which structure is tightening against the over-extension?
questions.why: The raphe runs from the hamulus to the retromolar region and tightens on wide opening, lifting a base that extends too far distally.

questions.stem:
A 79-year-old has a severely resorbed, knife-edged mandibular ridge.
Which features may need relief in the fitting surface?
options: The mental foramen, now near the crest
questions.why: Genial tubercles, a crestal mental foramen, a sharp mylohyoid ridge and a knife-edged crest are all mandibular relief areas in severe resorption.

questions.stem:
A patient on anticholinergic medication complains of a dry mouth at rest.
Which gland produces most of the unstimulated saliva?
questions.why: The submandibular gland produces most unstimulated (resting) saliva.
questions.others: The parotid dominates stimulated flow.

questions.stem:
A patient has had radiotherapy to both parotid glands.
Which saliva is reduced most?
options: None, because the submandibular glands compensate fully
questions.why: The parotid contributes most of the stimulated saliva, so its loss reduces flow during eating most.

questions.stem:
You see a small salivary stone at the duct opening beside the lingual frenum.
Which duct opens here?
options: Submandibular (Wharton's) duct, at the sublingual papilla
questions.why: It opens at the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenum, the common site for salivary stones.

questions.stem:
You explain parotid secretomotor supply to a student.
What is the correct parasympathetic pathway?
options: Facial nerve, chorda tympani, lingual nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve, lesser petrosal nerve, otic ganglion, auriculotemporal nerve
Superior cervical ganglion, external carotid plexus
Facial nerve, greater petrosal nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion
questions.answerText: IX, lesser petrosal, otic ganglion, auriculotemporal.
questions.why: This is the parasympathetic route to the parotid.
questions.others: A is the submandibular route; E supplies the lacrimal and nasal glands.

questions.stem:
A patient has reduced submandibular flow after a middle-ear operation.
Which parasympathetic pathway supplies the submandibular gland?
options: Facial nerve, chorda tympani, lingual nerve, submandibular ganglion
questions.answerText: VII, chorda tympani, lingual nerve, submandibular ganglion.
questions.why: The chorda tympani passes through the middle ear, so ear surgery can reduce submandibular and sublingual secretion.

questions.stem:
A patient has a ranula-like swelling in the floor of the mouth.
Which statement about the sublingual gland is correct?
options: It drains through a single duct opposite the upper second molar
It is supplied by the otic ganglion
It produces most of the stimulated saliva
It is mainly mucous and drains through multiple ducts of Rivinus on the sublingual fold
questions.answerText: Mainly mucous, with multiple ducts of Rivinus.
questions.why: The sublingual gland drains through many small ducts on the sublingual fold and shares the submandibular parasympathetic supply.

questions.stem:
A patient has TMJ inflammation and the vascular supply is discussed.
Which arteries supply the TMJ?
questions.why: The TMJ is supplied by branches of these two vessels.

questions.stem:
A student asks how to classify the TMJ.
Which description is correct?
questions.why: It hinges (rotation, lower compartment) and glides (translation, upper compartment).

questions.stem:
During an inferior alveolar block, the solution may be deflected by a ligament running from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula.
Which ligament is this?
questions.why: It runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula, medial to the nerve at the mandibular foramen, and is an accessory TMJ ligament.

questions.stem:
A new lower denture is retentive at rest but is displaced whenever the patient speaks or smiles.
What should you do first?
options: Assess the border extension and polished-surface contours against muscle action
questions.answerText: Assess borders and polished surfaces against muscle action.
questions.why: A denture retentive at rest but displaced in function suggests over-extension or polished-surface contours that conflict with muscles. Diagnose the functional border first.
questions.others: Adhesive, occlusal changes or a remake do not address the cause.

questions.stem:
On a lower complete denture, the lingual flange in the molar region ends 4 mm short of the functional depth of the floor of the mouth.
What is the most likely consequence?
options: Ulceration of the floor of the mouth
Loss of the peripheral seal and reduced retention
questions.why: A short lingual flange fails to contact the floor of the mouth, breaking the seal and reducing retention.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old complete denture wearer reports 6 weeks of numbness of the left lower lip. The denture fits well and does not press on the mental foramen.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Urgent referral to investigate the cause, including malignancy
Relieve the denture and review in 6 months
questions.why: Unexplained, persistent lip numbness with no denture cause may signal malignancy or neuropathy and must be investigated.
questions.others: Relieving and reviewing in 6 months delays diagnosis.

questions.stem:
A patient with a lower molar infection has a temperature of 38.6°C, trismus of 15 mm and difficulty swallowing.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Prescribe amoxicillin and review in a week
Extract the tooth under LA in the practice
Refer urgently to the maxillofacial team
questions.why: Fever, trismus and dysphagia show a spreading infection that may threaten the airway.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old with an atrophic mandible is assessed for an implant-retained overdenture.
Which structure most often limits safe implant placement in the premolar region?
options: The mental foramen and the anterior loop of the inferior alveolar nerve
questions.answerText: Mental foramen and anterior loop of the inferior alveolar nerve.
questions.why: In atrophy the foramen lies high on the ridge and the nerve may loop forward, limiting premolar implant sites. Recognise it and refer for appropriate imaging and planning.

questions.stem:
You are deciding the posterior extent of a new upper complete denture.
What should be assessed before planning the posterior palatal seal?
options: Soft-palate form and movement at the vibrating line
questions.why: The posterior seal depends on the vibrating line, and its position varies with soft-palate form; examine it before deciding the seal.

questions.stem:
An edentulous patient has large undercuts on both maxillary tuberosities.
What is the usual approach?
options: Choose a path or block out one side, reducing surgically only if both still prevent insertion
questions.answerText: Choose a path or block out one side.
questions.why: A suitable path of insertion or relief on one side usually allows insertion; surgery is reserved for undercuts that still prevent it.

questions.stem:
A partially dentate patient needs a lower Kennedy Class I RPD. Large bilateral mandibular tori leave no room for a lingual bar.
What is appropriate?
options: A lingual bar over the tori
A lingual plate over the tori
A labial bar, or surgical removal of the tori if a sound design needs it
questions.answerText: Labial bar, or removal of the tori.
questions.why: Tori block a lingual connector; a labial bar avoids them, or the tori are removed if a sound design needs a lingual connector.

questions.stem:
A patient with an inferior alveolar block infection develops severe trismus and dysphagia.
Infection in the pterygomandibular space can spread directly to which space?
questions.why: The pterygomandibular space communicates with the lateral pharyngeal space, which can lead to airway compromise.

questions.stem:
After a successful inferior alveolar block, the lower lip is numb but the first molar pulp is still sensitive.
Supplementary anaesthesia of which nerve is most likely to help?
questions.why: It can give accessory supply to lower molars; supplementary lingual infiltration or intraligamentary anaesthesia may help.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old taking amitriptyline and oxybutynin complains that her dentures are loose. Her unstimulated whole saliva flow is 0.08 mL/min.
How should this result be interpreted?
options: It cannot be interpreted without a stimulated sample
questions.why: Unstimulated flow below 0.1 mL/min is hyposalivation (normal is about 0.3–0.4 mL/min). Amitriptyline and oxybutynin are both anticholinergic.
questions.others: A stimulated sample adds information, but the resting value alone already meets the definition.

questions.stem:
A student asks how saliva retains a complete denture.
Which factors contribute?
options: Atmospheric pressure through the peripheral seal
questions.why: Retention comes from a thin saliva film (adhesion to mucosa and base, cohesion within the film), interfacial surface tension, viscosity, and atmospheric pressure maintained by the border seal.

questions.stem:
Two edentulous patients have similar ridges and well-made dentures. One has thin, watery saliva; the other has thick, ropy saliva.
Which saliva usually gives better retention?
options: Thick saliva in the mandible only
questions.why: A thin film gives better adhesion and surface tension. Thick, ropy saliva forms a thicker film that reduces retention and can push the denture down.

questions.stem:
A dentate 64-year-old with Sjögren's syndrome asks what to use for her dry mouth. She has several root caries lesions.
What is most appropriate?
options: A neutral mucin- or carboxymethylcellulose-based substitute, with high-fluoride toothpaste
questions.why: Substitutes for dentate patients must be pH-neutral; acidic products demineralise teeth. High-fluoride toothpaste protects against the high caries risk.
questions.others: Lemon, citric acid and sugared lozenges all increase caries or erosion.

questions.stem:
A patient with Sjögren's syndrome also has poorly controlled asthma.
Which treatment for her dry mouth is unsuitable?
questions.why: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist that can provoke bronchospasm; it is contraindicated in uncontrolled asthma and glaucoma.

questions.stem:
A patient sips an acidic drink and stimulated saliva begins to neutralise it.
What is the main buffer in stimulated saliva?
questions.why: Bicarbonate concentration rises with flow rate and is the main buffer of stimulated saliva.

questions.stem:
You explain to a patient why saliva protects against infection.
Which are antimicrobial components of saliva?
questions.why: Lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA and histatins (antifungal) are all antimicrobial.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old with new complete dentures says they cannot chew steak as they did with natural teeth.
About what proportion of dentate bite force and chewing efficiency do complete denture wearers achieve?
questions.why: Complete denture wearers achieve about one-fifth to one-sixth of dentate bite force and chewing efficiency. Explaining this sets realistic expectations.

questions.stem:
You are explaining why complete denture wearers find fine biting control harder than dentate patients.
On which receptors does a complete denture wearer depend for feedback?
questions.why: Periodontal mechanoreceptors are lost with the teeth, so edentulous patients rely on mucosal and TMJ receptors for feedback.

questions.stem:
A patient with an implant crown asks whether the implant will "feel" like a tooth.
Compared with a natural tooth, feedback from an implant (osseoperception) is:
questions.why: Implants lack a periodontal ligament; their osseoperception is less sensitive than a natural tooth's feedback.

questions.stem:
A healthy 72-year-old has lost all four first and second molars but has sound premolars and anterior teeth in both arches. She is comfortable and chews well.
What is the most appropriate advice?
options: A removable partial denture to replace the molars
Extraction of the remaining teeth for complete dentures
No replacement; a shortened dental arch usually gives adequate function
questions.why: Käyser showed that premolar-to-premolar arches (about 3–5 occlusal units) usually give adequate function in older adults. A free-end RPD often adds little and risks plaque and caries.

questions.stem:
A public-health lecture quotes the WHO goal for tooth retention.
How many functional natural teeth should be retained throughout life?
questions.why: The WHO goal is retention of at least 20 functional teeth throughout life.

questions.stem:
An 84-year-old with Parkinson's disease has worn the same well-liked complete dentures for 12 years. They are worn and loose.
Which approach best suits her ability to adapt?
options: New dentures of a completely new design
questions.why: Ability to adapt falls with age and neuromuscular disease. Copying keeps the familiar shapes she has learned to control while correcting wear and fit.

questions.stem:
A patient edentulous for 30 years appears Class III, with the upper denture teeth set inside the lower ridge.
What explains this appearance?
options: The maxilla resorbs upwards and inwards, and the mandible downwards and outwards
questions.why: The upper arch becomes smaller and the lower wider, giving an apparent Class III relationship and posterior crossbite.

questions.stem:
You are explaining long-term ridge resorption to a patient after extractions.
In the long term, how much more height does the anterior mandible lose than the anterior maxilla?
questions.why: Tallgren showed the anterior mandible loses about four times the height of the anterior maxilla in the long term.

questions.stem:
A patient asks when her ridges will shrink most after extractions.
When is resorption fastest?
options: At a constant rate for life
questions.why: Resorption is fastest early after extraction and continues more slowly for life. This is why immediate dentures need relining.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old with two sound lower canines wants to slow the loss of her lower ridge.
Which measures help preserve the ridge?
questions.why: Retained roots and implants load the bone and preserve it; night removal reduces continuous loading of the ridge.

questions.stem:
A patient has worn the same ill-fitting dentures day and night for 15 years.
Which habit is most likely to have accelerated ridge resorption?
questions.why: Prosthetic factors (poor fit, continuous wear, inadequate support) accelerate resorption.

questions.stem:
A 56-year-old lost 36 ten years ago and wants it replaced. 26 has over-erupted by 3 mm.
What is the main consequence for planning?
options: Reduced interocclusal space, so the over-erupted tooth must be managed first
questions.why: Over-eruption after tooth loss reduces the space for a replacement; the opposing tooth may need adjustment, a restoration or orthodontic intrusion first.

questions.stem:
An 80-year-old drinks sweet tea through the day and has several root caries lesions.
At about what pH does root dentine begin to demineralise?
questions.why: Root dentine and cementum demineralise at a higher pH than enamel (5.5), so root caries starts with milder acid challenges.

questions.stem:
Patient X has sugar in ten cups of tea a day. Patient Y has the same total sugar in one dessert.
What is the most important caries advice for patient X?
options: Use a mouthwash after every cup
Reduce the frequency of sugar intake
Rinse with water after each cup
questions.why: The Stephan curve shows each intake drops plaque pH for 30–60 minutes. Frequency, not total quantity, drives caries.

questions.stem:
A partially dentate patient with recession has multiple root caries lesions.
Which organism is particularly associated with root caries?
questions.why: Actinomyces is particularly associated with root caries; Streptococcus mutans initiates coronal caries and Lactobacillus drives progression.

questions.stem:
A histology slide shows an early enamel caries lesion.
Which zone shows the greatest demineralisation?
questions.why: Deep to surface, the zones are translucent, dark, body and surface; the body has the greatest mineral loss.
questions.others: The surface zone stays relatively intact.

questions.stem:
A deep carious lesion on 36 is close to the pulp. The tooth is vital with no symptoms of irreversible pulpitis.
What is the most appropriate caries removal approach?
options: Remove all softened dentine to hard dentine over the pulp
Leave infected dentine at the periphery
Remove infected dentine, leave affected dentine near the pulp, and seal
questions.why: Remove soft, infected dentine; leave affected, remineralisable dentine over the pulp and seal well, avoiding pulp exposure.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old has high caries risk and active root caries.
Which toothpaste does Delivering Better Oral Health recommend?
questions.why: Delivering Better Oral Health (2021) recommends 5000 ppm for high-risk patients aged 16 and over.

questions.stem:
An adult with partial dentures is at high caries risk.
Which professional fluoride application is recommended?
options: Fluoride varnish 22,600 ppm at least twice a year
226 ppm rinse daily in the surgery
questions.answerText: 22,600 ppm varnish at least twice yearly.
questions.why: This is the DBOH recommendation for adults at higher caries risk.

questions.stem:
A 76-year-old with a Co-Cr RPD, poor dexterity and gingival recession is reviewed.
Which factors increase her root caries risk?
questions.why: Recession exposes roots, hyposalivation removes protection, and partial dentures retain plaque around clasps and saddles. Poor dexterity adds to the risk.

questions.stem:
A 21-year-old has palatal erosion of the upper anterior teeth, bilateral parotid enlargement and calluses on her knuckles.
What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Palatal erosion (perimylolysis), parotid enlargement and Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) together point to bulimia.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old has smooth, silky enamel on the upper incisors, cupped cusps, and amalgam restorations standing proud of the surrounding tooth.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acid dissolves tooth around the restorations, leaving them standing proud, with smooth, silky enamel and cupped cusps.
questions.others: In attrition, restorations wear flush with the tooth.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old has flat, shiny wear facets that match on opposing teeth, fractured cusps and hypertrophic masseters.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Matching facets on opposing teeth, fractured cusps and masseteric hypertrophy show tooth-to-tooth wear from bruxism.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old has sharp-edged, V-shaped cervical notches on the upper canines and premolars, worse on the left. She is right-handed and brushes hard.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Sharp, V-shaped cervical notches from a foreign object (the toothbrush) are worst on the side opposite the brushing hand — the left for a right-handed patient.

questions.stem:
A bruxist has wedge-shaped cervical lesions with sharp internal angles, some extending below the gingival margin, on teeth with heavy lateral contacts.
Which process is proposed to explain these lesions?
options: Abfraction (flexural stress at the cervical margin)
questions.why: Abfraction is the proposed (debated) flexural-stress mechanism for wedge-shaped cervical lesions with sharp angles, sometimes subgingival, on teeth under heavy lateral load.

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old has slow, localised wear of the upper anterior teeth over many years, yet the posterior teeth still meet and there is no space to restore the worn teeth.
Why is there no interocclusal space?
options: Compensatory alveolar growth has kept the worn teeth in contact
questions.why: In slow wear, dentoalveolar compensation keeps worn teeth in contact and maintains the OVD, leaving no space. This is the rationale for the Dahl approach.
questions.others: OVD is usually maintained, not lost.

questions.stem:
You screen a new patient's tooth wear with the BEWE.
How is the BEWE scored?
options: Using the Smith and Knight index
0–3 for the worst surface in each sextant, with the sum guiding management
questions.answerText: 0–3 per sextant; the sum guides management.
questions.why: BEWE scores the most affected surface in each sextant 0–3; the cumulative score directs prevention, monitoring or treatment.
questions.others: A describes Smith and Knight.

questions.stem:
You need to record wear on each surface for a research audit.
Which index scores 0–4 on every tooth surface?
options: Smith and Knight Tooth Wear Index
questions.answerText: Smith and Knight Tooth Wear Index.
questions.why: It scores every surface 0–4 and suits detailed research or monitoring rather than screening.

questions.stem:
You suspect an eating disorder in a 19-year-old with palatal erosion, who denies vomiting.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Approach with empathy, liaise with her GMP with consent, and focus on prevention and monitoring before restoration
questions.answerText: Empathy, liaison with the GMP, prevention first.
questions.why: Patients may be secretive. A non-judgemental approach, consent-based liaison with the GMP, and protective, monitoring-led care come before any restoration.

questions.stem:
An upper denture wearer has nodular, papillary tissue in the centre of the palate under the denture.
Which Newton type of denture stomatitis is this?
questions.why: Type III is papillary hyperplasia of the central palate. Type I is pinpoint hyperaemia; type II is diffuse erythema.

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old has diffuse erythema of the palate under an ill-fitting upper acrylic denture that she wears day and night. She has no symptoms.
What is the most appropriate first management?
options: Denture hygiene, removal at night, soaking, and correcting the fit
questions.answerText: Hygiene, night removal, soaking and correcting fit.
questions.why: Denture stomatitis is driven by denture biofilm and continuous wear; treat the denture first. Antifungals are added only if it persists.

questions.stem:
A patient on warfarin has denture stomatitis that has not settled with hygiene and night removal.
Which antifungal is most appropriate?
questions.why: Miconazole (even as gel or cream) and systemic azoles interact with warfarin and raise the INR. Nystatin is not absorbed.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old denture wearer has painful fissures at both corners of the mouth.
Which investigations are indicated?
options: A swab and no other tests
Full blood count, haematinics and blood glucose
questions.why: Angular cheilitis is predisposed by haematinic deficiency, diabetes and immunosuppression, as well as low OVD and denture infection.

questions.stem:
A patient with angular cheilitis grows both Candida and Staphylococcus aureus from swabs. He is not on any interacting drugs.
Which topical treatment covers both organisms?
questions.why: Miconazole is active against both Candida and Staphylococcus aureus. Treat the denture as the source as well.

questions.stem:
A leaf of firm tissue lies in the lower labial sulcus under an over-extended flange of a 10-year-old denture.
What is the most appropriate management?
options: Excise it immediately without adjusting the denture
Trim the flange, use a tissue conditioner, and excise with histology if it does not resolve
questions.answerText: Trim, condition, excise with histology if it persists.
questions.why: Removing the irritant and using a tissue conditioner often lets the hyperplasia shrink. Persistent tissue is excised and examined histologically.

questions.stem:
An ulcer under a lower flange is still present 3 weeks after the flange was adjusted.
What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Adjust the flange again and review in 3 months
Urgent referral on the suspected cancer pathway
questions.why: An ulcer persisting 3 weeks after removing the cause must be treated as possible malignancy.

questions.stem:
An edentulous upper anterior ridge is mobile and displaceable. The patient has natural lower anterior teeth.
Which statement is correct?
options: It should be compressed in a putty impression
It is fibrous replacement of bone, best recorded with a mucostatic or selective-pressure impression
questions.answerText: Fibrous replacement of bone; mucostatic or selective-pressure impression.
questions.why: A flabby ridge, often opposed by lower natural anteriors (combination syndrome), is recorded undisplaced with a windowed tray so it does not rebound under the denture.
questions.others: Excision loses ridge height and is rarely needed.

questions.stem:
A 62-year-old smoker has a well-demarcated red patch on the floor of the mouth that does not wipe off.
Which lesion carries the highest risk of malignant transformation?
questions.why: Erythroplakia carries the highest malignant transformation risk of the potentially malignant disorders.

questions.stem:
You are performing a soft-tissue examination on a high-risk patient.
Which sites carry the highest risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma?
options: Dorsum of the tongue and lips
Lateral border of the tongue and floor of the mouth
questions.answerText: Lateral tongue and floor of mouth.
questions.why: These are the highest-risk sites for oral squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem:
A new patient smokes 20 a day, drinks 30 units a week and chews areca nut.
Which of these are risk factors for oral cancer?
questions.why: Tobacco and alcohol act synergistically; areca nut is an independent carcinogen. HPV, immunosuppression and previous cancer also raise risk.

questions.stem:
At a denture review you find a red and white patch on the lateral tongue that the patient had not noticed.
What does NICE NG12 advise?
options: Urgent referral on the suspected cancer pathway
questions.why: NICE NG12 lists a red or red-and-white patch, persistent ulceration over 3 weeks, or a persistent lump as triggers for urgent referral.

questions.stem:
A 79-year-old's teeth respond weakly to cold testing, and root canal access on a molar proves difficult.
What explains both findings?
options: Secondary dentine deposition, giving smaller pulp chambers and lower sensibility responses
questions.why: Ageing teeth lay down secondary dentine, shrinking the pulp, lowering sensibility responses and making access harder.
questions.others: A weak response does not mean necrosis.

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old has glossitis, recurrent ulcers, angular cheilitis and a burning tongue.
What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.why: Deficient iron, B12 or folate causes glossitis, angular cheilitis, recurrent ulcers and a burning sensation.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has periodontitis.
How are the two conditions related?
options: Periodontitis improves diabetes, but not the reverse
questions.why: Poor glycaemic control worsens periodontitis, and periodontal inflammation worsens glycaemic control.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old with osteoporosis asks about implants. She has not been prescribed drugs for it.
Which statement is correct?
options: Osteoporosis is generally not a contraindication; antiresorptive drug treatment is the bigger issue
A bone density scan is required before any denture
questions.answerText: Not a contraindication; antiresorptives matter more.
questions.why: Osteoporosis itself does not preclude implants. Antiresorptive drugs carry the MRONJ risk.

questions.stem:
A patient asks how to clean her cobalt–chromium partial denture.
Which advice is correct?
options: Soak it overnight in household bleach
Do not soak it in hypochlorite, because it damages Co-Cr; use a suitable non-abrasive cleaner
questions.why: Sodium hypochlorite corrodes cobalt–chromium frameworks. Use non-abrasive cleaners suitable for metal.

questions.stem:
An 86-year-old care-home resident with poor dexterity needs replacement of missing teeth. Attendance and cleaning are unreliable.
Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.why: When cleaning and attendance are unreliable, favour designs the patient and carers can maintain over elaborate fixed or implant work.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old with generalised periodontitis wants a bridge.
What is the usual sequence of periodontal care before definitive prosthodontics?
options: Hygiene and risk-factor control, subgingival instrumentation, surgery where needed, then supportive care
Extraction of all mobile teeth first
questions.answerText: OHI and risk control, instrumentation, surgery, supportive care.
questions.why: This is the stepwise periodontal sequence; definitive prosthodontics follows stability.

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old has lost 47 only. There is no drifting or over-eruption and he has no complaints.
What is the most appropriate advice?
options: No replacement is a valid option
questions.answerText: No replacement is a valid option.
questions.why: Not every missing tooth needs replacing. A single missing second molar with a stable occlusion and no complaint can be left, after the options are discussed.

questions.stem:
A 62-year-old has a dry mouth from her antidepressant and has new root caries.
Which measures are appropriate?
options: Ask her GMP whether the medication can be reviewed
questions.why: Treat the cause where possible (a medication review with the GMP), stimulate saliva without sugar, and protect the teeth with high fluoride.

questions.stem:
After head and neck radiotherapy, a patient's saliva is scant, thick and ropy, and his upper denture keeps dropping.
What explains the poor retention?
options: Thick, scant saliva gives a poor adhesive and cohesive film
questions.answerText: Thick, scant saliva gives a poor film.
questions.why: Retention depends on a thin continuous saliva film. After radiotherapy, saliva is reduced and viscous, so adhesion and cohesion fail.

questions.stem:
You review a patient's medication list for causes of dry mouth.
Which drug group is least associated with dry mouth?
questions.why: Antidepressants, antihistamines, antimuscarinics and diuretics commonly cause dry mouth; penicillins do not.

questions.stem:
A patient with frequent sugar intake and low saliva develops rapidly progressive caries.
Which concept explains the shift towards acid-producing species?
questions.why: Environmental change, such as frequent sugar and low saliva, selects for acidogenic, aciduric species, shifting the plaque towards caries.

questions.stem:
A technician designs a cobalt–chromium clasp to engage a 0.25 mm undercut, whereas a cast gold clasp on the same tooth would engage 0.5 mm.
Which property of Co-Cr explains the difference?
options: Higher elastic modulus (about 220 GPa, roughly twice that of Type IV gold)
questions.why: Co-Cr (about 220 GPa) is about twice as stiff as Type IV gold (90–100 GPa). A stiffer clasp generates more force per unit of flexure, so it must engage a shallower undercut (0.25 mm against 0.5 mm).
questions.others: Density affects weight, not clasp design.

questions.stem:
A clasp arm must flex over the height of contour every time the denture is inserted and still return to its original shape.
Which property must the strain not exceed?
questions.why: Below the proportional limit a clasp recovers fully; above it the clasp deforms permanently and loosens.
questions.others: UTS is the stress at fracture, far beyond the working range.

questions.stem:
A patient repeatedly bent her Co-Cr clasp to tighten it, and it snapped at the shoulder.
Which property of Co-Cr made this likely?
questions.why: Co-Cr has little permanent strain before fracture, so repeated bending work-hardens and cracks it. Wrought wire tolerates adjustment better.

questions.stem:
A patient with Parkinson's disease drops her upper denture in the sink every few weeks.
Which property should the new denture base be chosen for?
questions.why: Toughness is energy absorbed before fracture. High-impact acrylic, with a rubber phase, resists breakage when dropped.
questions.others: Resilience is energy absorbed elastically, relevant to liners and mouthguards.

questions.stem:
An upper complete denture opposing natural lower teeth cracks down the midline after 3 years, without ever being dropped.
What is the failure mechanism?
questions.why: Repeated sub-critical flexing, worsened by natural opposing teeth, a deep frenal notch or a torus, causes the classic midline fracture.
questions.others: Impact fracture follows a single event such as dropping.

questions.stem:
A sports mouthguard and a soft denture liner both need to absorb energy without permanent deformation.
Which property describes this?
questions.why: Resilience is the energy absorbed elastically (the area under the elastic part of the stress–strain curve).

questions.stem:
A clinician chooses zirconia rather than a glass ceramic for a posterior bridge in a heavy biter.
Which property gives zirconia its advantage in resisting crack growth?
questions.why: KIc measures resistance to crack propagation; zirconia's is much higher than glass ceramics'.
questions.others: High modulus means stiffness, not crack resistance.

questions.stem:
An elastomeric impression is removed slowly over several seconds and the casts do not fit.
Why should it be removed with a snap?
options: Viscoelastic materials recover better when deformed quickly
questions.answerText: Viscoelastic recovery is better with fast deformation.
questions.why: Elastomers behave more elastically under a rapid load; slow removal allows permanent deformation.

questions.stem:
A wax pattern for a crown is left on the bench overnight before investing. The casting does not seat.
What has happened to the wax?
questions.why: Wax has high thermal expansion and stores stresses that release over time, distorting the pattern. Invest promptly.

questions.stem:
A researcher measures the hardness of a thin glaze layer on porcelain.
Which hardness test suits brittle materials and thin coatings?
questions.why: Knoop's elongated, shallow indenter suits brittle materials and thin coatings.

questions.stem:
A large acrylic restoration repeatedly leaks at its margins with hot and cold drinks.
How does the thermal expansion of acrylic compare with tooth?
options: Acrylic (about 80 ppm/°C) expands far more than tooth (about 11 ppm/°C)
questions.why: Acrylic is about 80 ppm/°C against about 11 ppm/°C for tooth, so temperature change opens the margins.

questions.stem:
A technician explains why the porcelain on a metal–ceramic crown resists cracking on cooling.
How should the coefficient of thermal expansion of the porcelain relate to the metal?
options: Slightly lower than the metal, so the porcelain cools into compression
questions.why: The metal contracts slightly more on cooling and leaves the porcelain in compression, which brittle materials resist well.

questions.stem:
A clinician wants a post whose stiffness is close to dentine, to spread stress more evenly in a root-filled premolar.
Which post has a modulus closest to dentine (15–20 GPa)?
questions.why: Glass-fibre posts (about 20–40 GPa) are closest to dentine (15–20 GPa). Their failures tend to be debonds rather than root fractures.

questions.stem:
A sales representative says a material with a high elastic modulus must be the best choice for a posterior crown.
What does a high elastic modulus necessarily mean?
options: The material has high flexural strength
None of these; modulus describes stiffness only
questions.why: Modulus tells you stiffness. It says nothing about toughness, wear, bond strength or flexural strength — a classic exam trap.

questions.stem:
You need a mucostatic impression of a flabby ridge and do not need to record undercuts.
Which material records tissue at rest but cannot record undercuts?
questions.why: Plaster is mucostatic and accurate but brittle, so it fractures over undercuts.

questions.stem:
A primary impression in compound is distorted, with soft surface and hard centre.
Why must compound be softened thoroughly?
options: It has low thermal conductivity, so heat penetrates slowly
questions.why: Compound must be heated through; a soft surface over a hard core distorts the impression.

questions.stem:
A patient complains of a burning feeling after a wash impression with zinc oxide–eugenol paste.
Which is a disadvantage of ZOE impression paste?
options: Eugenol irritation, and it cannot record undercuts
questions.why: ZOE paste is rigid when set, so it cannot record undercuts, and eugenol can irritate.

questions.stem:
An alginate impression for study casts is left in a sealed bag over the weekend before pouring.
What is the main problem?
options: Syneresis and imbibition distort it; alginate should be poured within about 10–15 minutes
questions.why: Alginate loses water (syneresis) or absorbs it (imbibition) and distorts; pour within about 10–15 minutes unless it is an extended-pour product.

questions.stem:
An alginate impression tears in the interproximal areas.
Which design feature helps prevent tearing?
options: A metal stock tray with no adhesive
At least 3–4 mm bulk of material
questions.why: Alginate has low tear strength; adequate bulk, a perforated or adhesive tray and snap removal reduce tearing.

questions.stem:
A condensation silicone impression was poured 2 days after it was taken. The crown made on it is tight.
Why?
questions.why: Condensation silicone gives off ethanol as a by-product and keeps shrinking; pour promptly.

questions.stem:
An addition silicone wash stays sticky around a preparation where the nurse handled the retraction cord with gloved fingers.
What is the most likely cause?
options: Sulphur from latex gloves inhibiting the set
questions.why: Sulphur compounds in latex poison the platinum catalyst of addition silicone. Use vinyl or nitrile gloves when handling cord near the preparation.

questions.stem:
Casts poured immediately from an addition silicone impression have bubbly, porous die surfaces.
What explains this?
options: Hydrogen release from the set material; wait about an hour or use a material with a hydrogen absorber
questions.why: Set addition silicone can release hydrogen, causing porous die surfaces if poured immediately. Wait about an hour unless the product contains a hydrogen absorber.

questions.stem:
A polyether impression is taken for a lower implant case with large embrasure spaces. The stone dies break on removal.
Which property of polyether caused the problem?
questions.why: Set polyether is very rigid, so it is hard to remove from undercuts and can fracture stone dies.

questions.stem:
A clinician wants an elastomer that wets a moist preparation well without added surfactant.
Which material is inherently hydrophilic?
questions.why: Polyether is inherently hydrophilic; addition silicone needs added surfactant.

questions.stem:
A patient has a flabby anterior maxilla that must be recorded undisplaced.
Which technique records the tissue at rest?
options: Heavy-bodied silicone in a close-fitting tray
A low-viscosity material in a spaced (or windowed) tray
questions.answerText: Low-viscosity material in a spaced or windowed tray.
questions.why: Mucostatic recording avoids displacing the flabby tissue, which would otherwise rebound under the denture.

questions.stem:
A special tray is made for an alginate secondary impression.
What spacer thickness is typical?
questions.why: Alginate needs about 3 mm bulk for strength; elastomers use 1–3 mm depending on viscosity; ZOE is close-fitting.

questions.stem:
Several casts from one practice are distorted. The practice uses thin plastic stock trays without adhesive for elastomers.
What is the main cause?
options: Tray flexure and lack of adhesive
questions.answerText: Tray flexure and lack of adhesive.
questions.why: A flexible tray distorts during removal and springs back afterwards; elastomers also need the matching adhesive.

questions.stem:
A one-stage (simultaneous) putty–wash impression shows putty at the preparation margin.
What is the recognised risk of this technique?
options: The putty displaces the wash from the margins
questions.why: In a simultaneous technique the stiff putty can push the wash away from the margins.

questions.stem:
A two-stage putty–wash impression gives a tight crown.
What is the recognised risk of this technique?
options: Distortion if the set putty is reseated without adequate relief
questions.answerText: Distortion when the set putty is reseated without relief.
questions.why: Reseating set putty over the wash compresses it; it rebounds after removal, giving undersized dies and tight crowns.

questions.stem:
A nurse asks how to disinfect an alginate impression before sending it to the laboratory.
What is correct?
options: Rinse it, then use a material-specific disinfectant for the time on the label, avoiding prolonged immersion
questions.why: Follow the label time; prolonged immersion distorts alginate and polyether.

questions.stem:
A technician adds extra water to stone so it pours easily.
What is the effect on the cast?
options: Weaker, with less expansion and a slower set
questions.why: Extra water leaves more porosity in the set gypsum.

questions.stem:
A technician spatulates stone for twice the recommended time.
What is the effect?
options: A faster set and more expansion
questions.why: Spatulation breaks up crystals and creates more nuclei for crystallisation.

questions.stem:
A cast poured from an impression with blood on it has a soft, chalky surface.
Why?
options: Blood and saliva retard the setting of gypsum, so impressions should be rinsed
Blood reacts with the tray adhesive
questions.answerText: Blood and saliva retard the set.
questions.why: They leave a soft, chalky cast surface; rinse impressions before disinfecting and pouring.

questions.stem:
A technician wants a quicker-setting stone for a chairside cast.
Which additive accelerates gypsum setting?
questions.why: Potassium sulphate, gypsum seed and low-concentration sodium chloride accelerate; borax, citrates and acetates retard.

questions.stem:
A setting stone cast is left under water in a soaking bath and comes out oversized.
What explains this?
questions.why: Gypsum immersed in water while setting expands more than when it sets in air.

questions.stem:
A crown on a 3 mm high, over-tapered molar preparation has come off twice, despite resin cement.
What is most appropriate?
options: Improve resistance form (grooves or boxes, or crown lengthening) before a new crown
questions.why: A short, over-tapered preparation cannot be rescued by cement. Add grooves or boxes, or gain height by crown lengthening.

questions.stem:
Dies for a metal–ceramic bridge are being poured.
Which gypsum is appropriate?
questions.why: Dies need high strength and abrasion resistance; plaster and Type III stone are too weak.

questions.stem:
Base-metal castings consistently fit tightly on Type IV dies.
Which gypsum could compensate?
options: Type V high-strength, high-expansion die stone
questions.why: Its greater setting expansion compensates for the higher casting shrinkage of base-metal alloys.

questions.stem:
A technician uses gypsum-bonded investment for a cobalt–chromium framework. The casting is rough and brittle.
Why is gypsum-bonded investment unsuitable?
options: Calcium sulphate breaks down above about 700°C, releasing sulphur dioxide
questions.answerText: Calcium sulphate breaks down above about 700°C.
questions.why: It releases sulphur dioxide and contaminates the casting, so gypsum-bonded investment is for gold alloys only.

questions.stem:
A metal–ceramic crown framework is to be cast in a high-fusing alloy.
Which investment is appropriate?
questions.why: It withstands the higher temperatures of metal–ceramic and base-metal alloys.

questions.stem:
A gold crown casting shrinks about 1.4% as it cools.
How is this shrinkage compensated?
options: By setting, hygroscopic and thermal expansion of the investment
By casting at a lower temperature
questions.answerText: Setting, hygroscopic and thermal expansion of the investment.
questions.why: The mould is expanded to match the alloy's casting shrinkage (gold about 1.4%; Co-Cr more).

questions.stem:
A wax pattern is finished at 5 p.m. and the technician plans to invest it the next morning.
What is the best advice?
options: Invest promptly, because wax has high thermal expansion and releases stresses on standing
Store it in the fridge overnight
Re-wax the margins in the morning
questions.why: Wax relaxes and distorts as stored stresses release; delays reduce casting accuracy.

questions.stem:
A student asks how heat-cured PMMA polymerisation starts.
What is the initiator?
questions.why: Benzoyl peroxide in the powder decomposes on heating to free radicals. In self-cure acrylic a tertiary amine activates it.
questions.others: Camphorquinone is the light-cure initiator; hydroquinone is the inhibitor.

questions.stem:
Liquid monomer in an old bottle has stayed liquid for two years.
Which component prevents premature polymerisation?
questions.why: It is the inhibitor in the monomer, giving shelf life.

questions.stem:
Acrylic denture teeth from one manufacturer resist crazing around the necks better than another brand.
Which component improves craze resistance?
questions.why: Ethylene glycol dimethacrylate cross-links the polymer and improves resistance to crazing.

questions.stem:
A technician mixes heat-cure acrylic and waits for it to pass through its stages.
At which stage should it be packed into the flask?
questions.why: The stages are sandy, stringy, dough, rubbery, stiff. Pack at dough, when the mix is no longer sticky and flows under pressure.

questions.stem:
A processed complete denture has bubbles confined to the thick palatal and tuberosity areas.
What is the most likely cause?
options: Too little dough in the flask
Heating too fast, so monomer boiled (gaseous porosity)
Dough left uncovered on the bench
questions.why: Monomer boils at about 100.3°C. If heated too fast, the exothermic thick sections overheat and form bubbles.

questions.stem:
A processed denture shows irregular voids throughout, including at the surface.
What is the most likely cause?
options: Too little dough or packing pressure (contraction porosity)
questions.why: Insufficient dough or pressure leaves voids throughout and at the surface.
questions.others: Monomer evaporation from uncovered dough gives granular porosity.

questions.stem:
A patient develops mucosal irritation under a chairside self-cure reline but not under her heat-cured denture.
What explains the difference?
options: Self-cure acrylic has much higher residual monomer (about 2–5% against 0.2–0.5%)
questions.why: Self-cure acrylic leaves about 2–5% residual monomer against 0.2–0.5% for heat-cure; monomer is an irritant and allergen.

questions.stem:
A patient sterilises her acrylic dentures by soaking them in boiling water. They no longer fit.
Why?
options: Stress relief and warpage occur well below the glass transition temperature (about 105°C)
questions.answerText: Warpage below the glass transition temperature.
questions.why: Stresses relieve and the base warps well below about 105°C. Advise against hot or boiling water.

questions.stem:
An upper denture has fractured twice at a deep labial frenal notch. The patient has a full lower natural dentition.
What is the most effective remedy?
options: A metal palate or fibre reinforcement, and reducing stress concentration at the notch
A thicker layer of self-cure acrylic
questions.answerText: Metal palate or reinforcement, and reduce the notch stress.
questions.why: Fatigue fracture beside a stress-raising notch against natural teeth needs a stronger base (metal or high-impact acrylic) and a gentler notch.

questions.stem:
A practice switches to digitally milled, pre-polymerised PMMA denture bases.
What is the main material advantage?
options: Very low residual monomer and porosity, with no polymerisation shrinkage in the clinic
questions.answerText: Very low residual monomer and porosity.
questions.why: Industrially polymerised blocks are milled, so there is no processing shrinkage and the fit is better.

questions.stem:
A patient may have swallowed a fragment of a fractured acrylic partial denture, but it is not visible on the chest radiograph.
Why?
options: The fragment was too small to matter
questions.why: Standard acrylic does not show on radiographs, which matters when fragments may be swallowed or inhaled.

questions.stem:
A complete denture with porcelain posterior teeth opposes natural lower premolars and molars.
What is the main risk?
options: Abrasion of the opposing natural teeth
questions.why: Porcelain teeth resist wear but abrade enamel; they also click, are brittle and need more space. Acrylic teeth are preferred opposite natural teeth.

questions.stem:
A tissue conditioner is used on inflamed mucosa before new impressions.
What is it made from?
options: PEMA powder with an aromatic ester plasticiser in ethanol
questions.why: This gel stays viscoelastic for days to weeks, conditioning traumatised mucosa and allowing functional impressions.

questions.stem:
A tissue conditioner placed 4 weeks ago has become hard and rough.
Why?
options: Ethanol and plasticiser have leached out; it should be changed every few days to weeks
The base has reacted with it
It has polymerised further from heat
questions.why: The material hardens and roughens, harbouring Candida; replace it every few days to weeks.

questions.stem:
A silicone long-term soft liner has partly separated from the base and is colonised by Candida.
Which statement about silicone soft liners is correct?
options: They bond less well to the base and support Candida growth
They are best trimmed with hot burs
questions.why: Silicone liners stay resilient longer but bond poorly to PMMA, are hard to trim and polish, and support Candida.

questions.stem:
A patient with a Co-Cr RPD and an acrylic complete denture asks how to soak them overnight.
Which advice is correct?
options: Hypochlorite only for the all-acrylic denture; an alkaline peroxide cleaner for the Co-Cr
questions.answerText: Hypochlorite for acrylic only; alkaline peroxide for Co-Cr.
questions.why: Hypochlorite is antifungal but bleaches and corrodes metals.

questions.stem:
A technician asks why cobalt–chromium frameworks resist corrosion in saliva.
What provides corrosion resistance?
options: A passive chromium oxide film (chromium content about 25–30%)
questions.why: At least 12–13% chromium is needed for passivation; Co-Cr has about 25–30%.

questions.stem:
A Co-Cr clasp fractured on first insertion. The laboratory reports a high carbon content in the alloy.
What does excess carbon do?
options: Forms excess carbides, making the alloy brittle
questions.why: Carbon forms carbides that harden the alloy, but too much makes it brittle.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old woman with a nickel allergy needs a resin-bonded bridge.
Which statement about nickel–chromium alloys is correct?
options: Nickel allergy is rare in women
Ni-Cr is safe for anyone with a nickel allergy
Beryllium in some Ni-Cr alloys is harmless
Nickel allergy is more common in women; avoid Ni-Cr and consider Co-Cr
questions.answerText: Nickel allergy is commoner in women; avoid Ni-Cr.
questions.why: Co-Cr is the usual alternative for a base-metal framework. Some Ni-Cr alloys also contain toxic beryllium.

questions.stem:
A clinician compares implant abutment metals.
What is the elastic modulus of titanium, and how is it protected from corrosion?
options: About 110 GPa; a titanium dioxide film
questions.why: Titanium is about half as stiff as Co-Cr and forms a passive TiO2 layer.

questions.stem:
A clasp on a lower premolar needs to engage a 0.5–0.75 mm undercut and be adjustable.
Which material is most suitable?
options: Wrought wire with a cold-worked, fibrous grain structure
questions.why: The cold-worked, fibrous grain gives flexibility and adjustability, suiting 0.5–0.75 mm undercuts.

questions.stem:
A cast gold clasp is planned for a premolar abutment.
Which undercut should it engage?
questions.why: Cast gold engages 0.5 mm; Co-Cr 0.25 mm; wrought wire 0.5–0.75 mm.

questions.stem:
A patient feels a sharp twinge when foil touches a new gold crown that contacts an amalgam in the opposing tooth.
What explains this?
options: Galvanic current between dissimilar metals in saliva
questions.why: Dissimilar metals in saliva form a cell; contact creates a current felt as a shock.

questions.stem:
A technician explains how porcelain bonds to a metal coping.
Which bond mechanism is most important?
options: Chemical bonding through the metal oxide layer
questions.answerText: Chemical bonding via the oxide layer.
questions.why: Tin and indium oxides on noble alloys, or chromium oxide on base metals, bond chemically to porcelain. Mechanical, compressive and van der Waals forces contribute less.

questions.stem:
Porcelain repeatedly delaminates from a base-metal coping fired with a thick, dark oxide layer.
What explains the failure?
options: An oxide layer that is too thick weakens the bond
questions.why: Base metals form a thick oxide that fails cohesively, weakening the bond.

questions.stem:
The incisal edge of a metal–ceramic upper central crown has chipped. The porcelain at the incisal edge was 3 mm thick with no metal support.
What is the design rule?
options: Porcelain should be at least 3 mm thick everywhere
Unsupported porcelain should not exceed about 2 mm
Metal should be at least 2 mm thick
Porcelain does not need metal support
Opaque porcelain should be 1 mm thick
questions.answerText: Unsupported porcelain should not exceed about 2 mm.
questions.why: Porcelain needs uniform metal support; excess unsupported bulk chips.

questions.stem:
A metal–ceramic crown on 11 looks opaque and bulky.
What labial reduction is usually needed for a metal–ceramic crown?
questions.why: Space is needed for metal (0.3–0.5 mm), opaque (about 0.2 mm) and body porcelain; less reduction gives an opaque, bulky crown.

questions.stem:
A lithium disilicate onlay is to be bonded to a premolar.
What is the correct surface treatment of the restoration?
options: Hydrofluoric acid (about 5–10%), silane, then resin cement
Air abrasion and MDP primer only
questions.why: HF etches the glass phase of the silica-based ceramic and silane couples it to resin.

questions.stem:
A monolithic zirconia crown with limited retention is to be cemented.
What surface treatment is recommended?
options: No treatment and zinc oxide eugenol
Low-pressure air abrasion (about 50 µm alumina) with an MDP-containing primer or cement
questions.why: Zirconia has no glass phase to etch; MDP bonds chemically to its oxide. Conventional GIC or RMGIC is acceptable when the preparation is retentive.

questions.stem:
A clinician applies silane alone to the fitting surface of a zirconia crown before resin cementation. It debonds.
Why did silane fail?
options: Silane needs a silica-based surface; zirconia contains no glass phase
Resin cement cannot bond to tooth
questions.why: Zirconia is polycrystalline with no silica. Use MDP, or tribochemical silica coating before silane.

questions.stem:
A student asks why zirconia resists crack propagation.
What is transformation toughening?
options: Cubic to tetragonal change on heating
Stress at a crack tip converts tetragonal to monoclinic zirconia, with about 3–5% volume expansion that closes the crack
questions.answerText: Tetragonal to monoclinic with volume expansion.
questions.why: The 3–5% expansion at a crack tip compresses and arrests the crack.

questions.stem:
A zirconia hip implant failed in the 1990s after roughening in body fluids.
What is this phenomenon?
options: Low-temperature degradation (ageing): spontaneous tetragonal to monoclinic change in moisture
questions.why: In moisture, zirconia can transform spontaneously, roughening and weakening its surface.

questions.stem:
A laboratory mills a zirconia bridge noticeably larger than the final size.
Why?
options: It is milled pre-sintered and shrinks about 20–25% linearly on sintering
questions.why: Zirconia is milled pre-sintered (green or white state) and enlarged to compensate.

questions.stem:
A chairside lithium disilicate crown is blue after milling.
Why?
options: It is milled in the lithium metasilicate state and then crystallised
The block was the wrong shade
questions.answerText: Milled as lithium metasilicate, then crystallised.
questions.why: The blue, softer state is easy to mill; firing produces lithium disilicate with its final shade and strength.

questions.stem:
A patient's lower incisors are wearing rapidly against new upper ceramic crowns that were adjusted chairside and not repolished.
Which surface is most abrasive to opposing enamel?
questions.why: It is the most abrasive surface; polished monolithic zirconia is relatively kind. Always polish after adjustment.

questions.stem:
A patient feels sensitivity after a gold crown is cemented with zinc phosphate.
Which property of zinc phosphate explains this, and how is it mixed?
options: High pH; mixed quickly in bulk
Fluoride release; mixed on a warm slab
Moisture sensitivity; mixed on a pad
Low initial pH; mixed incrementally on a cool glass slab because the reaction is exothermic
questions.answerText: Low initial pH; incremental mixing on a cool slab.
questions.why: The acid can irritate the pulp; incremental mixing on a cool slab controls the exothermic reaction and prolongs working time.

questions.stem:
A leucite-reinforced glass-ceramic crown cracked a month after it was cemented with resin-modified glass ionomer.
What is the likely cause?
options: Hygroscopic expansion of the RMGIC fracturing a weak glass ceramic
questions.why: RMGIC absorbs water and expands, which can crack weak glass ceramics; use resin cement for them.

questions.stem:
A glass ionomer cement is chosen for a metal–ceramic crown on a patient with high caries risk.
What are its main properties?
options: High bond to zirconia via MDP
Fluoride release, CTE close to tooth, and sensitivity to moisture early on
The highest bond strength of any cement
questions.answerText: Fluoride, tooth-like CTE, early moisture sensitivity.
questions.why: GIC releases fluoride and expands like tooth, but must be protected from moisture while it sets.

questions.stem:
Porcelain veneers are to be fitted to four upper incisors.
Which cement is essential?
questions.why: Thin, weak feldspathic or leucite veneers need an adhesive resin bond; light-cure resin gives colour stability.

questions.stem:
Provisional crowns are cemented with a eugenol-containing temporary cement before definitive resin-bonded crowns.
What is the problem?
options: Eugenol inhibits polymerisation of the later resin cement
questions.why: Use eugenol-free temporary cement when definitive resin bonding is planned.

questions.stem:
A crown does not seat fully and the cement layer is thick.
What is the ISO maximum film thickness for luting cements?
questions.why: ISO sets 25 µm as the maximum film thickness for luting cements.

questions.stem:
You are bonding a resin-bonded bridge to enamel.
What is the standard enamel etch?
questions.why: This produces the type I–III etch patterns; enamel bonding is the most reliable bond in dentistry.

questions.stem:
After etching dentine with phosphoric acid, an assistant dries the cavity with prolonged air until it looks chalky.
What is the consequence?
options: Collagen collapse and a weaker bond
questions.answerText: Collagen collapse and a weaker bond.
questions.why: Etched dentine must stay moist so resin can infiltrate the collagen and form a hybrid layer.

questions.stem:
A composite is placed in a sclerotic cervical wear lesion in a 70-year-old.
How can bonding be improved?
options: Roughening the sclerotic dentine and selectively etching the enamel
questions.why: Sclerotic dentine bonds poorly; roughening removes the hypermineralised surface and enamel etching adds a reliable bond.

questions.stem:
A resin-bonded bridge is made with a cobalt–chromium wing.
What is the current standard for bonding the wing?
options: Air-abraded base metal bonded with an MDP-containing resin cement
questions.why: Modern RBB wings use air-abraded base metal bonded with MDP-containing cement (for example Panavia); Rochette, Maryland and Virginia are historical.

questions.stem:
A resin-bonded bridge is cast in a high-gold alloy.
What extra step is needed for a chemical bond?
options: Phosphoric acid etching of the metal
Hydrofluoric acid etching of the metal
Tin plating or a noble-metal primer
questions.answerText: Tin plating or a noble-metal primer.
questions.why: Noble alloys form little oxide, so they need an added layer to bond chemically.

questions.stem:
A root-filled premolar is to be crowned with a post-retained core.
Which factor is most important for the long-term survival of the tooth?
options: A ferrule of 1.5–2 mm of sound dentine all round
