questions.why: The ferrule, not the post, protects the root. A post only retains the core; it does not reinforce the tooth.

questions.stem:
A clinician plans a full-arch zirconia bridge from an intraoral scan of an edentulous maxilla.
Which statement about intraoral scanner accuracy is correct?
options: It is greatest over full arches
It is greatest over short spans and lower over full arches and mobile, featureless edentulous mucosa
It equals conventional impressions in every situation
It is best for edentulous ridges
questions.why: Errors accumulate as images are stitched across long spans, and mobile, featureless mucosa scans poorly.

questions.stem:
A healthy 60 kg adult needs extensive crown preparations under local anaesthetic. You use the dental-text maximum of 4.4 mg/kg for lidocaine with adrenaline.
About how many 2.2 mL cartridges of 2% lidocaine with 1:80,000 adrenaline is that?
questions.why: 4.4 mg/kg × 60 kg = 264 mg. One 2.2 mL cartridge of 2% lidocaine holds 44 mg, so 264 ÷ 44 = 6.

questions.stem:
Buccal infiltration in the lower first molar region gives good anaesthesia with one agent but not another.
Why is articaine effective for mandibular buccal infiltration?
options: It has a very long half-life
It diffuses well through bone, and its ester side chain allows rapid plasma metabolism
questions.why: Articaine is an amide with an ester side chain. It diffuses well through bone, so buccal infiltration can reach mandibular molars, and plasma esterases give it a short half-life.

questions.stem:
A patient who is 36 weeks pregnant needs an urgent extraction for a painful tooth.
Which local anaesthetic is best avoided?
questions.why: Felypressin has oxytocic action, so avoid it in late pregnancy. Large doses of prilocaine also cause methaemoglobinaemia.

questions.stem:
Minutes after several cartridges, a patient reports tingling around the lips and ringing in the ears, then becomes drowsy.
What is happening?
options: Early local anaesthetic toxicity, which affects the CNS first
questions.why: Toxicity affects the CNS first (perioral tingling, tinnitus, drowsiness, convulsions), then depresses the cardiovascular system. Stop, call for help and support the airway.

questions.stem:
A patient taking propranolol receives several cartridges of lidocaine with adrenaline.
What interaction may follow?
questions.why: Non-selective beta-blockers leave adrenaline's alpha effects unopposed. Limit the dose.

questions.stem:
An inferior alveolar block repeatedly fails on a lower molar with an acute periapical abscess.
What is the main pharmacological reason?
options: Low tissue pH reduces the non-ionised fraction of the anaesthetic
Accessory supply from the facial nerve
The patient is resistant to amides
questions.why: Inflamed, acidic tissue reduces the non-ionised (lipid-soluble) fraction that crosses the nerve membrane.
questions.others: Accessory supply comes from the mylohyoid nerve or cervical plexus, not the facial nerve.

questions.stem:
A patient with trismus of 15 mm needs anaesthesia for a lower molar.
Which technique is designed for limited opening?
questions.why: It is given with the teeth together, suiting trismus. Gow-Gates is another alternative to the standard block.

questions.stem:
An inhalation sedation machine is being checked before use.
What is the minimum oxygen concentration it must deliver?
questions.why: Machines must deliver at least 30% oxygen (maximum 70% nitrous oxide), with fail-safe and scavenging.

questions.stem:
An anxious patient asks for inhalation sedation for impressions.
Which of these is a relative contraindication?
questions.why: It is a relative contraindication, with nasal obstruction, severe COPD, recent middle-ear or eye surgery with gas, and B12 deficiency.

questions.stem:
During IV sedation with midazolam, a patient's respiratory rate falls and they become unresponsive.
Which drug reverses midazolam?
questions.why: It is the benzodiazepine antagonist. Naloxone reverses opioids.

questions.stem:
A patient is to have IV midazolam sedation for a lengthy procedure.
What post-operative instruction is correct?
options: They may drive home after an hour
They may return to work that afternoon
They may drink alcohol that evening
A responsible adult escort, and no driving or operating machinery until the next day
questions.answerText: Escort; no driving or machinery until the next day.
questions.why: IACSD standards require an escort after IV sedation, because of residual sedation and amnesia.

questions.stem:
A patient with poorly controlled heart failure (ASA III) asks for IV sedation in your practice.
Which patients are generally suitable for sedation in primary care?
questions.why: ASA III and above are generally treated in secondary care.

questions.stem:
A patient has a dental abscess with facial swelling, a temperature of 38.5°C and malaise. You have drained it.
Which antibiotic regimen does SDCEP recommend?
options: Clindamycin 150 mg four times daily for 14 days
Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days (or amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily)
questions.answerText: Phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days.
questions.why: For spreading infection with systemic signs, SDCEP recommends this, or amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily, after drainage.

questions.stem:
The patient in the previous scenario is allergic to penicillin.
What is an appropriate alternative?
options: Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily (or metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for anaerobes)
questions.why: These are the SDCEP alternatives for penicillin allergy.
questions.others: Co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin are penicillins.

questions.stem:
A smoker has painful, bleeding, punched-out interdental papillae and halitosis.
What antimicrobial, if indicated, is recommended?
options: Metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 3 days
questions.answerText: Metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 3 days.
questions.why: It is the SDCEP regimen for necrotising periodontal disease, alongside debridement and oral hygiene.

questions.stem:
A patient has a localised abscess on a lower premolar. There is no spreading swelling and no systemic upset.
What is the first-line management?
options: Drainage and removal of the cause; antibiotics are not needed
Analgesics only and review in a month
questions.answerText: Drainage and removal of the cause.
questions.why: Antibiotics are not a substitute for drainage and are not indicated without spreading infection or systemic involvement.

questions.stem:
A patient taking simvastatin and warfarin has denture stomatitis that has not settled with hygiene and night removal.
Which antifungal must be avoided?
options: Hypochlorite soaks for the acrylic denture
questions.why: Azoles potentiate warfarin (raising the INR) and raise statin levels (myopathy). Use nystatin and denture measures.

questions.stem:
A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve needs crown preparation with retraction cord.
What is the current guidance on antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: Not routinely recommended; for patients at special risk, consider it in consultation with the cardiologist
questions.answerText: Not routine; consider with the cardiologist for special risk.
questions.why: NICE CG64 does not recommend routine prophylaxis. SDCEP advises considering it for special-risk patients (previous endocarditis, prosthetic valves, some congenital heart disease) with the cardiologist.

questions.stem:
A patient uses 0.2% chlorhexidine mouthwash straight after brushing and finds it ineffective.
Why?
options: Sodium lauryl sulphate in toothpaste inactivates it; wait about 30 minutes
questions.why: Wait about 30 minutes after brushing. Chlorhexidine also stains and alters taste.

questions.stem:
You plan analgesia after a difficult extraction for several patients.
Which patient should not be given ibuprofen?
options: A patient with a penicillin allergy
questions.why: NSAIDs can trigger bronchospasm. Also avoid or take care with peptic ulcer, renal impairment, anticoagulants and third-trimester pregnancy.

questions.stem:
A 48 kg, 82-year-old woman with mild hepatic impairment needs paracetamol.
What is correct?
options: The usual maximum is 4 g in 24 hours, reduced for low body weight and hepatic impairment
questions.answerText: Maximum 4 g in 24 hours, reduced in low weight or hepatic impairment.
questions.why: The dose is reduced in low body weight, hepatic impairment and alcohol dependence.

questions.stem:
A healthy adult has moderate pain after crown preparation.
Which analgesic approach is most effective?
questions.why: The combination is more effective than either drug alone for dental pain.

questions.stem:
A patient on warfarin needs an extraction before a partial denture. Her INR this morning is 3.2.
What is appropriate?
options: Proceed in primary care with local haemostatic measures
Defer until the INR is below 2
questions.why: SDCEP: check the INR ideally within 24 hours; if it is below 4, treat in primary care with haemostatic measures.

questions.stem:
A patient on warfarin has an INR of 4.6 on the day of a planned extraction.
What should you do?
options: Halve the next warfarin dose and proceed
Defer treatment and seek advice from the anticoagulation service
questions.why: An INR of 4 or above is outside the threshold for primary care treatment.

questions.stem:
A patient taking apixaban twice daily needs several extractions (a higher bleeding-risk procedure).
What does SDCEP advise?
questions.why: For twice-daily apixaban or dabigatran and a higher-risk procedure, SDCEP advises missing the morning dose; low-risk procedures need no interruption.

questions.stem:
A patient taking rivaroxaban once each morning needs a higher-risk extraction.
What does SDCEP advise?
options: Delay the morning dose until about 4 hours after haemostasis
questions.answerText: Delay the morning dose until 4 hours after haemostasis.
questions.why: That is the SDCEP advice for once-daily rivaroxaban or edoxaban and a higher-risk procedure.

questions.stem:
A patient on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel) after a coronary stent needs a tooth extracted before a denture.
What is correct?
options: Do not stop either; use local haemostatic measures
questions.why: Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy after a stent risks thrombosis. Use local measures.

questions.stem:
A patient with moderate haemophilia A needs a lower molar extracted.
What is the safe approach?
options: Liaise with the haemophilia centre; avoid an inferior alveolar block without factor cover
Proceed with an inferior alveolar block and sutures
Prescribe tranexamic acid and proceed with no liaison
questions.why: An inferior alveolar block without factor cover risks a pterygomandibular haematoma and airway compromise.

questions.stem:
A patient on apixaban needs crown preparation with retraction cord and impressions.
How should the apixaban be managed?
options: No interruption; these are low bleeding-risk procedures
questions.why: Crown preparation with cord, impressions and denture work are low bleeding-risk procedures.

questions.stem:
A patient has exposed bone in the lower lingual region after a sore spot from a denture. She has taken alendronic acid for 7 years and has never had radiotherapy.
When does this meet the definition of MRONJ?
options: When the bone has been exposed for more than 8 weeks
questions.why: MRONJ is exposed (or probeable) bone for over 8 weeks, with antiresorptive or antiangiogenic history and no jaw radiotherapy or metastasis.

questions.stem:
A patient stopped denosumab 18 months ago; another stopped IV zoledronic acid 18 months ago.
Which statement is correct?
options: Denosumab's effect wears off within months; bisphosphonates persist in bone for years
Bisphosphonate effects wear off in weeks
Neither drug is associated with MRONJ
questions.answerText: Denosumab wears off in months; bisphosphonates persist for years.
questions.why: Denosumab is a RANKL antibody; bisphosphonates bind to bone and persist.

questions.stem:
You are assessing MRONJ risk in several patients.
Who is at highest risk?
options: Osteoporosis patient on oral alendronate for 2 years
Osteoporosis patient with no drug treatment
Cancer patient on high-dose IV zoledronic acid
Patient who stopped alendronate 10 years ago after 1 year
questions.answerText: Cancer patient on high-dose IV zoledronic acid.
questions.why: High-dose IV bisphosphonate or denosumab for cancer carries the highest MRONJ risk.

questions.stem:
A cancer patient on IV zoledronic acid has a lower canine with a heavily broken-down crown but a sound root. A denture is planned.
What is the preferred management of the canine?
options: Extract it before making the denture
Retain the root (root treatment and decoronation as an overdenture abutment)
questions.why: In high-risk patients, root treatment and decoronation avoid an extraction and support the denture as an overdenture abutment.

questions.stem:
A patient on oral bisphosphonates for 6 years needs a simple extraction.
What does SDCEP advise about a drug holiday?
options: Drug holidays are not recommended for routine dental care
questions.answerText: No drug holidays for routine care.
questions.why: SDCEP does not recommend interrupting antiresorptives for routine dentistry.

questions.stem:
An oncologist plans IV zoledronic acid for a patient with bone metastases. The patient has an ill-fitting partial denture and a broken-down tooth.
What should happen first?
options: Start the drug and see the dentist later
A dental assessment, getting the mouth healthy before treatment starts if possible
questions.why: Getting the mouth healthy before antiresorptive therapy, including well-fitting dentures, reduces MRONJ risk.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old will start radiotherapy for an oropharyngeal cancer, with both parotids in the field. A lower molar has a poor prognosis.
When should it ideally be extracted?
options: At least 10–14 days before radiotherapy, to allow healing
questions.why: Teeth of poor prognosis in the field should be removed early enough to heal before irradiation, reducing later osteoradionecrosis risk.

questions.stem:
A dentate patient finished head and neck radiotherapy 6 months ago and now has rampant cervical caries, a dry mouth and limited opening.
Which measures are appropriate?
options: 5000 ppm toothpaste, fluoride gel in custom trays, saliva substitutes and trismus exercises
questions.answerText: 5000 ppm, fluoride trays, saliva substitutes, trismus exercises.
questions.why: Radiation caries, xerostomia and trismus are managed preventively; avoid extractions in the field where possible.

questions.stem:
A patient who had mandibular radiotherapy 8 years ago asks whether the risk of osteoradionecrosis has gone.
Which statement is correct?
options: The risk is lifelong, dose-dependent and much higher in the mandible than the maxilla
The maxilla is at higher risk
The risk applies only during radiotherapy
questions.answerText: Lifelong, dose-dependent, mandible far more than maxilla.
questions.why: Osteoradionecrosis risk persists for life and rises with doses above about 50–60 Gy.

questions.stem:
A patient who had a maxillectomy and radiotherapy needs an obturator and asks about implants in the irradiated bone.
At which NHS complexity level is this care?
questions.why: Obturators and implants in irradiated bone are Level 3 (specialist) care under the NHS restorative standard.

questions.stem:
A patient's GP letter gives an HbA1c result.
At or above which value is diabetes diagnosed?
questions.why: An HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or above diagnoses diabetes.

questions.stem:
An undiagnosed 54-year-old with periodontitis and recurrent candidosis has an HbA1c of 45 mmol/mol.
What does this indicate?
questions.why: 42–47 mmol/mol is prediabetes. Refer to the GMP for confirmation and management, as the Level 2 curriculum expects.

questions.stem:
A patient with insulin-treated diabetes is booked for a long denture appointment.
Which arrangement is best?
options: A morning appointment after a normal meal and medication, with oral glucose available
Ask the patient to omit insulin
questions.answerText: Morning, after a normal meal, glucose available.
questions.why: This minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia during treatment.

questions.stem:
Minutes after an impression, a patient develops wheeze, facial swelling, urticaria and a falling blood pressure.
What is the first drug and dose?
options: Adrenaline 1:1000, 500 micrograms IM into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed
questions.why: Give it into the anterolateral thigh and repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. IV adrenaline is for specialists only.

questions.stem:
An 8-year-old develops anaphylaxis in the surgery.
What is the IM adrenaline dose?
questions.why: Children aged 6–12 receive 300 micrograms; under 6, 150 micrograms.

questions.stem:
A 65-year-old with known angina develops central chest tightness during a crown preparation.
What is the first drug to give?
questions.why: GTN is the first drug for angina; it can be repeated.

questions.stem:
The chest pain in the previous patient is unrelieved after GTN and lasts over 20 minutes. He is pale and sweaty.
What should you do?
options: Give more GTN and send him home
Call 999, give aspirin 300 mg chewed, and give oxygen if he is hypoxic
Lie him flat with legs raised and wait
questions.answerText: 999, aspirin 300 mg chewed, oxygen if hypoxic.
questions.why: Persistent pain unrelieved by GTN suggests myocardial infarction.

questions.stem:
A patient with asthma becomes wheezy and breathless during an appointment but can still speak.
What is the first treatment?
options: Salbutamol 100 micrograms per puff, 4–6 puffs via a spacer, repeated up to 10 puffs
questions.why: Give 4–6 puffs, repeating up to 10. Call 999 if it is life-threatening or not improving.

questions.stem:
A patient with diabetes becomes sweaty, confused and irritable but can still swallow.
What should you give?
questions.why: A conscious patient able to swallow is given 15–20 g of oral glucose.

questions.stem:
The same patient becomes unconscious and cannot swallow.
What should you give?
options: Oral glucose gel between the cheeks
questions.why: An unconscious patient cannot swallow safely; give glucagon IM and call for help.

questions.stem:
A patient with epilepsy has a tonic–clonic seizure in the chair that is still continuing after 5 minutes.
What should you give?
options: Nothing; wait for it to stop
questions.why: For a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, protect the patient from injury and give buccal midazolam.

questions.stem:
A young patient becomes pale, sweaty and dizzy, then briefly loses consciousness during an injection. The pulse is slow but present.
What is the immediate management?
options: Lie the patient flat, raise the legs and give oxygen
questions.why: Vasovagal syncope restores cerebral perfusion quickly when the patient is laid flat with the legs raised.

questions.stem:
A patient on long-term corticosteroids collapses with profound hypotension after a stressful procedure.
What is appropriate?
options: Call 999 and give hydrocortisone if prescribed and you are trained
questions.answerText: 999 and hydrocortisone if prescribed and trained.
questions.why: Adrenal crisis needs urgent steroid replacement and transfer.

questions.stem:
A patient collapses, is unresponsive and is not breathing normally.
What is correct adult CPR?
options: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, at 100–120 a minute and 5–6 cm deep, with an AED as soon as available
Wait for the ambulance before compressions
questions.why: These are the Resuscitation Council UK adult standards.

questions.stem:
A patient inhales part of a crown preparation's debris, coughs ineffectively and cannot speak. She is conscious.
What is the first action?
options: Up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts
questions.why: For ineffective coughing in a conscious adult: up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated.

questions.stem:
A patient becomes acutely unwell in the surgery.
How should oxygen be given?
questions.why: High-flow oxygen is given to the acutely ill patient.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old with poorly controlled epilepsy has lost 11 and 21 and takes phenytoin.
Which prosthodontic approach is most appropriate?
options: Prefer a fixed option, avoiding small removable prostheses that could be inhaled or fractured
A small acrylic partial denture worn at night
Porcelain teeth on an acrylic base
No replacement because of the epilepsy
questions.why: In uncontrolled epilepsy, small removable prostheses can be inhaled or fracture during a seizure. Metal-based or reinforced dentures are used if removable. Check for phenytoin-induced gingival overgrowth.

questions.stem:
A patient is 10 weeks pregnant and asks when to have elective bridge work.
When is the safest time for necessary dental treatment?
options: Second trimester; elective prosthodontics can usually wait until after delivery
questions.answerText: Second trimester; elective work can wait.
questions.why: Necessary care is safest in the second trimester; take radiographs only if justified.

questions.stem:
A patient on haemodialysis three times a week needs crown work.
Which arrangement is appropriate?
options: Treat on a non-dialysis day and avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic drugs
questions.why: Heparin is used during dialysis, and NSAIDs and nephrotoxic drugs harm residual renal function; bleeding and infection risk are raised.

questions.stem:
A patient with a confirmed latex allergy needs addition silicone impressions.
Which precaution is needed?
options: Latex gloves are fine with a barrier cream
Premedicate with an antihistamine and use latex
Use non-latex gloves and dam; latex also inhibits the setting of addition silicone
questions.why: Latex allergy requires a latex-free environment. Latex also inhibits addition silicone setting.

questions.stem:
A denture wearer has a confirmed methyl methacrylate allergy on patch testing.
Which base material may be considered?
options: Fully cured heat-cured PMMA, polyamide or polycarbonate
questions.answerText: Fully cured heat-cured PMMA, polyamide or polycarbonate.
questions.why: True allergy is to residual monomer; fully cured or methacrylate-free bases avoid it.
questions.others: Self-cure and chairside resins contain the most residual monomer.

questions.stem:
A patient with an implanted cardiac defibrillator needs gingival management before an impression.
Which instrument needs caution?
questions.why: Electrosurgery, and some ultrasonic devices, may interfere with pacemakers and ICDs.

questions.stem:
A colleague has told a patient to stop rivaroxaban for 3 days before impressions for a new denture.
What is the best response?
options: Continue the rivaroxaban; denture impressions are low bleeding risk and need no interruption
Agree, and stop it for a week instead
Refer to hospital for the impressions
questions.answerText: Continue; denture impressions are low risk.
questions.why: Do not tell patients to stop anticoagulants for low-risk procedures; follow procedure-specific guidance.

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old wants a 3-unit bridge. She has active, untreated periodontitis with bleeding and 6 mm pockets around the proposed abutments.
What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Prepare the bridge now and treat the periodontitis later
Use resin-bonded bridges to avoid preparation
Stabilise the periodontal disease first, then reassess before any definitive bridge
questions.why: Uncontrolled periodontal disease is not a suitable foundation for definitive bridgework; reassess after therapy.

questions.stem:
A patient on IV zoledronic acid is considering an RPD or implants.
What should the consent discussion include?
options: The medical risks (such as MRONJ) and the maintenance needs
questions.why: Shared decision-making covers benefit, alternatives (including no treatment), medical risks and maintenance, and is documented.

questions.stem:
An 85-year-old care-home resident with Parkinson's disease needs replacement complete dentures.
Which approach is most appropriate?
options: An entirely new design to improve appearance
Copy dentures with minimal changes, and labelling for identification
questions.why: Neuromuscular disease limits adaptation; copying keeps learned control. Labelling prevents loss in care homes.

questions.stem:
A patient on long-term oral prednisolone for arthritis needs a new partial denture.
Which consequence is most relevant to the prosthodontic care?
options: Steroid cover is needed for impressions
Increased risk of candidosis and delayed healing
questions.why: Adrenal suppression is rarely relevant for routine prosthodontics; infection and healing are.

questions.stem:
An edentulous patient with Sjögren's syndrome has poor retention despite well-made complete dentures.
Which option should be considered?
questions.why: Without saliva, physical retention fails; implants provide mechanical retention.

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old has erosion from gastro-oesophageal reflux that is not yet controlled. She wants her worn teeth crowned.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Manage the cause with her GMP first; delay definitive restorations until the condition is stable
questions.why: Ongoing acid would undermine new restorations; stabilise with the GMP, then restore.

questions.stem:
A patient with recently diagnosed, unstable angina asks for a complex bridge.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Stabilise oral disease, liaise with her physician, and defer elective definitive prosthodontics until her condition is stable
Proceed with all treatment in one long session
questions.why: With unstable disease, stabilise oral disease and defer elective definitive care until it is medically safe.

questions.stem:
An ASA III patient with severe COPD requests IV sedation for implant-supported overdenture work.
What is most appropriate?
options: Use inhalation sedation at 80% nitrous oxide
Treat without sedation regardless of anxiety
Refer to a secondary care setting
questions.why: ASA III patients, and severe COPD, are outside primary-care sedation standards.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old attends saying, "I want new teeth." She has an upper complete denture and a lower RPD.
What is the most important first step in the history?
options: Record her complaint in her own words and what she expects from treatment
questions.answerText: Her complaint in her own words, and her expectations.
questions.why: The history starts with the presenting complaint and expectations; they shape the whole plan and its prospects of success.

questions.stem:
You are assessing edentulous patients' attitudes using House's classification.
Which category carries the worst prognosis?
questions.why: House ranks attitudes philosophical (best), exacting, indifferent, hysterical (worst prognosis).

questions.stem:
A 32-year-old wants a bridge to replace 21. When she smiles broadly, more than 3 mm of gingiva shows.
Why is this finding important?
options: It is a sign of bruxism
A high smile line increases the aesthetic risk of the margins and pontic
questions.why: A high smile line shows more than 3 mm of gingiva, so margins, gingival contour and pontic emergence are all visible.

questions.stem:
A new patient has a BPE code 4 in one sextant and code 2 elsewhere.
What does the BSP recommend?
options: A full six-point periodontal chart of the whole dentition
A chart of that sextant only
A repeat BPE in a year
questions.answerText: Full six-point charting of the whole dentition.
questions.why: BSP guidance: code 4 or * in any sextant prompts full charting; code 3 prompts charting of that sextant after initial therapy.

questions.stem:
You examine an 80-year-old's existing complete dentures before planning replacements.
What should the assessment include?
options: None; the old dentures are irrelevant
questions.why: Existing dentures show what works and what failed: retention, stability, support, extension, OVD, occlusion, aesthetics, hygiene and wear.

questions.stem:
An upper arch is missing 16, 17, 26 and 27. The third molars are absent and will not be replaced.
What is the Kennedy classification?
questions.why: Bilateral free-end spaces behind the remaining teeth; unreplaced missing third molars are ignored.

questions.stem:
A lower arch is missing 46, 47 and 35. 48 is absent and will not be replaced.
What is the Kennedy classification?
questions.why: The right free end (46, 47) sets Class II; the 35 space is one modification.

questions.stem:
An upper arch is missing 14 and 15 only.
What is the Kennedy classification?
questions.why: A unilateral bounded space with teeth in front and behind.

questions.stem:
An upper arch is missing 12, 11, 21 and 22 only.
What is the Kennedy classification?
questions.why: A single bilateral anterior space crossing the midline.

questions.stem:
A lower arch is missing 36 and 37. 38 is present and will be used as an abutment.
What is the Kennedy classification?
questions.why: A third molar present and used as an abutment counts, so the space is bounded.

questions.stem:
A lower arch is missing 44, 45 and 46. 47 has a hopeless prognosis and will be extracted before the denture is made.
How should the arch be classified?
questions.why: Applegate: classify after planned extractions. Once 47 is removed the space becomes free-ended.

questions.stem:
A student classifies an arch as "Kennedy Class IV modification 1".
Why is this wrong?
options: Modifications apply only to Class I
Class IV has no modifications; any space behind it would make it a different class
questions.why: Any space behind the anterior space would itself be the most posterior and set a different class.

questions.stem:
An upper arch is missing 17 (not to be replaced), 24 and 25. All other teeth are present.
What is the Kennedy classification?
questions.why: A missing second molar that will not be replaced is ignored, leaving the bounded 24–25 space.

questions.stem:
A lower RPD will be supported by rests on the abutments and by the free-end saddle on the ridge.
What is its Craddock class?
questions.why: Support comes from teeth (rests) and mucosa (the free-end saddle). Class 1 is tooth-borne; Class 2 mucosa-borne.

questions.stem:
A mandibular ridge has adequate height but a narrow, sharp crest.
What is its Cawood and Howell class?
questions.why: Cawood and Howell IV: adequate height, inadequate width.

questions.stem:
An edentulous mandible has a flat ridge of inadequate height and width.
What is its Cawood and Howell class?
questions.why: A flat ridge, inadequate in height and width.

questions.stem:
An edentulous mandible is depressed, with loss of basal bone.
What is its Cawood and Howell class?
questions.why: A depressed ridge with basal bone loss.

questions.stem:
You are predicting retention for a new upper complete denture.
Which palatal vault form gives the best retention and resistance to lateral displacement?
questions.why: It gives the best retention and resistance to lateral displacement; V-shaped is unstable and flat resists lateral movement poorly.

questions.stem:
The soft palate of an edentulous patient drops steeply at about 70° from the hard palate.
What is its House class and implication?
options: Class III: a narrow post-dam area and poorer posterior seal
Class I: the widest post-dam area
Class III: the best posterior seal
It has no effect on the post-dam
questions.why: A steep soft palate gives a narrow post-dam area and a poorer posterior seal.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old's worst interproximal bone loss reaches the middle third of the root.
What is the BSP stage?
questions.why: Stage is set by the worst interproximal site: coronal third is Stage II, mid third Stage III, apical third Stage IV.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old has 40% interproximal bone loss at the worst site.
What is the BSP grade?
questions.why: Percentage bone loss ÷ age = 0.89, within 0.5–1.0.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old has 60% interproximal bone loss at the worst site.
What is the BSP grade?
questions.why: 60 ÷ 30 = 2.0, above 1.0, showing rapid progression.

questions.stem:
A patient's periodontitis affects 6 of 26 teeth.
Is the extent localised or generalised?
options: Generalised, because more than 5 teeth are affected
Localised, because fewer than 30% of teeth are affected
Generalised, because more than 25% are affected
questions.why: 6 of 26 teeth is 23%, under the 30% threshold, so the extent is localised; 30% or more of teeth is generalised.

questions.stem:
After treatment, a patient has bleeding on probing at 6% of sites, all pockets 4 mm or less, and no bleeding at 4 mm sites.
What is the periodontal status?
questions.why: BOP under 10%, PPD 4 mm or less and no BOP at 4 mm sites.

questions.stem:
A treated patient has bleeding on probing at 15% of sites, all pockets 4 mm or less, and no bleeding at 4 mm sites.
What is the periodontal status?
questions.why: BOP 10% or more, but PPD 4 mm or less with no BOP at 4 mm sites.

questions.stem:
A treated patient still has several 5 mm pockets that bleed.
What is the periodontal status?
questions.why: Any PPD of 5 mm or more, or a 4 mm site with bleeding, is unstable.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old has lost 6 teeth to periodontitis, has fewer than 20 teeth, and has drifting with masticatory dysfunction.
Which stage is this likely to be?
options: Stage IV, which usually needs complex rehabilitation
questions.why: Stage IV involves tooth loss from periodontitis and a need for complex rehabilitation (fewer than 20 teeth, masticatory dysfunction, drifting).

questions.stem:
After steps 1 and 2 of periodontal therapy in primary care, a patient has Stage III Grade A periodontitis.
At what NHS complexity level does further care sit?
questions.why: NHS standard: after steps 1–2 in primary care, Stage III Grade A is Level 2.

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old has Stage III Grade C periodontitis.
At what NHS complexity level does care sit?
questions.why: Stage III Grade B or C, and all Stage IV, are Level 3.

questions.stem:
During a BPE, the black band of the probe is partly visible in a sextant.
What code is this?
questions.why: The band partly visible means a 3.5–5.5 mm pocket; code 4 is the band disappearing (over 5.5 mm).

questions.stem:
A lower incisor moves more than 1 mm horizontally and can be depressed.
What is its Miller mobility grade?
questions.why: Over 1 mm horizontal and/or vertical (depressible) mobility.

questions.stem:
A lower first molar has a furcation lesion that a probe passes right through from buccal to lingual.
What is the Hamp furcation grade?
questions.why: Hamp III is through-and-through; I is under 3 mm horizontal loss; II is over 3 mm but not through.

questions.stem:
On BEWE screening, the worst surface in a sextant shows a distinct defect with less than 50% of the surface lost.
What is the score?
questions.why: 0 none, 1 initial loss of texture, 2 distinct defect under 50%, 3 loss of 50% or more.

questions.stem:
A patient's BEWE scores across the six sextants sum to 15.
What does this indicate?
options: High risk: oral hygiene and dietary assessment, find the cause, monitor, and consider restoration
questions.why: A cumulative BEWE of 14 or more is high risk: identify the cause, prevent, monitor and consider restoration.

questions.stem:
A patient's upper central incisors are retroclined with a deep overbite, and the lower incisal edges lie behind the cingulum plateau.
What is the incisor relationship?
questions.why: Retroclined upper centrals with lower edges behind the cingulum plateau.

questions.stem:
A patient's lower incisal edges lie anterior to the cingulum plateau of the upper incisors.
What is the incisor relationship?
questions.why: Lower incisal edges lie anterior to the upper cingulum plateau (BSI classification).

questions.stem:
A lateral cephalogram shows an ANB angle of 3°.
What is the skeletal pattern?
questions.why: A normal ANB angle is about 2–4°.

questions.stem:
You assess a lower premolar as a bridge abutment.
What are the ideal and minimum acceptable crown–root ratios?
questions.why: A crown longer than its root in bone gives an unfavourable lever for an abutment.

questions.stem:
You need to assess bone level, root form and periapical status of a proposed bridge abutment.
Which radiograph is most appropriate?
options: Periapical radiograph using the paralleling technique
questions.why: It shows bone level, crown–root ratio, root form, periapical status and root-filling quality with least distortion.

questions.stem:
A patient with moderate periodontitis needs bone levels recorded in the posterior segments.
Which radiograph is best?
questions.why: Vertical bitewings show crestal bone in periodontitis; horizontal bitewings are for caries.

questions.stem:
A panoramic radiograph shows a hazy radiopacity over the right ramus. The patient has an earring in the left ear.
Which statement explains the artefact?
options: It is a calcified lymph node
It appears on the same side, smaller and lower
It is a ghost image, projected on the opposite side, higher and larger
questions.answerText: Ghost image: opposite side, higher, larger.
questions.why: Objects between the source and the rotation centre project as blurred ghosts on the opposite side, higher and magnified.

questions.stem:
A colleague asks for CBCT on every new denture patient "as a baseline".
What is the correct principle?
options: CBCT is suitable for routine screening
CBCT is justified only for a three-dimensional question that lower-dose imaging cannot answer
CBCT has a lower dose than a bitewing
questions.answerText: CBCT only for a justified three-dimensional question.
questions.why: CBCT has the highest dental dose; it is never routine screening.

questions.stem:
Under IR(ME)R 2017, a dental nurse takes a radiograph requested by the dentist.
Who justifies the exposure?
questions.why: Under IR(ME)R the practitioner justifies, the operator exposes, the referrer requests and the employer sets procedures.

questions.stem:
An audit finds radiographs in the notes with no written findings.
What does IR(ME)R require of every exposure?
options: Justification, optimisation (ALARP) and a recorded clinical evaluation
questions.answerText: Justification, optimisation and a recorded evaluation.
questions.why: Every exposure must be justified, kept as low as reasonably practicable and clinically evaluated with a written report.

questions.stem:
A patient worried about radiation asks which dental radiograph gives the highest dose.
What is the order from lowest to highest effective dose?
questions.why: Roughly 0.001–0.008, 0.003–0.024 and 0.02–1 mSv respectively.

questions.stem:
You need a reliable sensibility test on a lower premolar abutment.
Which thermal test is more reliable?
options: Cold, using tetrafluoroethane or ethyl chloride on a pledget
questions.why: Tetrafluoroethane or ethyl chloride cold tests are more reliable than heat.

questions.stem:
An upper central incisor showed no response to the electric pulp test 2 weeks after a sporting injury. There is no discolouration or tenderness.
What is the correct interpretation?
options: The pulp is necrotic; start root canal treatment now
The EPT measures nerve response, not blood flow; recently traumatised teeth may not respond, so monitor
The EPT is always accurate after trauma
questions.why: After trauma, nerve conduction may be lost temporarily while the blood supply survives; a single negative result does not justify root canal treatment.

questions.stem:
A researcher wants to measure true pulpal vitality (blood flow) in traumatised teeth.
Which test assesses blood flow?
options: Laser Doppler flowmetry or pulse oximetry
questions.why: These assess pulpal blood flow, true vitality; thermal and electric tests assess sensibility only.

questions.stem:
A patient has sharp pain on biting with a lower molar that has a large amalgam; the pain stops on release.
Which test helps confirm a cracked cusp?
options: A bite test on individual cusps (for example a Tooth Slooth)
questions.why: Pain on release when loading a single cusp localises a crack; transillumination also helps.

questions.stem:
You are planning a lower Co-Cr RPD and a crown on an abutment.
What is the main value of mounted study casts on a semi-adjustable articulator with a facebow and RCP record?
options: To assess interocclusal space, plan a wax-up and survey the RPD design
questions.why: Mounted casts in RCP show space, guidance and interferences, and let you survey the RPD path and design.

questions.stem:
A patient wants composite build-ups for worn incisors but is unsure about the look.
What is the best way to test aesthetics and the proposed OVD before treatment?
options: A diagnostic wax-up and intraoral mock-up
questions.why: They test aesthetics and OVD reversibly and help communication with patient and laboratory.

questions.stem:
A denture wearer with angular cheilitis and glossitis has a full blood count showing a low MCV.
What deficiency is most likely?
questions.why: A low MCV (microcytosis) suggests iron deficiency; confirm with ferritin.

questions.stem:
A patient with a sore tongue and recurrent ulcers has a high MCV.
What does this suggest?
questions.why: A high MCV (macrocytosis) suggests B12 or folate deficiency.

questions.stem:
A heavily restored lower premolar is being assessed as a key abutment.
Which features support restorability?
options: A possible ferrule of 1.5–2 mm without harmful crown lengthening
An acceptable crown–root ratio and strategic value
questions.why: The restorability checklist covers a feasible ferrule, no vertical root fracture, an acceptable crown–root ratio and strategic value.

questions.stem:
A patient asks for root canal treatment of a lower molar under the NHS before a crown.
What does the NHS standard require for the tooth to enter endodontic care?
options: The tooth must already be crowned
Sound coronal tissue above the crest (about 2 mm high and 1 mm wide, or over 30% of the original crown)
A periapical lesion must be present
questions.answerText: Sound coronal tissue above the crest.
questions.why: The NHS entry criteria require about 2 mm high and 1 mm wide sound tissue, or over 30% of the original crown.

questions.stem:
A post-crowned upper premolar has a deep, narrow, isolated periodontal pocket and a J-shaped radiolucency.
What is the most likely diagnosis and prognosis?
questions.why: An isolated deep, narrow pocket and a J-shaped lesion on a post-crowned tooth suggest a vertical fracture, which is unrestorable.

questions.stem:
A colleague orders a full radiographic survey for a patient attending only for denture adjustment, with no clinical indication.
Which principle does this break?
options: Radiographs must be taken every visit
Investigations should be chosen only when their results may change the diagnosis, prognosis or plan
Imaging is optional if the patient pays
questions.answerText: Investigate only if it may change the plan.
questions.why: Choose investigations whose results could alter diagnosis, prognosis or treatment.

questions.stem:
A denture wearer has a persistent, indurated ulcer under the lower flange. A panoramic radiograph looks normal.
What should you do?
options: Reassure, because the radiograph is normal
Refer urgently; a normal radiograph does not overrule a suspicious clinical finding
Adjust the flange and review in 3 months
questions.why: A normal radiograph does not overrule a suspicious clinical lesion; an indurated persistent ulcer needs the suspected cancer pathway.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old presents in pain from a periapical abscess. She also has active caries, untreated periodontitis and missing teeth she wants replaced.
What is the correct sequence of care?
options: Urgent care, stabilisation, re-evaluation, definitive treatment, supportive maintenance
questions.why: This five-phase sequence ensures definitive work rests on controlled disease.

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old has lost 25 and asks what can be done.
Which options should be discussed?
options: Leaving the space, a resin-bonded bridge, a conventional bridge, an RPD or an implant, with their pros and cons
questions.answerText: All options, including leaving the space.
questions.why: Compare preparation, reversibility, aesthetics, cost, longevity, cleaning and failure for each, including no treatment.

questions.stem:
A patient needs a single crown on 36. She has a stable, comfortable intercuspal position with no symptoms.
Which occlusal approach is appropriate?
options: A conformative approach, matching the existing ICP
questions.why: A stable, comfortable ICP is kept when space and function allow.
questions.revise: Unit 5 treatment strategies note 03, Unit 9 · LO 2c.19

questions.stem:
A patient with generalised severe wear needs an increase in OVD and restoration of most teeth.
What is the appropriate level of care?
options: Complex reorganisation with careful diagnostic testing, usually with specialist involvement (Level 3)
Single-visit composite in general practice without planning
questions.why: OVD change and full-mouth rehabilitation need diagnostic testing and usually specialist involvement.

questions.stem:
You are consenting a patient for a conventional bridge.
Which principle does Montgomery establish?
options: The dentist decides what risks to mention
Material risks and reasonable alternatives, including no treatment, must be discussed
questions.why: Montgomery (2015) requires disclosure of what this patient would consider material, plus alternatives including no treatment.
questions.revise: Unit 5 treatment strategies note 04, Unit 13 · LO 3b.1

questions.stem:
You refer a patient with a complex failing dentition to a restorative consultant.
What should the referral contain?
options: The diagnosis, key-tooth prognosis, proposed phases, responsibilities and relevant records
questions.answerText: Diagnosis, prognosis, phases, responsibilities and records.
questions.why: A good referral lets the receiving clinician act without repeating the assessment.

questions.stem:
A patient with active periodontitis requests four new crowns on the upper anteriors.
What is the main flaw in starting with the crowns?
options: Crowns are not available on the NHS
Definitive restorations before disease control are unsound
questions.answerText: Definitive work before disease control is unsound.
questions.why: Active periodontitis threatens margins, abutments and long-term outcome; stabilise first.

questions.stem:
A complete denture wearer has angular cheilitis, deep nasolabial folds and a prominent chin when the dentures are in occlusion.
What does this suggest, and how would you confirm it?
options: Reduced OVD; compare the rest vertical dimension with the occlusal vertical dimension (freeway space)
questions.answerText: Reduced OVD; compare RVD with OVD.
questions.why: Overclosure produces deep folds, a prominent chin and angular cheilitis. An excessive freeway space confirms it.

questions.stem:
You measure the freeway space of a complete denture wearer.
What is the normal range?
questions.why: It is usually about 3 mm. Less suggests excessive OVD; more suggests overclosure.

questions.stem:
Before preparing several crowns, you find a 2 mm slide from RCP to ICP.
Why should this be recorded?
options: It may affect whether a conformative or reorganised approach is needed
It means the patient has TMD
questions.why: A significant slide with symptoms or interferences may favour reorganisation; a stable one may be conformed to.

questions.stem:
You are examining an edentulous mouth before complete dentures.
Which features should be recorded?
questions.why: Ridge form, flabby tissue, undercuts, tori and mucosa all shape impression technique and design.

questions.stem:
A complete denture wearer complains of poor retention and a dry mouth.
How is unstimulated whole saliva flow measured?
options: Timed collection by spitting or drooling for 5–15 minutes
questions.why: Unstimulated flow is collected by spitting or drooling over a set time; under 0.1 mL/min is hyposalivation.

questions.stem:
You are grading the difficulty of edentulous and partially dentate cases.
What does the ACP Prosthodontic Diagnostic Index grade?
options: Complete and partial edentulism by ridge height, ridge relationship, muscle attachments and complicating factors
questions.answerText: Edentulism by ridge, relationship, muscle attachments and complicating factors.
questions.why: The ACP PDI grades complete and partial edentulism into classes I–IV of difficulty.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old has bone loss confined to the incisors and first molars.
How is the extent described in the 2017 classification?
questions.why: The 2017 classification describes extent as localised, generalised or molar–incisor pattern.

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old has localised Stage III Grade B periodontitis after initial therapy.
At what NHS complexity level is further care?
questions.why: Stage III Grade B is Level 3, whatever the extent.

questions.stem:
You need to check for proximal caries on the abutments of an RPD.
Which radiograph is best?
questions.why: They are the standard view for proximal caries and restoration margins.

questions.stem:
A colleague uses panoramic radiographs alone to screen for early caries.
Why is this inadequate?
options: Focal trough distortion and overlap limit fine detail; they are not suitable for detecting early caries
questions.why: Panoramic images give an overview, not the fine detail needed for early caries.

questions.stem:
A patient asks how much radiation a CBCT gives compared with a periapical.
Which approximate figures are correct?
options: Intraoral about 0.001–0.008 mSv; CBCT about 0.02–1 mSv depending on field of view
questions.why: The CBCT dose depends heavily on the field of view.

questions.stem:
An anxious patient reports a response to the electric pulp test on a tooth with a periapical radiolucency.
What could explain a false-positive result?
options: Anxiety, or liquefactive necrosis conducting the current
questions.why: Both can give a false-positive EPT response.

questions.stem:
An 82-year-old's lower canine, with a sound restoration and no radiographic lesion, does not respond to the EPT.
What is a likely explanation?
options: Calcification and reduced pulp size with age, giving a false negative
questions.why: Older and calcified teeth often fail to respond despite vital pulps.

questions.stem:
An arch has one large free-end saddle and two small bounded spaces.
How are the bounded spaces handled in Kennedy classification?
options: They are counted as modification spaces by number, whatever their size
questions.why: Applegate: the extent of a modification is not considered, only how many extra spaces there are.

questions.stem:
You are deciding whether to keep a compromised lower molar.
Which factors determine its prognosis?
questions.why: Prognosis integrates periodontal support, restorability, endodontic status, strategic value and patient risk factors.

questions.stem:
You have surveyed a study cast for a lower RPD and are about to draw the design.
What is decided first?
options: The outline of the saddles (which spaces will be restored)
questions.why: The design sequence is saddles, support, retention, bracing and reciprocation, connection, review. First decide which spaces need restoring.

questions.stem:
You have outlined the saddles on a design for an upper RPD.
Which design element comes next?
questions.why: Support (tooth, mucosa or both) follows the saddles; clasps come later.

questions.stem:
A Co-Cr RPD rocks sideways when the patient chews.
Which components resist lateral forces?
options: Bracing and reciprocal elements, and guide planes
questions.answerText: Bracing, reciprocal elements and guide planes.
questions.why: The three forces are towards the tissues (support), away from them (retention) and lateral (bracing).

questions.stem:
A healthy 74-year-old has premolars and anterior teeth in both arches and chews comfortably. Her molars were lost years ago.
What should you consider first when outlining saddles?
options: Whether the posterior spaces need restoring at all (shortened dental arch)
questions.answerText: Whether the spaces need restoring at all.
questions.why: A shortened dental arch may give adequate function; not every space needs filling.

questions.stem:
You are measuring undercuts on 35 for a cast Co-Cr clasp.
Which undercut gauge do you use?
questions.why: Stiff Co-Cr clasps engage 0.25 mm; gauges are 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 mm.

questions.stem:
A student marks the survey line on a premolar.
What does the survey line represent?
options: The greatest convexity of the tooth relative to the chosen path of insertion
questions.answerText: Greatest convexity relative to the path.
questions.why: The undercut lies gingival to the survey line, which changes with the chosen tilt.

questions.stem:
You are choosing the path of insertion on the surveyor.
Which factors determine it?
questions.why: Guide planes, retention, interference and aesthetics together determine the path.

questions.stem:
You tilt a lower cast on the surveyor table by lowering its front (heels up).
What happens to the undercuts?
questions.why: Lowering the front tips the crowns mesially relative to the rod. Lowering the heels increases distal undercuts.

questions.stem:
You have chosen a tilt for the cast and need the laboratory to reproduce it.
What should you do?
questions.why: Three marks at the same height let the technician reproduce the tilt exactly.

questions.stem:
Guide planes are being prepared on abutments for an upper Co-Cr RPD.
How high should they typically be?
options: 2–4 mm, parallel to the path of insertion
questions.why: Guide planes define a single path, add frictional retention, brace and reduce food trapping.

questions.stem:
The survey line on the lingual of 34 is so high that a reciprocal arm would sit above the occlusal third.
How can this be corrected?
options: Recontour the enamel to lower the height of contour
questions.why: Enameloplasty lowers the height of contour so the reciprocal arm sits correctly.

questions.stem:
15 has no retentive undercut on the buccal surface for the chosen path.
How can an undercut be created conservatively?
options: Add composite to create a contour with a suitable undercut
Tilt the cast until any undercut appears
questions.why: Additive composite can create retentive contour or a rest seat without crowning.

questions.stem:
A student lists the functions of an occlusal rest.
Which is NOT a function of a rest?
options: Transmitting load along the long axis of the tooth
Providing retention by engaging an undercut
Maintaining the vertical position of the denture
questions.why: That is a clasp's job. Rests support, keep the denture in position, protect the gingiva, keep clasps placed, act as indirect retainers and prevent over-eruption.

questions.stem:
You are preparing an occlusal rest seat on 36 for a Co-Cr framework.
Which description is correct?
options: A box with a floor angled away from the tooth centre
Half the buccolingual width, 3 mm deep
Spoon-shaped, about 1–1.5 mm deep and one-third of the buccolingual width, with the floor angled under 90° to the minor connector
Placed on the buccal cusp tip
questions.why: This directs load along the long axis and gives enough metal thickness for Co-Cr.

questions.stem:
You plan guide planes and rest seats on several abutments.
When are rest seats prepared?
options: After the guide planes, before the master impression
After the guide planes and after the master impression
questions.answerText: After guide planes, before the impression.
questions.why: Guide planes alter proximal contours; rest seats follow, then the master impression records both.

questions.stem:
A rest is needed on a lower canine for an RPD.
Which rest is preferred?
options: A cingulum rest (on a natural or composite-built cingulum)
A rest on the labial surface
A rest on the cusp tip
questions.why: It is less visible, gives a shorter lever and directs load better than an incisal rest.

questions.stem:
45 is the terminal abutment of a lower free-end saddle.
Where should its rest be placed?
questions.why: A mesial rest tips the abutment towards the arch rather than distally when the saddle sinks (RPI principle).

questions.stem:
An embrasure clasp is planned between 34 and 35.
What rest arrangement is needed?
questions.why: They support the clasp and stop it wedging the teeth apart.

questions.stem:
A student lists the requirements of a clasp unit.
How much of the tooth's circumference should the clasp encircle?
questions.why: Encirclement stops the tooth escaping from the clasp. Other requirements are retention, support, reciprocation, passivity and bracing.

questions.stem:
47 is tipped mesially into the space of 46 and has a mesiolingual undercut.
Which clasp suits 47?
options: A ring clasp with a supporting strut
questions.why: It reaches the mesiolingual undercut of a tipped molar; its long, flexible arm needs a bracing strut.

questions.stem:
A Kennedy Class II lower arch has no modification space on the dentate side.
How is retention usually gained on that side?
options: An embrasure clasp, with the embrasure prepared for space
A ring clasp on the canine
questions.why: It gives cross-arch retention and bracing on the dentate side of a Kennedy II; prepare enough embrasure space.

questions.stem:
An RPI clasp assembly is planned for 44.
Which finding contraindicates the I-bar?
options: A sulcus under about 4 mm, a soft-tissue undercut or a prominent frenum
questions.answerText: Shallow sulcus, soft-tissue undercut or prominent frenum.
questions.why: A gingivally approaching I-bar needs a sulcus of about 4 mm or more and no tissue undercut.

questions.stem:
A free-end abutment needs a flexible clasp engaging a 0.5–0.75 mm undercut.
Which clasp is suitable?
questions.why: Wrought wire is flexible, adjustable and suits 0.5–0.75 mm undercuts on free-end abutments.

questions.stem:
A technician makes a clasp arm twice as long as planned.
How does its flexibility change?
questions.why: Flexibility rises with the cube of length.

questions.stem:
You review a clasp design on a premolar.
Where should the reciprocal arm sit?
options: On or above the survey line, contacting the tooth before or with the retentive arm
questions.answerText: On or above the survey line, contacting first.
questions.why: It must resist the retentive arm's push as that arm flexes over the height of contour.

questions.stem:
The retentive arm of a new clasp is pressing on the tooth when the denture is fully seated.
What is the correct position of the retentive tip?
options: In the occlusal third, under tension
In the gingival third undercut, passive when fully seated
questions.why: An active clasp at rest moves the tooth orthodontically.

questions.stem:
A patient asks why her lower free-end RPD moves while her other partial denture does not.
What explains the problem of free-end saddles?
options: Teeth move about 0.02–0.1 mm under load, while mucosa compresses about 0.4–2 mm
Mucosa is less compressible than teeth
questions.why: Teeth move 0.02–0.1 mm; mucosa compresses 0.4–2 mm. The saddle rotates about the fulcrum line and torques the abutment.

questions.stem:
You are planning the extension of a lower free-end saddle.
What should it cover?
options: Half the length of the ridge
The retromolar pad and buccal shelf
questions.why: Maximum extension spreads load over the largest supporting area.

questions.stem:
A lower Kennedy Class I RPD is planned for a patient with a resorbed, displaceable ridge.
Which impression technique records the saddle area functionally?
options: A one-stage impression of the teeth and ridge in compound
questions.why: It records the saddle area under functional load on the framework, matching tooth and mucosal support.

questions.stem:
An RPI clasp is designed for 34, the abutment of a free-end saddle.
What are its three components?
options: Mesial rest, distal proximal plate and buccal I-bar
Distal rest, mesial plate and lingual arm
questions.answerText: Mesial rest, distal proximal plate, buccal I-bar.
questions.why: That is Kratochvil and Krol's RPI assembly.

questions.stem:
A patient bites on the free-end saddle of a lower RPD with an RPI assembly on 34.
What happens to the I-bar and proximal plate?
options: They move gingivally and mesially, disengaging from the tooth and reducing torque
They lock the denture in place
questions.why: Releasing from the tooth under load minimises torque on the abutment.

questions.stem:
44 is the terminal abutment of a free-end saddle, but the buccal sulcus is 3 mm deep with a soft-tissue undercut.
Which clasp assembly is appropriate?
options: RPA, replacing the I-bar with an Akers-type arm
questions.why: Eliason's RPA replaces the I-bar with an Akers-type arm when a gingivally approaching clasp is contraindicated.

questions.stem:
You are designing indirect retention for a lower Kennedy Class I RPD.
Where does the fulcrum line run?
options: Through the rests nearest to the free-end saddles
questions.answerText: Through the rests nearest the free-end saddles.
questions.why: The saddle rotates about this line.

questions.stem:
A patient's lower bilateral free-end RPD lifts at the back when she eats toffee.
Where should an indirect retainer be placed?
options: As far anterior to the fulcrum line as possible
questions.answerText: As far anterior to the fulcrum line as possible.
questions.why: The longer the lever arm, the better the indirect retainer resists lifting.

questions.stem:
A student asks what else indirect retainers achieve besides resisting rotation.
What is correct?
options: They give support and stop the major connector settling
questions.why: Indirect retainers also support anterior extensions and stop the major connector sinking.

questions.stem:
A long lower free-end saddle on a resorbed ridge is being set up.
How should the saddle teeth be arranged?
options: Extra teeth to the retromolar pad
Narrow, reduced occlusal tables in harmonious occlusion
questions.why: Narrower tables reduce the load on the resorbing ridge and the torque on abutments.

questions.stem:
At review, pressing on the lower free-end saddle lifts the canine rests from their seats.
What is needed?
questions.why: Lifting rests on pressing the saddle show ridge resorption and rotation.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old has only 13–23 remaining. The palate is flat and resorbed.
Which maxillary connector is appropriate?
questions.why: Few teeth, long saddles and a flat palate need maximum support and retention.

questions.stem:
An upper arch has short bounded saddles on both sides (16 and 26 missing).
Which maxillary connector is appropriate?
options: Mid-palatal strap, at least 8 mm wide
questions.answerText: Mid-palatal strap, at least 8 mm wide.
questions.why: Short bounded saddles on both sides need a thin, rigid strap.

questions.stem:
An upper arch has anterior and posterior saddles and a large torus that the patient will not have removed.
Which connector is appropriate?
options: Full palatal plate over the torus
Narrow mid-palatal strap over the torus
questions.why: It is rigid with less coverage and avoids the torus.

questions.stem:
A student asks which maxillary connector is least rigid.
Which is it, and when is it used?
options: Horseshoe; for anterior saddles only or an inoperable torus
questions.why: It is the least rigid maxillary connector, used only for anterior saddles or an inoperable torus.

questions.stem:
A lower RPD is planned. From the gingival margin to the functional floor of the mouth there are 9 mm.
Which connector and dimensions are correct?
options: Lingual plate, because the sulcus is deep
Lingual bar: half-pear, about 4 mm high, at least 3 mm clear of the gingival margin
questions.why: At least 7–8 mm of sulcus allows a half-pear bar about 4 mm high and 3 mm clear of the gingiva.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old has mobile lower incisors, a 6 mm lingual sulcus, and may lose more teeth.
Which lower connector is appropriate?
questions.why: A shallow sulcus, mobile incisors needing splinting and likely additions favour a plate.

questions.stem:
A shallow lingual sulcus would place a lingual bar on the gingivae, but the incisors are healthy.
Which connector lies deeper in the sulcus and needs a functional impression?
questions.why: It sits deeper in the sulcus and is recorded in a functional impression.

questions.stem:
A patient has markedly lingually inclined lower premolars and large tori.
Which connector is indicated?
questions.why: It is used for lingually inclined teeth or large tori, despite its bulk.

questions.stem:
A dental bar (continuous clasp) on the cingula is suggested for a patient with recession.
What is its main drawback?
questions.why: A continuous clasp gives indirect retention but lies on the cingula, where food collects.

questions.stem:
You review the edges of a Co-Cr major connector.
How should they relate to the gingival margins?
options: They should end on the gingival margin
At least 3 mm (mandible) to 6 mm (maxilla) away, or covering the margin fully with relief
questions.answerText: 3 mm (mandible) to 6 mm (maxilla) clear, or fully covered with relief.
questions.why: Never end a connector on the gingival margin.

questions.stem:
A minor connector runs from a lingual bar to a rest on 34.
How should it cross the gingival margin?
options: At right angles, as narrow as possible, lying in the embrasure
questions.answerText: At right angles, narrow, in the embrasure.
questions.why: This minimises gingival coverage and is least noticed by the tongue.

questions.stem:
A technician proposes a thin, flexible lingual bar to improve comfort.
Why is this wrong?
options: Thin bars are more expensive to cast
Major connectors must be rigid so that forces spread across the arch
questions.why: Rigidity distributes forces across the arch; a flexible bar concentrates load on single abutments.

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old has worn a mucosa-borne acrylic RPD covering the gingival margins for 10 years.
What is the typical consequence?
options: Gingival stripping, with more periodontal disease and caries
questions.answerText: Gingival stripping, periodontal disease and caries.
questions.why: Mucosa-borne acrylic RPDs covering the margins are known as "gum strippers".

questions.stem:
Several teeth of uncertain prognosis remain, and further extractions are likely within a year.
Which RPD is most appropriate?
options: A Co-Cr framework with precision attachments
questions.why: Acrylic is easy to add to as teeth are lost; a Co-Cr framework would be wasted on teeth of uncertain prognosis.

questions.stem:
An upper acrylic RPD is designed with point contacts on the teeth, open embrasures, free gingival margins and distal stabilising wires.
What design is this?
questions.why: Every (1949): point contacts, open embrasures, free gingival margins and distal stabilising wires maximise gingival health in an acrylic design.

questions.stem:
A patient needs a small, interim replacement for 11 with no gingival contact.
Which design is this?
questions.why: A small upper anterior mucosa-borne interim denture with no gingival contact.

questions.stem:
A patient has missing anterior teeth and periodontally compromised remaining teeth with labial undercuts, where conventional clasps work poorly.
Which design is indicated?
questions.why: A hinged labial bar engages labial undercuts of many teeth, suiting compromised teeth where conventional clasps fail.

questions.stem:
A patient asks for a flexible nylon denture because she dislikes metal clasps.
What is its main disadvantage?
options: It is hard to adjust, reline or add to
questions.answerText: Hard to adjust, reline or add to.
questions.why: Nylon is aesthetic and clasp-free but mainly mucosa-borne and difficult to modify.

questions.stem:
A patient asks about precision attachments for a lower RPD.
What is correct?
options: They need crowned abutments and usually lie beyond Level 2
They cannot be used with Co-Cr
questions.why: Attachments need crowns, laboratory precision and maintenance.

questions.stem:
26 has over-erupted into a lower edentulous space where an RPD is planned.
What is appropriate before designing?
options: Correct the over-eruption and occlusal plane (pre-prosthetic optimisation, a Level 2 task)
questions.why: Correct over-eruption, tilts and the occlusal plane before design; this is within Level 2.

questions.stem:
The metal framework of a Co-Cr RPD is tried in before the teeth are set.
What should be checked?
options: That clasps are passive and the occlusion is not disturbed
questions.why: At framework try-in check fit with disclosing medium, full seating of rests, passive clasps and undisturbed occlusion before setting teeth.

questions.stem:
A patient removes her new RPD by pulling on the clasp tips.
What instruction should she be given?
options: Remove it only at the dentist
Use a tool on the clasps
Insert and remove it along the path of insertion, using the saddles, not the clasps
questions.answerText: Along the path, using the saddles.
questions.why: Pulling on clasp tips distorts them and loosens retention.

questions.stem:
A new Co-Cr RPD is fitted.
When should it first be reviewed?
options: About 1 week, then at regular recalls
questions.why: Early review catches pressure points and high rests.

questions.stem:
A patient has worn a Co-Cr RPD for 5 years.
What is the most important long-term maintenance?
options: Monitoring caries and periodontal health at the abutments, and relining saddles as needed
questions.why: Caries and periodontal disease at abutments, and ridge resorption under free-end saddles, are the main long-term risks.

questions.stem:
A patient is worried that an RPD will damage her remaining teeth.
What does the evidence (Bergman) show?
options: A well-designed, tooth-supported Co-Cr RPD with good hygiene and recall does little harm
questions.why: Bergman showed tooth-supported Co-Cr RPDs, with good hygiene and recall, do little harm to the remaining teeth.

questions.stem:
A laboratory returns a Co-Cr framework with clasps on different teeth from those planned.
Who is responsible for the design?
options: The dentist, whose prescription must specify every component
questions.why: The dentist is responsible for the design; the prescription must specify every component.
questions.revise: Unit 6, In one minute, Unit 13 · LO 2c.3, 3a.3

questions.stem:
A student designs a retentive clasp on 45 with no reciprocal element.
Why is the design incomplete?
options: Without reciprocation, the retentive arm pushes the tooth as it flexes
questions.answerText: Without reciprocation the tooth is pushed.
questions.why: A retentive clasp without reciprocation is not a complete design.

questions.stem:
A patient has pain on biting on 36 a week after fitting a Co-Cr RPD. A rest on 36 marks heavily with articulating paper.
What is the likely cause and remedy?
options: A high rest; adjust the rest or deepen the seat
questions.why: Adjust the rest or deepen the seat; pain after fitting is often from a high rest, over-extension or tissue pressure.

questions.stem:
An upper arch is missing 24, 25 and 26 only, with sound 23 and 27.
What support and indirect retention does this design need?
options: Tooth support from rests at both ends; indirect retention is generally not needed
questions.answerText: Tooth-borne with rests at both ends.
questions.why: A Kennedy III saddle is tooth-supported, so it does not rotate about a fulcrum; indirect retention is generally unnecessary.

questions.stem:
A Kennedy Class IV RPD replaces 12 to 22.
Which design principles apply?
options: Rests on the teeth next to the anterior saddle
Attention to aesthetics and lip support
questions.why: A Kennedy IV saddle needs rests on the adjacent teeth, indirect retention posteriorly, and attention to appearance and lip support.

questions.stem:
A lower Kennedy Class I RPD is planned with 33 to 44 remaining and a deep lingual sulcus.
Which design is most appropriate?
options: Mesial rests and RPI clasps on 34 and 44, cingulum rests on the canines, a lingual bar and maximum saddle extension
Distal rests and Akers clasps on the premolars
A labial bar with no rests
questions.answerText: Mesial rests, RPI, canine cingulum rests, lingual bar, maximum extension.
questions.why: This classic free-end design controls torque and rotation.

questions.stem:
An upper arch has 13, 12, 22 and 23 remaining, with bilateral free-end saddles and a high, well-formed vault.
Which connector gives the best support and retention?
questions.why: With only four teeth and bilateral free ends, palatal coverage gives most support and retention.

questions.stem:
A student asks when guide planes and rest seats should be prepared for a Co-Cr RPD.
What is the correct sequence?
options: Prepare freehand at the first visit
Survey the study cast and plan, prepare the teeth, then take the master impression
questions.answerText: Survey and plan, prepare, then the master impression.
questions.why: Preparing teeth to a surveyed design ensures guide planes and rests match the path.

questions.stem:
An RPI assembly is planned on 34.
How long should the distal guide plane be?
options: Short, about 2–3 mm, so the plate can disengage under load
questions.why: A short guide plane lets the proximal plate move gingivally and disengage.

questions.stem:
35 has a 0.75 mm undercut on its buccal surface.
Which clasp suits this depth?
questions.why: Wrought wire engages 0.5–0.75 mm; Co-Cr 0.25 mm; cast gold 0.5 mm.

questions.stem:
You tilt a lower cast on the surveyor so that its heels are lowered.
What happens to the undercuts?
questions.why: Lowering the heels tips the crowns distally relative to the rod.

questions.stem:
A technician makes a Co-Cr clasp arm twice as thick as planned.
How does its flexibility change?
questions.why: Flexibility falls with the cube of thickness.

questions.stem:
A patient dislikes the buccal circumferential clasp showing on 13.
Which is a more aesthetic option if the sulcus allows?
options: A gingivally approaching I-bar into a mesiobuccal undercut, or moving retention to a premolar
questions.answerText: I-bar, or move retention to a premolar.
questions.why: A gingivally approaching bar is less visible; retention can also be placed on less visible teeth or gained from guide planes.

questions.stem:
A lower lingual plate is planned for a patient with mobile incisors.
What is required for it to succeed?
options: Excellent oral hygiene, as it covers the gingival margins
questions.why: A lingual plate covers the gingival margins, so plaque control is critical.

questions.stem:
A patient with xerostomia and high caries risk needs an RPD.
Which design principle is most important?
options: A minimal, open design with little tooth and gingival coverage
questions.why: Reducing tooth and gingival coverage limits plaque stagnation in a high-risk mouth.

questions.stem:
A patient asks how to soak her Co-Cr RPD overnight.
What is correct?
questions.why: Hypochlorite corrodes Co-Cr.

questions.stem:
A patient asks whether to wear her new RPD at night.
What is the standard advice?
questions.why: Night removal rests the tissues and reduces candidosis and plaque stagnation.

questions.stem:
A lower Kennedy Class II RPD fitted 6 years ago now rocks, and the indirect retainer lifts when the saddle is pressed.
What is the correct management?
questions.why: Rocking and lifting indirect retainers mean ridge resorption; tightening clasps would add torque.

questions.stem:
An abutment tooth has over-erupted slightly since the patient stopped wearing her RPD.
Which function of rests helps prevent this?
options: Preventing over-eruption and maintaining tooth position
questions.why: Occlusal rests maintain the abutment's vertical position as well as supporting the denture.

questions.stem:
A bounded saddle abutment is tilted towards the space, so the denture cannot be inserted without a gap.
What helps?
options: Preparing guide planes parallel to the path of insertion
questions.answerText: Guide planes parallel to the path.
questions.why: Preparing parallel guide planes on a tilted abutment removes the obstruction to a single path.

questions.stem:
Food collects between a saddle and the abutment of a Co-Cr RPD.
What design feature is likely missing?
options: A proximal plate on a guide plane
questions.answerText: A proximal plate on a guide plane.
questions.why: Close contact between plate and guide plane reduces food trapping.

questions.stem:
A Co-Cr RPD is being set up for a patient with a stable natural occlusion.
How should the denture occlusion be arranged?
options: Balanced occlusion like a complete denture
With heavy contacts on the saddle teeth
Without contact on the saddle teeth
In harmony with the existing ICP
questions.answerText: In harmony with the existing ICP.
questions.why: RPD occlusion conforms to the natural occlusion; balanced occlusion is for complete dentures.

questions.stem:
A tilted lower molar and over-erupted upper molar complicate an RPD design.
How is correcting them before design classed?
questions.why: Adjusting over-eruption and tilts before design is part of Level 2 care.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old has grade 2 mobile lower incisors with stable periodontal disease and needs a free-end RPD.
Which lower connector helps?
questions.why: A lingual plate splints mobile incisors and provides indirect retention.

questions.stem:
A lower lingual bar has sunk onto the lingual gingiva of the incisors.
What is the most likely cause?
options: Inadequate rest support, so the denture settles
questions.why: Without seated rests the denture settles and the bar impinges on the gingiva.

questions.stem:
A lower Kennedy Class I RPD needs indirect retention.
Which components can act as indirect retainers?
options: Canine cingulum rests, a lingual plate or rests on premolars, placed anterior to the fulcrum line
Clasp tips behind the fulcrum line
questions.answerText: Cingulum rests, lingual plate or premolar rests anterior to the fulcrum.
questions.why: Any rigid component seated well forward of the fulcrum line can act as an indirect retainer.

questions.stem:
A student designs an RPD by first choosing an attractive clasp for each tooth.
What is wrong with this approach?
options: Clasps should be chosen last of all
It reverses the design logic; support and the path of insertion come before clasp selection
questions.why: Support and the path of insertion come first; clasps are chosen to suit them.

questions.stem:
A patient's RPD lifts at the back when she eats sticky food. The only rests are on the premolars next to the saddles.
Where should an extra rest be added?
options: As far forward of the fulcrum line as possible, such as a cingulum rest on a canine
questions.answerText: Far forward, such as a canine cingulum rest.
questions.why: An indirect retainer far anterior to the fulcrum resists the saddle lifting.

questions.stem:
A distal-extension RPD is being planned.
How is it supported?
questions.why: A distal-extension RPD is tooth- and mucosa-borne (Craddock 3).

questions.stem:
A colleague plans Akers clasps engaging the distobuccal undercuts of the terminal abutments of a lower free-end RPD.
What is the problem?
options: The clasps will torque the abutments distally as the saddle moves; mesial rests with RPI or RPA are better
questions.answerText: Distal torque; use mesial rests with RPI or RPA.
questions.why: Rigid clasps in distal undercuts lever the abutments as the saddle sinks.

questions.stem:
