A patient has lost several anterior teeth and the remaining teeth have reduced support with labial undercuts.
Which design gives retention without conventional clasps?
questions.why: It gains retention from labial undercuts across many teeth through a hinged labial bar.

questions.stem:
An RPD is needed while a patient's periodontal treatment outcome is uncertain.
Which type is most appropriate?
options: A Co-Cr RPD with precision attachments
questions.why: It suits uncertain prognosis and can be modified as treatment progresses.

questions.stem:
A patient requests an RPD with precision attachments on crowned canines.
At what level is this care usually provided?
questions.why: Precision attachments on crowned abutments are usually specialist care.

questions.stem:
A Co-Cr framework will not seat. Disclosing medium shows contact on the inner surface of a minor connector.
What should you do?
options: Adjust only the marked area and re-check
questions.answerText: Adjust the marked area and re-check.
questions.why: Disclosing medium identifies the interference; relieve only where it marks. Remake only if no interference explains the misfit.

questions.stem:
A week after fitting, a patient reports a sore abutment. The rest on it marks heavily in occlusion.
What should you do?
questions.why: A high rest overloads the abutment and causes tenderness.

questions.stem:
You send a Co-Cr RPD case to the laboratory.
What must the prescription include?
options: A request to "design as you see fit"
A drawn design specifying every component, on a surveyed cast with tripod marks
questions.answerText: A full drawn design on a surveyed, tripoded cast.
questions.why: The prescription must specify every component; the laboratory must not design it.

questions.stem:
A patient lisps on "s" with a new upper Co-Cr RPD whose anterior strap is thick over the rugae.
What should be adjusted?
options: The thickness and position of the anterior strap
questions.why: Bulk over the anterior palate disturbs tongue contact for "s"; thin or reposition it.

questions.stem:
A patient asks why a well-made Co-Cr RPD is kinder to the remaining teeth than an acrylic one.
Which features reduce harm?
questions.why: Tooth support, minimal gingival coverage, hygiene and recall together explain why Co-Cr RPDs do little harm.

questions.stem:
A new upper complete denture stays up at rest but slides sideways when the patient chews.
Which property is deficient?
questions.why: Stability resists horizontal and rotational forces; it depends on ridge form, flange extension, balanced occlusion and teeth in the neutral zone. Retention resists displacement away from the tissues.

questions.stem:
A student asks what holds a complete denture in place.
Which factors contribute to retention?
options: Physical factors such as adhesion, cohesion and the peripheral seal
Muscular factors such as polished-surface shape and the neutral zone
Mechanical factors such as undercuts, implants or adhesive
questions.why: Retention has physical, muscular and mechanical components.

questions.stem:
A lower denture sinks into a soft, flat ridge under load, causing pain.
Which property describes resistance to movement towards the tissues, and how is it improved?
options: Support; by maximum extension over the stress-bearing areas
questions.why: Support resists movement towards the tissues and is improved by covering all stress-bearing areas.

questions.stem:
A well-fitting lower denture is displaced by the cheeks and tongue during speech.
Which group of retentive factors is failing?
options: Muscular factors: polished-surface shape and the neutral zone
questions.why: Polished surfaces shaped to the neutral zone let the tongue and cheeks hold the denture in function.

questions.stem:
You prescribe special trays for complete dentures from primary impressions.
How far should the tray borders be from the sulcus depth?
options: About 2 mm short, to allow border moulding
questions.why: It leaves room for border moulding to record the functional sulcus.

questions.stem:
You take primary impressions of an edentulous patient in stock trays.
What is the main aim?
options: A mucostatic record of the ridge only
Recording the full sulcus depth so that special trays can be made
questions.why: The primary cast must show the whole denture-bearing area so special trays can be made.

questions.stem:
You are border moulding a special tray before the secondary impression.
Which material is traditionally used?
questions.why: Its thermoplastic handling allows sectional border moulding.

questions.stem:
The laboratory pours the secondary impressions for complete dentures.
Which stone is used for the master casts?
questions.why: Dental stone gives adequate strength for denture master casts; die stone is for crowns.

questions.stem:
You are taking secondary (master) impressions in close-fitting special trays.
Which materials are suitable?
options: ZOE paste, light-bodied silicone or polyether
questions.why: These record detail in a close-fitting, border-moulded special tray.

questions.stem:
You are at the jaw registration visit with wax rims.
What is recorded at this visit?
options: OVD, RCP, occlusal plane, centre and canine lines, lip line, tooth mould and shade
questions.answerText: OVD, RCP, plane, lines, mould and shade.
questions.why: Everything the technician needs to set the teeth is recorded at this visit, with a facebow if a semi-adjustable articulator is used.

questions.stem:
At the wax try-in of new complete dentures, everything looks satisfactory.
What else should be done before processing?
options: Record the patient's approval and mark the post-dam
questions.why: Try-in is the last chance to change appearance; approval is recorded and the vibrating line marked for the post-dam.

questions.stem:
You are fitting new complete dentures.
How do you identify pressure points on the fitting surface?
questions.why: It shows exactly where the fitting surface presses on the mucosa.

questions.stem:
New complete dentures have been fitted.
When is the first review usually arranged?
questions.why: Early review lets you adjust ulcers and occlusion.

questions.stem:
You are contouring an upper wax rim for lip support.
How far anterior to the centre of the incisive papilla do the labial surfaces of the central incisors usually lie?
questions.why: This rule of thumb restores lip support.

questions.stem:
You set the incisal level of an upper wax rim for a 45-year-old.
How much rim usually shows below the relaxed upper lip?
questions.why: Incisal display reduces with age.

questions.stem:
You check the upper occlusal rim with a Fox's plane guide.
How should the occlusal plane be oriented?
options: Parallel to the lower ridge only
Parallel to the interpupillary line anteriorly and to the ala–tragal line (Camper's plane) posteriorly
questions.answerText: Interpupillary line anteriorly, Camper's plane posteriorly.
questions.why: These references orient the occlusal plane.

questions.stem:
You set the lower posterior occlusal plane.
What is the usual landmark?
options: About two-thirds up the retromolar pad, level with the lateral border of the tongue
The top of the retromolar pad
questions.why: At this height, level with the lateral border of the tongue, the lower plane is stable.

questions.stem:
You mark guidelines on the upper rim.
What do the centre line and canine lines follow?
options: The facial midline (philtrum) and the corners of the mouth at rest
The lower midline and the commissures in a smile
The nose tip and the pupils
The labial frenum and the buccal frena
questions.answerText: Philtrum, and the corners of the mouth at rest.
questions.why: They locate the midline and the distal of the canines.

questions.stem:
An edentulous patient's rest vertical dimension measures 70 mm.
What OVD would you aim for?
options: About 67 mm (a freeway space of about 3 mm)
questions.why: OVD = RVD minus a freeway space of 2–4 mm (average about 3 mm).

questions.stem:
You use a Willis gauge during jaw registration.
What does it measure?
options: Base of the nose to the underside of the chin
questions.answerText: Base of the nose to the underside of the chin.
questions.why: Willis noted this roughly equals the pupil-to-stomion distance.

questions.stem:
You test the OVD of trial dentures phonetically.
What is the normal closest speaking space on "s"?
questions.why: If the teeth touch on "s", the OVD is too high.

questions.stem:
Rest vertical dimension readings vary between visits for the same patient.
Why, and how should you respond?
options: Rest position is fixed for life
Rest position varies with posture, fatigue and emotion; measure several times with the patient upright and relaxed
Use the old denture's OVD only
questions.answerText: Rest position varies; measure several times.
questions.why: Head posture, fatigue and emotion all change it.

questions.stem:
A week after fitting, a patient complains of generalised soreness of the lower ridge. Her teeth click when she speaks and her lips look strained.
What is the most likely cause?
options: OVD too high (freeway space too small)
questions.why: Generalised soreness, clicking and strained lips are classic signs of too little freeway space.

questions.stem:
A patient's old dentures give him a collapsed appearance, angular cheilitis and a prominent chin.
What do these signs indicate?
options: OVD too low (freeway space too large)
questions.why: Overclosure causes commissural folds (angular cheilitis), a collapsed look and a prominent chin.

questions.stem:
A colleague builds the OVD of new dentures well above the rest position.
Which long-term consequences may follow?
options: Muscle fatigue, soreness and faster ridge resorption
questions.why: Constant loading without rest accelerates resorption and fatigues the muscles.

questions.stem:
A student asks why complete dentures are made in the retruded contact position.
What is the reason?
options: It is the position patients habitually use
questions.why: With no teeth to guide ICP, RCP is the repeatable reference.

questions.stem:
You are recording the horizontal jaw relation.
Which technique is appropriate?
options: Ask the patient to bite hard in any position
Guide the mandible gently to the retruded arc, with the patient relaxed and the tongue curled back
Record it with the patient lying flat and asleep
questions.answerText: Gentle guidance, patient relaxed, tongue curled back.
questions.why: Force or protrusion gives false records.

questions.stem:
You use a Gothic arch (needle-point) tracer because registration is unreliable.
Where is RCP recorded?
options: At the end of the right lateral path
In the centre of the tracing
At the apex of the arrowhead
questions.why: It marks the most retruded, reproducible position.

questions.stem:
At try-in, the posterior teeth on one side do not meet and there is a slide on closure.
What is the correct action?
options: Grind the teeth until they meet
Process the dentures and adjust at fit
Take a new RCP registration and re-articulate
questions.why: Grinding the teeth to fit a wrong record makes things worse.

questions.stem:
A technician uses an average-value articulator for complete dentures.
What are its fixed settings?
options: Condylar guidance about 30° and a Bonwill triangle with sides of about 10 cm
Settings taken from a protrusive record
questions.why: These fixed averages are adequate for most complete dentures.

questions.stem:
A semi-adjustable articulator is used with a facebow.
How is its condylar guidance set?
questions.why: The protrusive record positions the condylar elements at the patient's guidance angle.

questions.stem:
A technician needs the Bennett angle but has no lateral records.
Which formula estimates it from condylar guidance (H)?
questions.why: Hanau's formula estimates the Bennett angle (L) from the horizontal condylar guidance (H).

questions.stem:
A student is comparing articulators.
What defines an arcon articulator?
options: Its condylar element is on the upper member
Its condylar element is on the lower member, as in the anatomy (for example Whip Mix, Denar)
questions.answerText: Condylar element on the lower member.
questions.why: Arcon designs (Whip Mix, Denar) mimic the anatomy; non-arcon (Dentatus, Hanau H2) have it on the upper member.

questions.stem:
A facebow record is taken for complete dentures on a semi-adjustable articulator.
What does it record?
options: The relationship of the maxillary arch to the hinge axis
questions.why: It makes the arcs of closure on the articulator match the patient's.

questions.stem:
In protrusion, the posterior parts of the record rims separate.
What is this phenomenon, and what does balanced occlusion need?
questions.why: The condyles move down the eminence in protrusion; a compensating curve keeps posterior contact.

questions.stem:
A technician refers to Hanau's quint when setting balanced occlusion.
What are its five factors?
options: OVD, RCP, shade, mould, lip line
Freeway space, OVD, overjet, overbite, post-dam
Condylar guidance, incisal guidance, cusp angle, plane of orientation, compensating curve
Ridge height, width, shape, saliva, tongue
questions.why: Condylar guidance, incisal guidance, cusp angle, plane of orientation and compensating curve must be balanced together.

questions.stem:
A student asks why bilateral balanced occlusion is used in complete dentures.
What is its purpose?
options: Simultaneous contacts on working and non-working sides keep the dentures stable in excursions
questions.why: They stop the dentures tipping in excursions.

questions.stem:
A technician sets a lingualised occlusion.
How is it arranged?
options: Only the upper palatal cusps contact the lower central fossae
Only the lower buccal cusps contact
questions.answerText: Upper palatal cusps into lower central fossae.
questions.why: Lingualised occlusion gives good stability on resorbed ridges with acceptable appearance.

questions.stem:
A patient has a severely resorbed mandible, a Class III jaw relationship and poor neuromuscular control.
Which posterior teeth are most suitable?
questions.why: Zero-degree teeth generate the least horizontal force, which suits severe resorption, Class III and poor control.

questions.stem:
You estimate the width of an upper central incisor for a patient without pre-extraction records.
Which guide (Berry) relates it to facial width?
options: About one-sixteenth of the bizygomatic width
questions.why: Berry's proportion is one guide, alongside the canine lines and inter-alar width.

questions.stem:
A colleague insists that tooth shape must match the face form (Williams) and personality (dentogenics).
What is the evidence position?
options: They are required by the GDC
They guide shape but are weakly evidence-based
They are discredited and must never be used
questions.why: Williams' face form and Frush and Fisher's dentogenics can guide shape but lack strong evidence.

questions.stem:
An 80-year-old wants new dentures and asks for "bright white, perfect teeth".
Which approach to shade is best?
options: Involve her in the choice, usually favouring a darker, characterised shade that suits her age
questions.answerText: Involve her; favour an age-appropriate shade.
questions.why: Very light teeth create a "denture look"; shared decision-making avoids later disputes.

questions.stem:
A technician sets the lower second molar on the ascending slope of the ramus.
What is the consequence?
options: The lower denture is pushed forward in function
questions.why: Occlusal force on an inclined surface drives the denture anteriorly; lower posteriors go over the crest, never up the ramus.

questions.stem:
A patient has a severely resorbed maxilla that is much narrower than the mandible.
How are the posterior teeth usually set?
options: In crossbite, with the upper teeth possibly buccal to the resorbed ridge
questions.why: Centripetal maxillary resorption makes the upper arch narrower; setting in crossbite keeps teeth over the ridges.

questions.stem:
A patient's lower denture has been unstable for years on a resorbed ridge.
How is the neutral zone recorded?
options: With alginate in a stock tray
With a mouldable material on a lower base, shaped during swallowing and speaking
questions.why: Tissue conditioner, compound or soft wax on a lower base records where tongue and cheek forces balance.

questions.stem:
A colleague asks when a neutral-zone technique is most useful.
Which case suits it best?
options: A resorbed lower ridge with a history of unstable lower dentures
A first-time denture wearer with excellent ridges
questions.answerText: Resorbed lower ridge with unstable dentures.
questions.why: That is where muscle control matters most.

questions.stem:
A patient keeps biting his cheeks with new complete dentures.
What setting feature prevents this?
questions.why: Horizontal overlap keeps the cheek out from between the teeth.

questions.stem:
You are carving the post-dam on an upper master cast.
Where is it deepest?
options: About 1–1.5 mm deep either side of the midline, shallower over the raphe
questions.answerText: 1–1.5 mm either side of the midline.
questions.why: It is deepest over the compressible glandular tissue and shallower over the thin raphe.

questions.stem:
A student asks why a post-dam is needed.
Which is one of its functions?
options: It adds retention by engaging an undercut
It compensates for polymerisation contraction lifting the posterior border
It reduces the weight of the denture
questions.why: The post-dam also completes the posterior seal and reduces food entry and gagging.

questions.stem:
You mark the vibrating line for an upper complete denture.
How are the posterior and anterior vibrating lines identified?
options: Posterior: by asking the patient to say "ah"; anterior: with the Valsalva manoeuvre
questions.why: Saying "ah" shows the posterior vibrating line; the Valsalva manoeuvre shows the anterior one.

questions.stem:
At try-in, a patient's "f" sounds like "v".
What does the "f/v" test check?
options: That the upper incisal edges touch the wet–dry line of the lower lip (upper incisor length and labial position)
questions.answerText: Upper incisal edges touching the wet–dry line.
questions.why: The f/v sounds test upper incisor length and labial position.

questions.stem:
A patient whistles on "s" with new dentures.
What is a likely cause?
options: A narrow anterior palate or anterior teeth set too far palatally
questions.answerText: Narrow anterior palate or palatally set teeth.
questions.why: Whistling on "s" suggests too little anterior tongue space.

questions.stem:
A patient develops a lisp with a new upper denture.
Which feature is most likely to blame?
options: Lower incisors set too far labially
Excessive palatal thickness in the rugae area
questions.answerText: Excess palatal thickness at the rugae.
questions.why: The tongue contacts the rugae area for many sounds; bulk there causes a lisp.

questions.stem:
A new upper complete denture drops when the patient talks or opens wide.
What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: The coronoid process moves forward on opening and pushes the flange down.

questions.stem:
A new upper denture is loose even at rest, with no displacement on opening.
What is the most likely cause?
options: An inadequate post-dam or peripheral seal
questions.why: Looseness at rest means air enters at the border; under-extension or poor fit are other causes.

questions.stem:
A new lower complete denture lifts when the patient swallows.
What is the most likely cause?
options: An over-extended lingual flange (mylohyoid) or retromolar region
questions.why: Mylohyoid rises on swallowing; teeth outside the neutral zone also displace the denture.

questions.stem:
A patient's denture-bearing areas are sore all over after a week. The occlusion and extension look satisfactory, and she has anaemia.
Which causes of generalised soreness should be considered?
options: Excessive OVD, an RCP error, parafunction, inadequate support, or systemic factors such as anaemia or diabetes
questions.answerText: OVD, RCP error, parafunction, support or systemic factors.
questions.why: Generalised soreness points to overload or systemic susceptibility rather than a local fault.

questions.stem:
A patient has a single ulcer in the depth of the lower labial sulcus.
What is the most likely cause?
options: An over-extended flange or sharp flange edge
questions.why: Sulcus ulcers match the flange edge; trim and polish.

questions.stem:
A patient has an ulcer on the crest of the lower ridge under a new denture.
What is the most likely cause?
options: An occlusal interference, a pressure spot or a sharp underlying bony crest
questions.answerText: Occlusal interference, pressure spot or sharp bone.
questions.why: Crestal ulcers usually come from occlusal or fitting-surface pressure.

questions.stem:
A patient with a severely resorbed mandible has pain and numbness of the lower lip with a new denture.
What is the cause?
options: The denture pressing on the mental nerve
questions.why: In a resorbed mandible the foramen lies near the crest; relieve the fitting surface over it.

questions.stem:
A patient bites his cheeks with new complete dentures. The posterior teeth meet edge to edge.
What is the cause?
questions.why: Edge-to-edge posteriors and low OVD trap the cheek.

questions.stem:
A patient's teeth click together when he talks.
What are the likely causes?
options: Excessive OVD, porcelain teeth or loose dentures
questions.answerText: Excessive OVD, porcelain teeth or loose dentures.
questions.why: Clicking teeth with generalised soreness point to excessive OVD.

questions.stem:
A patient gags with a new upper denture. The posterior border is thick and slightly over-extended.
What is the management?
options: Correct the posterior border, and use a training base, desensitisation or palateless (implant) designs if needed
questions.answerText: Correct the border, then manage the gag reflex.
questions.why: Treat the technical cause first; training bases, desensitisation and palateless implant designs help persistent gaggers.

questions.stem:
A patient complains that food collects under her upper denture.
What is the most likely cause?
options: A poor peripheral seal or under-extension
questions.why: Gaps at the border let food under the denture.

questions.stem:
A denture wearer has a burning sensation under the upper denture.
Which causes should be considered?
options: Denture stomatitis, xerostomia, haematinic deficiency or diabetes, and very rarely monomer allergy
questions.answerText: Stomatitis, xerostomia, deficiency, diabetes, rarely allergy.
questions.why: Investigate local and systemic causes before assuming allergy or a psychological cause.

questions.stem:
An 80-year-old denture wearer has angular cheilitis.
Which factors are most likely to contribute?
options: Low OVD, Candida and haematinic deficiency
questions.why: Angular cheilitis is multifactorial.

questions.stem:
An upper complete denture has a midline fracture. The patient has a large midline torus and natural lower teeth.
What is the failure mechanism?
options: Fatigue from flexure over a midline fulcrum, worsened by opposing natural teeth
questions.why: Flexure over a torus or a poor fit, plus natural opposing teeth, causes midline fatigue fracture.

questions.stem:
The occlusion of newly processed complete dentures is uneven.
What is the most accurate way to correct processing errors?
options: A clinical remount: a new RCP record on the processed dentures, remounted and adjusted on the articulator
Grinding in the mouth by eye
Adding self-cure acrylic to the teeth
questions.why: It corrects processing errors more accurately than adjusting in the mouth.

questions.stem:
An 84-year-old who has worn the same dentures for 15 years needs replacements because they are loose and worn.
Which technique best preserves her adaptation?
options: Copy (replica) dentures, changing only what is necessary
questions.why: They keep the polished and occlusal surfaces the patient has learned, changing only what is needed.

questions.stem:
A patient asks whether an immediate upper denture can be made without a labial flange.
What is the disadvantage of an open-face (socketed) immediate denture?
options: Poor retention, and it cannot be relined labially
It needs more appointments to fit
questions.answerText: Poor retention; cannot be relined labially.
questions.why: Socketed immediates look natural at first but lose the labial seal as the ridge resorbs.

questions.stem:
An immediate upper denture is fitted after extractions.
What is the correct aftercare?
options: Remove it at night from the first day
Leave it in for the first 24 hours, review the next day, and reline at about 3–6 months
questions.answerText: 24 hours in, next-day review, reline at 3–6 months.
questions.why: Rapid early resorption loosens the denture.

questions.stem:
Two lower canines with good support remain under a planned complete lower denture.
How are they prepared as overdenture abutments?
options: Root-filled and reduced to 2–3 mm above the gingiva with domed surfaces
questions.why: This reduces leverage while preserving bone and proprioception; canines are ideal abutments.

questions.stem:
A patient with overdenture abutments asks how to protect them.
What is the key preventive measure?
options: Fluoride gel placed in the fitting surface of the denture, with meticulous hygiene
questions.answerText: Fluoride gel in the denture fitting surface.
questions.why: Caries and periodontitis are the main risks to overdenture abutments.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old with an atrophic mandible has struggled with lower complete dentures.
What do the McGill (2002) and York (2009) consensus statements recommend?
options: A two-implant mandibular overdenture as the minimum standard of care
A conventional denture as the standard
questions.why: This is the minimum standard of care for the edentulous mandible.

questions.stem:
An upper complete denture opposes lower natural anterior teeth and a lower free-end RPD that is rarely worn.
Which are features of combination syndrome (Kelly)?
options: Anterior maxillary resorption with a flabby ridge
Over-eruption of the lower anteriors and resorption under the lower free-end saddles
questions.why: Kelly's combination syndrome includes all these changes.

questions.stem:
You are planning for the patient in the previous question.
How is combination syndrome best prevented?
options: Restoring posterior support (a well-fitting lower RPD) and reducing anterior loading
questions.answerText: Restore posterior support and reduce anterior loading.
questions.why: Unsupported posterior lower segments throw load onto the premaxilla.

questions.stem:
An upper complete denture is needed over a flabby anterior ridge.
Which impression technique is appropriate?
options: A windowed special tray: a compressive material for the firm ridge, then low-viscosity material or plaster over the flabby tissue
questions.why: It records the firm ridge under load and the flabby tissue undisplaced.

questions.stem:
A lab note says a denture was "rebased" rather than "relined".
What is the difference?
options: A rebase adds a thin layer to the fitting surface
A rebase replaces the whole base; a reline adds a new fitting surface
questions.answerText: A rebase replaces the whole base.
questions.why: A reline adds a new fitting surface; a rebase replaces all the base material, keeping the teeth.

questions.stem:
After a closed-mouth laboratory reline, the patient's dentures feel "too tall".
What has likely happened?
options: The patient bit too firmly during the reline impression, increasing the OVD
questions.why: Closed-mouth relines raise the OVD if the patient bites into the material.

questions.stem:
A patient's dentures are unstable because of enlarged tuberosities and a shallow sulcus. Surgery is being considered.
At which level is pre-prosthetic surgery usually provided?
questions.why: Tuberosity reduction, vestibuloplasty and torus removal are usually specialist care.

questions.stem:
A chairside hard reline is planned for a loose lower denture.
What is its main drawback compared with a laboratory reline?
options: It cannot be polished at all
questions.why: Chairside reline is quick but more porous and less durable than a laboratory reline.

questions.stem:
A new lower denture keeps lifting because its lingual flange is over-extended. A colleague suggests adhesive and a higher OVD.
Why is this wrong?
options: Adhesive and OVD changes rarely cure an over-extended flange; correct the border
questions.why: Adhesive or OVD changes rarely cure an over-extended flange.

questions.stem:
A patient with failing complete dentures asks about implants at a Level 2 practice.
What is appropriate?
options: Tell the patient implants are never suitable
Discuss implant-assisted dentures as an option and refer for implant surgery
questions.why: Implant-assisted dentures should be offered; the surgery itself is beyond Level 2.

questions.stem:
At the try-in, only the left posterior teeth contact and the mandible slides on closure.
What does this indicate?
questions.why: Uneven contacts with a slide mean the jaw record is wrong.

questions.stem:
An upper denture was retentive in wax at the try-in but is loose after processing.
Which step is likely to have been missed?
options: Cutting the post-dam on the master cast along the marked vibrating line
questions.why: Without it, polymerisation contraction lifts the posterior border and breaks the seal.

questions.stem:
You use a Fox's plane guide at the jaw registration visit.
What does it check?
options: The occlusal plane against the interpupillary and ala–tragal lines
questions.why: Fox's guide checks the plane against the interpupillary and ala–tragal lines.

questions.stem:
A patient bites his tongue and the lower denture lifts. The lower posterior teeth are set lingual to the ridge crest.
What is the correction?
options: Reset the teeth over the ridge crest, in the neutral zone
questions.why: Teeth encroaching on tongue space trap the tongue and lift the denture.

questions.stem:
An 82-year-old with early dementia has loose but familiar dentures she manages well.
Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.why: Dementia limits adaptation; preserve the familiar shapes.

questions.stem:
A patient needs an upper complete denture against a full natural lower dentition.
Which design feature reduces the risk of fracture?
options: A metal (Co-Cr) or reinforced palate, with balanced contacts
questions.answerText: Metal or reinforced palate with balanced contacts.
questions.why: Natural opposing teeth overload a single denture and cause fatigue fracture.

questions.stem:
A student asks what mechanical retention means for a complete denture.
Which are mechanical retentive factors?
questions.why: These are mechanical, as opposed to physical or muscular, retention.

questions.stem:
With new dentures in, a patient's lips are apart at rest and look strained.
What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Lips that cannot meet at rest look strained.

questions.stem:
A patient has generalised soreness, clicking teeth and no freeway space with new dentures.
What is the definitive management?
options: Leaving them out for a week
Re-establish the OVD with a new jaw record and reset or remake the dentures
questions.answerText: New jaw record, then reset or remake.
questions.why: Excessive OVD can only be cured by re-establishing the correct vertical relation.

questions.stem:
A patient who had an immediate denture fitted removed it the same evening and now cannot reinsert it.
Why should an immediate denture be left in for 24 hours?
options: It acts as a splint and limits swelling
questions.answerText: It acts as a splint and limits swelling.
questions.why: Once swelling develops, reinsertion may be impossible.

questions.stem:
A 75-year-old, edentulous for 20 years, has a severely resorbed mandible and has failed with several well-made lower dentures.
What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Assessment and referral for a two-implant overdenture
questions.why: It is the minimum standard for the failing edentulous mandible.

questions.stem:
An edentulous patient asks whether she still needs dental check-ups.
What is the correct advice?
options: Yes: regular review of the oral mucosa and denture fit
No; edentulous patients need no recall
questions.why: Edentulous patients still need oral cancer screening, and their dentures loosen over time.

questions.stem:
Three weeks after new dentures, a patient says they are secure except with very fibrous food. Examination finds no fault.
What is the best response?
options: Explain realistic expectations and the adaptation period
questions.why: Denture wearers chew far less efficiently than dentate people; with no fault found, counselling is appropriate.

questions.stem:
You are selecting the mould of the upper anterior teeth.
Which anatomical guides help choose the width of the six anterior teeth?
options: The canine lines and inter-alar width
questions.why: They estimate the width of the six upper anterior teeth.

questions.stem:
A laboratory asks which articulator to use for routine complete dentures.
What is usually adequate?
options: A fully adjustable articulator with a kinematic facebow
questions.why: It is adequate for most complete dentures.

questions.stem:
A student asks which articulator uses a Bonwill triangle with sides of about 10 cm.
What is the answer?
questions.why: It uses a Bonwill triangle of about 10 cm and fixed condylar guidance of about 30°.

questions.stem:
You write the laboratory prescription for new complete dentures.
What should it include?
options: The post-dam and any relief areas
questions.why: The prescription specifies mould, shade, occlusal scheme, post-dam and relief.

questions.stem:
A colleague prepares a vital upper central incisor of a 22-year-old for an all-ceramic crown with 2.5 mm of axial reduction.
Which Shillingburg principle has been neglected?
options: Preservation of tooth structure and the pulp
questions.answerText: Preservation of tooth structure and the pulp.
questions.why: Excessive reduction on a young vital tooth risks pulpal damage. Shillingburg's other principles are retention and resistance, structural durability and preservation of the periodontium.

questions.stem:
You assess the convergence of a molar crown preparation.
What total occlusal convergence is typical and acceptable clinically?
questions.why: About 6° is the theoretical ideal; 10–20° is typical clinically. Retention falls sharply as convergence increases.

questions.stem:
A lower molar preparation is only 2.5 mm high after reduction.
What minimum axial wall heights are usually recommended?
options: About 3 mm for incisors and premolars, 4 mm for molars
questions.answerText: 3 mm for incisors and premolars; 4 mm for molars.
questions.why: Shorter walls lack resistance to tipping forces.

questions.stem:
A wide molar preparation is short.
Which ratio improves resistance form?
questions.why: Wide, short preparations rotate off easily; this ratio improves resistance.

questions.stem:
A crown on a short, tapered molar preparation keeps coming off.
What can improve retention and resistance?
options: Grooves or boxes, an adhesive cement, or crown lengthening
questions.answerText: Grooves or boxes, adhesive cement or crown lengthening.
questions.why: These add resistance and surface area; more cement or taper does not.

questions.stem:
You are preparing a vital molar for a crown.
Which measures protect the pulp?
options: Sharp burs, copious water spray, light intermittent pressure, avoiding desiccation and well-fitting temporaries
Leaving the tooth without a temporary
questions.answerText: Sharp burs, water, light pressure, no desiccation, good temporaries.
questions.why: Heat, desiccation and leakage injure the pulp.

questions.stem:
You prepare a lower molar for a full gold crown.
Where is the functional cusp bevel placed?
options: Buccal cusps of lower molars (and palatal cusps of upper molars)
questions.answerText: Lower buccal and upper palatal cusps.
questions.why: The functional (supporting) cusps need a bevel so the restoration has bulk where it is loaded.

questions.stem:
You plan a full-coverage cast metal crown on 36.
What reduction and margin are appropriate?
options: 3 mm occlusal reduction and a shoulder
0.5 mm occlusal reduction and a knife edge
2 mm occlusal reduction and a heavy chamfer
1.5 mm on functional and 1 mm on non-functional cusps, with a light chamfer margin
questions.answerText: 1.5 mm functional, 1 mm non-functional, light chamfer.
questions.why: Gold is strong in thin section, so less reduction is needed.

questions.stem:
You prepare 21 for a metal–ceramic crown.
What margin design is typical?
options: Labial shoulder (with or without a bevel) or heavy chamfer; lingual chamfer
questions.answerText: Labial shoulder or heavy chamfer; lingual chamfer.
questions.why: The labial margin must give space for metal, opaque and porcelain.

questions.stem:
You prepare 11 for a lithium disilicate crown.
What margin is typical?
options: Bevelled shoulder with sharp internal angles
Rounded shoulder or deep chamfer of about 1 mm, with rounded internal angles
questions.answerText: Rounded shoulder or deep chamfer of about 1 mm.
questions.why: Ceramics need even thickness and rounded internal angles to avoid stress concentration.

questions.stem:
You prepare 12 for a porcelain veneer.
How deep is the labial reduction?
questions.why: Bonding to enamel is the key to veneer survival.

questions.stem:
You are deciding where to place the margin of a molar crown with no aesthetic concern.
Where is it best placed?
questions.why: Supragingival margins are easier to clean, record, finish and inspect.

questions.stem:
You plan a subgingival margin on 21 for aesthetics.
How far should it stay from the bone crest?
options: About 3 mm (a supracrestal attachment of about 2 mm plus the sulcus)
questions.why: The supracrestal attachment averages about 2 mm (Gargiulo), plus the sulcus.

questions.stem:
A crown margin placed 1 mm from the bone crest has caused chronic gingival inflammation.
What has happened?
options: Invasion of the supracrestal tissue attachment, causing chronic inflammation, recession or bone loss
questions.why: It causes chronic inflammation, recession or bone loss.

questions.stem:
A crown on 46 is bulbous at its buccal furcation area, and the gingiva bleeds.
What is the cause?
options: Overcontour trapping plaque; emergence profiles should be flat
questions.why: Emergence profiles should be flat, especially over furcations.

questions.stem:
You need gingival retraction for 24 in a patient with poorly controlled hypertension.
Which retraction medicament should be avoided?
questions.why: Systemic absorption can raise blood pressure; use aluminium chloride, ferric sulphate or plain cord.

questions.stem:
A student asks why provisional crowns are needed.
What are their purposes?
options: To protect the pulp, keep tooth position, protect the gingiva, restore function and appearance, and test the planned shape or OVD
Only to keep the patient happy
questions.answerText: Pulp, position, gingiva, function and testing.
questions.why: Provisionals also let you trial the planned shape, OVD or occlusion.

questions.stem:
You make chairside provisional crowns.
Which material is commonly used, and why?
options: Bis-acryl composite, for its low exotherm and good strength
questions.why: It has a low exotherm and good strength; PMMA is stronger long-term but hotter and has more monomer.

questions.stem:
A lithium disilicate crown will be resin-bonded next week.
Which temporary cement should be used now?
questions.why: Eugenol inhibits polymerisation of the later resin cement.

questions.stem:
You are restoring a single crown on 36 in a patient with a stable, comfortable ICP.
Which occlusal approach is appropriate?
options: Conformative: restore to the existing ICP
questions.why: Single units and short bridges are restored to the existing ICP.

questions.stem:
Extensive restoration is planned with a change of OVD, and the ICP is unstable.
Which approach and level apply?
questions.why: An unstable ICP, extensive work or an OVD change needs a reorganised approach in RCP.

questions.stem:
You need a shade for a crown on 11.
When should the shade be taken?
options: Before preparation, because teeth dehydrate and lighten during treatment
questions.why: Teeth dehydrate and lighten during treatment, so later shades are too light.

questions.stem:
You are choosing a shade for an anterior crown.
Which dimension of colour is most important?
questions.why: Brightness errors are the most noticeable.

questions.stem:
A colleague takes a dual-arch (triple) tray impression for a 4-unit bridge.
Why is this inappropriate?
options: Dual-arch trays suit single units with stable intercuspation only
questions.answerText: Single units with stable intercuspation only.
questions.why: Dual-arch trays flex and cannot record longer spans accurately.

questions.stem:
The laboratory applies die spacer to the die.
What thickness is typical, and where does it stop?
options: About 20–40 µm, stopping short of the margin
questions.why: It gives room for cement without opening the margin.

questions.stem:
A lower first molar has had root canal treatment and has an MOD cavity.
What restoration improves survival?
questions.why: Sorensen and Martinoff showed much better survival for root-filled posterior teeth with cusp coverage.

questions.stem:
An upper central incisor has had root canal treatment through a small access cavity, with little other tissue loss.
What restoration is appropriate?
options: A composite restoration of the access cavity
questions.why: Anterior root-filled teeth with little tissue loss need no crown or post.

questions.stem:
A root-filled lower molar has a large pulp chamber and adequate remaining walls.
How can the core be retained without a post?
options: A Nayyar core (amalgam or composite retained in the pulp chamber)
questions.why: The pulp chamber retains an amalgam or composite core without a post.

questions.stem:
A molar has just had root canal treatment and will be crowned in 3 months.
What is important meanwhile?
options: A good coronal seal placed promptly, because coronal leakage contributes to failure
questions.why: Coronal leakage contributes to root canal failure.

questions.stem:
A root-filled upper premolar has no ferrule above the bone.
Which option can create a ferrule?
options: Surgical crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion, with appropriate specialist input
questions.why: A ferrule needs sound tooth above the bone; posts cannot replace it.

questions.stem:
A student mixes up bridge terms.
What is a retainer?
options: The restoration on the abutment tooth that holds the bridge
questions.why: The abutment is the tooth, the pontic the replacement, the connector the joint.

questions.stem:
You assess possible bridge abutments.
Which root form makes the best abutment?
options: Long roots, and divergent multi-rooted forms
questions.why: These give more support than conical or fused roots.

questions.stem:
A student quotes Ante's law.
What does it state?
options: The pontic should be wider than the abutment
Bridges should be no longer than three units
The total root surface area of the abutments should equal or exceed that of the teeth being replaced
questions.answerText: Abutment root area at least that of the replaced teeth.
questions.why: That is Ante's law.

questions.stem:
An examiner asks about the status of Ante's law.
What is correct?
options: It is supported by strong trial evidence
It is historical and not well supported by evidence, though still examined
questions.why: Ante's law is still examined but lacks good evidence.

questions.stem:
You are choosing a single-rooted upper abutment for a cantilever.
Which single-rooted upper tooth has the largest root surface area?
questions.why: The upper canine has the largest root of the single-rooted teeth.

questions.stem:
A bridge span is doubled in length with the same connectors.
How does its deflection change?
questions.why: Deflection increases with the cube of span length.

questions.stem:
A technician doubles the occlusogingival height of a bridge connector.
How does deflection change?
questions.why: Deflection decreases with the cube of connector thickness.

questions.stem:
A bridge replaces all four upper incisors between the canines.
What extra mechanical problem does arch curvature create?
options: The pontics lie outside the line joining the abutments and act as a lever arm
questions.why: Pontics outside the line between abutments tip the bridge labially.

questions.stem:
A fixed-fixed conventional bridge is planned between two heavily restored abutments.
What is a recognised drawback of this design?
options: The most tooth destruction, the need for parallel preparations, and a loose retainer may go unnoticed
It cannot be used for bounded spans
questions.answerText: Most destruction, parallel preparations, unnoticed loose retainer.
questions.why: These are the drawbacks of a fixed-fixed design.

questions.stem:
A young patient has lost 12; 13 is sound with a long root.
Which conventional design is suitable?
questions.why: A long-rooted canine supporting a lateral incisor pontic is a classic cantilever.

questions.stem:
You are designing a cantilever bridge.
What rules apply?
options: The pontic should be no larger than the abutment; avoid long or posterior distal cantilevers
The pontic should be larger than the abutment
questions.answerText: Pontic no larger than the abutment; avoid long posterior distal cantilevers.
questions.why: Cantilevers torque their abutment.

questions.stem:
47 is tilted mesially and will be the distal abutment of a bridge replacing 46, with 45 as the mesial abutment.
Which design avoids the need for parallel preparations?
options: A conventional fixed-fixed with deeper preparations
questions.why: A movable joint avoids preparing non-parallel abutments to a single path.

questions.stem:
You design a fixed-movable bridge.
Where is the keyway placed?
options: In the mesial of the distal retainer
In the distal of the mesial (minor) retainer, so mesial drift seats the key
questions.why: Mesial drift then seats the key.

questions.stem:
A student describes an old bridge with a palatal bar from a premolar to a distant incisor pontic.
What is it, and why is it rarely used?
options: A spring cantilever; the palatal bar is unhygienic
questions.why: It is historic and rarely used now.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old has lost 22. 23 is unrestored with plenty of enamel, and the occlusion is favourable.
What is usually the first choice?
questions.why: It is first choice for a single missing incisor or premolar with sound abutments.

questions.stem:
A two-winged fixed-fixed resin-bonded bridge has been in place for 4 years. The patient reports a bad taste.
What is the likely problem?
options: Differential movement has debonded one wing unnoticed, leading to caries
questions.why: Differential movement between two wings leads to caries; single-wing designs perform better.

questions.stem:
A bridge has a conventional retainer at one end and a resin-bonded retainer at the other.
What is this design called, and what joint is usually used?
options: Hybrid bridge; usually a movable joint
questions.answerText: Hybrid bridge, usually with a movable joint.
questions.why: It combines a conventional retainer at one end with a resin-bonded retainer at the other.

questions.stem:
A five-unit bridge from 13 to 17 has a pier abutment at 15. One terminal retainer keeps debonding.
Why, and what is the solution?
options: The span is too short; add a pontic
The pier acts as a fulcrum; use a non-rigid connector at the pier or separate bridges
questions.answerText: The pier acts as a fulcrum.
questions.why: Use a non-rigid connector at the pier, or separate bridges.

questions.stem:
A patient asks why a resin-bonded bridge is recommended over a conventional bridge.
What are its advantages?
options: Minimal or no preparation and no anaesthesia
Reversible and quicker, with the pulp not at risk
questions.why: RBBs are minimally invasive, reversible, quick, safe for the pulp and usually rebondable.

questions.stem:
A resin-bonded wing is planned on 23 but the occlusion is tight.
How much clearance does a Co-Cr wing need, and how can it be gained without preparation?
options: About 0.7 mm; using a Dahl approach
About 2 mm; by extracting the opposing tooth
About 0.1 mm; by grinding the wing thin
questions.answerText: About 0.7 mm, by a Dahl approach.
questions.why: Placing the wing at a slightly raised occlusion lets the teeth re-establish contact, avoiding preparation.

questions.stem:
You are designing a resin-bonded cantilever bridge from 13 replacing 12.
Which design features improve its success?
options: A thin wing covering the minimum enamel
Maximum enamel coverage within aesthetic limits, about 180° wraparound, a cingulum rest and minimal preparation for a path
questions.answerText: Maximum enamel coverage, wraparound, a rest and minimal preparation.
questions.why: These maximise the bond area and give resistance and a defined path.

questions.stem:
You are cementing a Co-Cr resin-bonded bridge wing.
What is the correct bonding protocol?
options: Air-abrade the metal (50 µm alumina), etch the enamel, and use an MDP-containing resin cement under rubber dam
questions.answerText: Air-abrade, etch enamel, MDP resin, rubber dam.
questions.why: MDP bonds chemically to the base-metal oxide; isolation protects the bond.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old bruxist with heavy anterior contacts asks for a resin-bonded bridge replacing 21.
What is the main concern?
options: Bruxism and heavy occlusion make debonding more likely
questions.why: They are the main risk factors for debonding.

questions.stem:
A single-wing resin-bonded bridge debonds after 3 years. The wing and pontic are intact and the abutment is sound.
What is the usual management?
questions.why: RBBs fail safely; an intact bridge on a sound abutment can be rebonded.

questions.stem:
A pontic is needed for 46 in a patient with no aesthetic concern.
Which pontic design is most hygienic?
options: Sanitary (hygienic), with no ridge contact and at least a 3 mm gap
questions.why: A gap of at least 3 mm suits lower posterior, non-aesthetic sites.

questions.stem:
A pontic replaces 14 in a patient who smiles broadly.
Which design balances appearance and hygiene?
options: Modified ridge lap, contacting the labial side of the ridge only
questions.why: Labial contact only balances appearance and hygiene in upper anterior and premolar sites.

questions.stem:
A patient with a thick ridge after socket preservation wants the most natural emergence for a 21 pontic.
Which pontic is indicated?
options: Ovate, sitting in a concavity in the ridge
questions.why: It gives the most natural emergence but needs a thick ridge or socket preservation.

questions.stem:
A bridge has a concave pontic covering the whole ridge, and the mucosa beneath is inflamed.
What is this pontic, and why has it failed?
options: A saddle (ridge lap) pontic; it is unhygienic
An ovate pontic; it is too small
A sanitary pontic; it traps food
A modified ridge lap; it is too narrow
A conical pontic; it is too short
questions.why: Its concave surface cannot be cleaned and causes inflammation.

questions.stem:
You check a new bridge pontic at try-in.
How should its tissue surface relate to the mucosa?
options: It should press hard enough to blanch the mucosa
Convex, smooth and glazed or highly polished, without pressing on the mucosa
Separated by 1 mm in the aesthetic zone
questions.answerText: Convex, smooth, glazed or polished; no pressure.
questions.why: Blanching pressure causes inflammation under fixed pontics.

questions.stem:
A posterior bridge is planned for a patient with heavy occlusal forces.
How can load on the pontic be reduced?
options: Narrow the buccolingual width of the pontic
questions.why: A narrower table reduces load on the abutments.

questions.stem:
A three-unit all-ceramic bridge fractures.
Where is the failure most likely?
questions.why: Connectors are the weakest point of all-ceramic bridges.

questions.stem:
A lithium disilicate bridge is planned from 13 to 15 replacing 14.
What is the minimum connector cross-section, and how far back can such a bridge extend?
options: About 16 mm² in the premolar region; three units, no further back than the second premolar
questions.answerText: About 16 mm² premolar; three units to the second premolar.
questions.why: Lithium disilicate bridges are limited in length and position; anterior connectors need about 12 mm².

questions.stem:
A three-unit posterior zirconia bridge is planned.
What approximate minimum connector cross-section is needed?
questions.why: That is for a three-unit posterior zirconia bridge; longer spans need more.

questions.stem:
A technician can enlarge a connector either in height or in width.
Which matters more, and why?
options: Width, because strength rises with the cube of width
Height, because strength rises with the square of height and deflection falls with its cube
questions.why: Strength rises with height squared and deflection falls with height cubed.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old has tetracycline staining that has not responded to bleaching and wants better-looking teeth.
Which indication supports porcelain veneers?
questions.why: That is a classic indication, with diastema closure, shape change and minor malalignment.

questions.stem:
A patient asks for veneers on her upper incisors.
Which finding contraindicates them?
options: Bruxism with an edge-to-edge incisor relationship
A request for minor shape change
questions.why: Heavy occlusion and edge-to-edge or Class III relationships fracture or debond veneers.

questions.stem:
You are choosing a preparation design for upper incisor veneers.
Which design is most common, for stress distribution and seating?
options: Incisal overlap with a palatal finish line
questions.answerText: Incisal overlap with a palatal finish line.
questions.why: It distributes stress and gives a positive seat.

questions.stem:
You are fitting feldspathic porcelain veneers.
What is the bonding protocol?
options: HF-etched, silanated ceramic and light-cured resin cement on etched enamel
questions.answerText: HF, silane, light-cured resin on etched enamel.
questions.why: This is the standard protocol for silica-based veneers.

questions.stem:
A lower first premolar has an MOD restoration, and its buccal cusp is less than half as wide as it is high.
What restoration is indicated?
questions.why: A cusp narrower than half its height is weak and needs protection.

questions.stem:
You prepare a cavity for a gold inlay.
How should the walls be shaped?
options: Diverging occlusally by about 6–10°, with no undercuts
questions.why: An intracoronal restoration needs a path of withdrawal.

questions.stem:
You write a laboratory prescription for a metal–ceramic bridge.
What must it contain?
options: Patient and clinician details, materials, design, shade, margin, pontic form, connector type and the delivery date
questions.answerText: All details of patient, clinician, materials and design.
questions.why: The prescription is a legal document.

questions.stem:
A crown arrives from the laboratory.
What regulatory documentation should accompany it?
options: A statement of manufacture, from a manufacturer registered with the MHRA
questions.answerText: Statement of manufacture from an MHRA-registered manufacturer.
questions.why: Custom-made devices fall under the UK Medical Devices Regulations; keep the records.

questions.stem:
A dental technician asks whether she must register with a professional regulator.
Who regulates dental technicians and clinical dental technicians?
questions.why: Technicians and clinical dental technicians are GDC registrants with their own scope of practice.

questions.stem:
A patient asks for a "Hollywood smile".
In what order should the smile be analysed?
options: From outside inward: face and midline, lips and smile line, incisal display and plane, then tooth proportions, shade and gingival contour
questions.why: Face and lips set the frame before teeth and gingiva are judged.

questions.stem:
A colleague insists every anterior restoration must follow the golden proportion.
What is correct?
options: It always applies to natural smiles
It is not a mandatory rule for a natural smile
questions.why: The golden proportion is not a natural-smile rule.

questions.stem:
A 25-year-old has a single darkened, root-filled upper incisor and asks for a crown.
What should be considered first?
options: Investigating the cause, then non-vital (internal) bleaching
questions.why: Least invasive first: whitening before any preparation.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old has white-spot lesions on the labial surfaces of the upper incisors after orthodontics.
What is the least invasive option?
questions.why: These treat white spots without preparation.

questions.stem:
A 17-year-old has peg-shaped upper lateral incisors after orthodontic space redistribution.
What is the most conservative restorative option?
questions.why: It is the most conservative option for peg laterals and spacing.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old has crowded, rotated upper incisors and wants them "straightened" with crowns.
What should be offered first?
options: Orthodontics, before any elective tooth preparation
questions.why: Malalignment is corrected before any elective tooth preparation.

questions.stem:
A patient insists on porcelain veneers for her upper incisors.
What should be done before any preparation?
options: A diagnostic wax-up and mock-up, assessment of enamel, parafunction and overbite, and a discussion of irreversibility and replacement
questions.why: Veneers are irreversible and will need replacing; test the result and discuss risks first.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old with sound, healthy upper incisors wants crowns because one is slightly darker.
Why are crowns inappropriate?
options: They are less conservative than whitening, orthodontics or composite, which can meet the aim
Crowns are illegal for aesthetic reasons
questions.why: Crowning sound teeth for a minor concern is a classic trap.

questions.stem:
At a 5-year review, a bridge is still in place but has recurrent caries and recession.
How should its outcome be described?
options: It has survived but is not a success
A failure, because it is present
questions.why: Success includes biological health, function and satisfaction, not just presence.

questions.stem:
A heavy bruxist needs a posterior crown.
How does parafunction influence the plan?
options: It favours monolithic materials and protective measures such as a night guard
questions.why: Layered ceramics chip under parafunction.

questions.stem:
A patient needs crowns or bridges on most teeth with an OVD increase.
At what level is this care?
questions.why: Full-mouth reconstruction with OVD change is specialist care.

questions.stem:
A patient with uncontrolled hypertension needs gingival retraction before an impression.
Which retraction method should be avoided?
questions.why: Systemic absorption can raise blood pressure.

questions.stem:
You are taking a shade for 11 in a busy surgery.
Which conditions improve accuracy?
options: Under the operating light, after preparation
In colour-corrected daylight, quickly, with photographs of shade tabs sent to the laboratory
questions.why: Eye fatigue and poor lighting distort shade; photos with tabs help the laboratory.

questions.stem:
A colleague plans to scan a full arch digitally for a 10-unit bridge.
Which statement about intraoral scans is correct?
options: They are most accurate for full arches
questions.why: Stitching errors accumulate across full arches.

questions.stem:
A patient with a 3-unit fixed-fixed bridge notices a bad taste. One retainer has come loose but the bridge has not fallen out.
What is the main risk?
questions.why: A partly debonded fixed-fixed bridge stays in place while leakage causes caries.

questions.stem:
A lower first molar has had root canal treatment and has an MOD cavity with thin cusps.
What is the appropriate restoration?
options: Cuspal coverage with an onlay or crown
questions.why: Root-filled posterior teeth with MOD cavities need cusp protection.

questions.stem:
You are choosing between an inlay, an onlay and a crown for a premolar with a large cavity.
Which statement is correct?
options: A crown always preserves most tooth
An adhesive onlay preserves more tooth than a crown while covering the cusps
questions.answerText: An adhesive onlay preserves more tooth.
questions.why: It covers cusps without full-coverage reduction.

questions.stem:
You are assessing the lower anterior teeth as abutments.
Which lower tooth has the smallest root surface area?
questions.why: In the mandible, root surface area runs 6 > 7 > 3 > 5 ≈ 4 > 2 > 1.

questions.stem:
46 is missing. 45 is upright, but 47 has tipped mesially by 25°.
Which approach is appropriate?
options: A fixed-fixed bridge with parallel preparations through 47
A fixed-movable bridge, or uprighting 47 orthodontically
questions.why: A tilted abutment cannot share a single path with an upright one.

questions.stem:
A patient wants 46 replaced by a cantilever pontic from 45 alone. He has a heavy bite.
What is the best advice?
options: Avoid it; long or posterior distal cantilevers torque the abutment
questions.why: Under heavy load it torques the single abutment.

questions.stem:
A rigid bridge from 13 to 17 (14 and 16 missing) has repeatedly debonded at 13.
What is the design problem and solution?
options: 15 acts as a pier fulcrum; use a non-rigid connector at the pier or separate bridges
questions.why: A rigid bridge rocks over the pier and debonds the terminal retainers.

questions.stem:
A patient with a deep overbite and bruxism requests upper incisor veneers.
What is the best response?
options: Explain that heavy occlusion contraindicates veneers, and discuss alternatives
questions.why: Discuss alternatives rather than proceeding.

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old finishes orthodontics with small lateral incisors and spaces, and growth is ongoing.
What is the preferred restoration?
questions.why: It is reversible and suits a young patient who is still growing.

questions.stem:
A patient has just finished whitening and wants composite bonding the next day.
Why should you wait?
options: The shade may still change and residual oxygen reduces the resin bond for a time
Composite cannot be used after whitening
There is no reason to wait
questions.answerText: Shade change and reduced bond strength.
questions.why: Residual oxygen after bleaching inhibits resin polymerisation for a period, and the shade settles.

questions.stem:
You use a double-cord technique before an impression for 21.
What is its purpose?
options: The first cord controls fluid and the second displaces the tissue until just before the impression
questions.why: The deep cord stays in; the upper cord is removed just before the impression.

questions.stem:
A crown on 36 is overcontoured buccally over the furcation, and the gingiva there is chronically inflamed.
What is the definitive solution?
options: Recontour or remake the crown with a flat emergence profile
questions.answerText: Recontour or remake with a flat emergence.
questions.why: The cause is the crown contour; mouthwash and antibiotics only mask it.

questions.stem:
You review a 5-year-old bridge.
What should be checked?
questions.why: Recall covers biological, technical and patient-reported outcomes.

questions.stem:
A student is asked to define ICP.
Which definition is correct?
options: The first contact on the retruded arc
The position of the mandible at rest
The condyles in their most superior position
Maximum intercuspation of the teeth, independent of condylar position
The position used for complete dentures
questions.answerText: Maximum intercuspation, independent of condylar position.
questions.why: ICP is defined by the teeth, not the joints.

questions.stem:
You guide a patient's mandible along the terminal hinge arc until the first tooth contact.
What position is this?
questions.why: RCP is the first tooth contact on the retruded (terminal hinge) arc.

questions.stem:
A colleague talks about recording centric relation.
What is centric relation?
options: A jaw-to-jaw relation with the condyles in their most superior-anterior position against the eminence, discs correctly interposed, independent of the teeth
questions.answerText: A jaw-to-jaw relation with condyles superior-anterior.
questions.why: Centric relation is independent of the teeth.

questions.stem:
On guiding a patient into RCP, you find a slide into ICP.
What is normal?
options: A slide occurs in fewer than 10% of people
A slide must always be eliminated
A slide of about 1 mm forwards occurs in about 90% of people
questions.why: A slide is normal and needs no treatment by itself.

questions.stem:
You measure a dentate patient's rest position.
What is the normal freeway space?
questions.why: The freeway space is the gap between rest position and occlusion.

questions.stem:
In right lateral excursion, only the right canines contact.
What is this guidance called?
questions.why: Only the canines contact on the working side and disclude all other teeth.

questions.stem:
In left lateral excursion, the left canine, premolars and mesiobuccal cusp of the first molar all contact.
What is this guidance called?
questions.why: Several working-side teeth share the load.

questions.stem:
A textbook describes an occlusion in which the anterior teeth protect the posteriors in excursions, and the posteriors protect the anteriors in ICP.
What is this?
questions.why: Anteriors protect posteriors in excursions; posteriors protect anteriors in ICP.

questions.stem:
In right lateral excursion, the left second molars contact heavily.
What is this and when is it desirable?
options: A non-working (balancing) interference; it is damaging in natural dentitions and desirable only in complete dentures
questions.why: It is most damaging in natural dentitions; desirable only in complete dentures (balanced occlusion).

questions.stem:
In right lateral excursion, the right first molars contact before the right canine.
What is this?
questions.why: A posterior contact prevents canine or group guidance on the working side.

questions.stem:
On closing, a contact on 17 diverts the mandible forward and sideways.
What is this?
questions.why: It diverts the mandible from its normal path of closure.

questions.stem:
A technician needs the angle of the non-working condyle path to the sagittal plane.
What is this, and its typical value?
questions.why: It is the angle of the non-working condyle path to the sagittal plane.

questions.stem:
You inspect the mediolateral curvature of the posterior occlusal plane.
What is it called?
questions.why: Wilson is mediolateral; Spee is anteroposterior.

questions.stem:
A patient's maximum mouth opening is 34 mm.
How should this be interpreted?
questions.why: Normal maximum opening is about 40–55 mm; under 40 mm is restricted.

questions.stem:
You record mandibular movements.
What are typical lateral excursion and protrusion ranges?
questions.why: Those are typical lateral excursion and protrusion ranges.

questions.stem:
A patient opens with pure hinge rotation of the condyles before translation.
About how much incisal opening does pure rotation give?
questions.why: Further opening needs condylar translation.

questions.stem:
You review the features of an "ideal" functional occlusion before restoration.
Which features apply?
options: A stable ICP with even, simultaneous contacts
Anterior guidance discluding the posteriors, with no non-working interferences
questions.why: These are the features of a functional ("ideal") occlusion.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old has aching cheeks, worse in the morning, and familiar pain when the masseters are palpated. Joint movements are painless.
What is the DC/TMD diagnosis?
questions.why: Familiar pain on palpating the masticatory muscles; it is the commonest TMD.

questions.stem:
A patient has pain localised to the left TMJ on palpation and when moving the jaw.
What is the DC/TMD diagnosis?
questions.why: Pain from the joint itself on palpation or movement.

questions.stem:
A patient has a click on opening and another on closing (reciprocal clicking), without pain or locking.
What is the DC/TMD diagnosis?
questions.why: A reciprocal click shows the disc is recaptured on opening.

questions.stem:
A patient has reciprocal clicking and occasional brief episodes when the jaw catches and will not open fully.
What is the DC/TMD diagnosis?
options: Disc displacement without reduction, with limited opening
Disc displacement with reduction, with intermittent locking
questions.why: Clicking plus episodes of limited opening.

questions.stem:
A patient's click stopped suddenly a week ago. She now opens 28 mm, deviating to the right, with restricted left lateral movement.
What is the diagnosis?
options: Disc displacement without reduction, with limited opening (right closed lock)
questions.answerText: DDwoR with limited opening (right closed lock).
questions.why: Opening under 40 mm, deflection to the affected side and restricted contralateral excursion.

questions.stem:
A patient had a closed lock 2 years ago. She now opens 44 mm without clicking.
What is the diagnosis?
options: Disc displacement without reduction, without limited opening
questions.why: A history of lock, now opening 40 mm or more.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old has crepitus in both TMJs, and a radiograph shows flattening and osteophytes on the condyles.
What is the diagnosis?
questions.why: Crepitus with radiographic change.

questions.stem:
After a wide yawn, a patient cannot close her mouth. The condyles are palpable in front of the eminences.
What is the diagnosis?
questions.why: The condyle is trapped anterior to the eminence and the patient cannot close.

questions.stem:
A patient has temporal headaches that worsen with chewing and are reproduced by palpating the temporalis.
What is the DC/TMD diagnosis?
questions.why: Temporal headache modified by jaw function.

questions.stem:
A patient asks whether her "bad bite" caused her TMD.
What is the current understanding of TMD aetiology?
options: It is multifactorial and biopsychosocial; occlusal factors have only a weak association
It is always caused by trauma
questions.why: Parafunction, trauma, stress, sleep and widespread pain contribute; occlusion has only a weak association.

questions.stem:
You are taking the history of a patient with TMD.
In which group is TMD commonest?
questions.why: That is the commonest demographic.

questions.stem:
A 25-year-old has a painless click on opening, with no locking or limitation.
What is the appropriate management?
questions.why: A click without pain or locking needs no treatment.

questions.stem:
A patient with masticatory myalgia asks what she can do herself.
Which self-care advice is appropriate?
options: Chew gum to exercise the muscles
A soft diet, avoiding wide opening and gum, warm compresses, jaw rest, and keeping "lips together, teeth apart"
Open as wide as possible several times a day
questions.answerText: Soft diet, jaw rest, warm compresses, habit control.
questions.why: Self-care is first-line and most TMD is self-limiting.

questions.stem:
A stabilisation splint is planned for a patient with myalgia.
Which design is correct?
options: Partial-coverage anterior bite plane worn continuously
Full-coverage hard acrylic (often maxillary), with even contacts in RCP and canine guidance
questions.answerText: Full-coverage hard acrylic with even RCP contacts and canine guidance.
questions.why: That is a stabilisation (Michigan-type) splint.

questions.stem:
A patient wants a soft splint for jaw pain because it is cheaper.
What is the concern?
options: They are for short-term use and may increase clenching in some patients
questions.why: Soft splints are not for long-term myalgia management.

questions.stem:
A patient has worn an anterior repositioning splint day and night for 9 months for a clicking joint.
What complication is likely?
questions.why: Long-term anterior repositioning changes the occlusion irreversibly.

questions.stem:
A patient has worn an anterior bite plane continuously for a year.
What complication may follow?
options: Over-eruption of the uncovered posterior teeth
questions.why: Partial-coverage appliances worn continuously let uncovered teeth erupt.

questions.stem:
A patient's left TMJ locked 2 days ago, with sudden loss of clicking and restricted opening.
What might be tried first?
options: Manipulation to try to recapture the disc, with reassurance, a splint and exercises
questions.why: A recent closed lock may be reduced; otherwise reassure, splint and exercise.

questions.stem:
A patient's jaw dislocates during an extraction. The condyles are anterior to the eminences.
How is it reduced?
options: Press the mandible downwards and backwards, with the thumbs on the lower molars or external oblique ridges
Ask the patient to bite hard
questions.why: This lowers the condyle below the eminence and guides it back into the fossa; then advise limited opening.

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old has new jaw pain on chewing that eases with rest, temporal headaches and a tender scalp.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Same-day medical referral for suspected giant cell arteritis (urgent ESR or CRP)
Ibuprofen and review in a month
questions.answerText: Same-day referral for giant cell arteritis.
questions.why: Jaw claudication over age 50 risks sight; ESR and CRP are urgent.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old has progressive trismus, numbness of the lower lip, unexplained weight loss and earache with a normal ear examination.
What must be excluded?
options: Malignancy (for example nasopharyngeal, parotid or infratemporal)
questions.why: Progressive trismus, numbness, weight loss and referred otalgia are red flags.

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old has jaw ache that comes on when climbing stairs and settles with rest.
What must be considered?
options: Cardiac pain referred to the jaw
questions.why: Exertional jaw pain can be angina.

questions.stem:
A patient has brief, electric-shock pains in the right cheek triggered by light touch when shaving.
What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?
options: Trigeminal neuralgia; carbamazepine via the GMP or a specialist
questions.why: Paroxysmal electric-shock pain triggered by light touch is characteristic.

questions.stem:
A colleague offers selective occlusal grinding to "cure" a patient's TMD.
What is the evidence position?
options: It is irreversible and not an evidence-based TMD treatment
questions.why: Selective grinding is not a TMD treatment.

questions.stem:
A patient's myofascial pain persists after 6 months of self-care, splint therapy and physiotherapy.
Which secondary-care options exist?
options: Arthrocentesis or arthroscopy for joint disorders
questions.why: Secondary care offers tricyclics, botulinum toxin, arthrocentesis, arthroscopy and surgery.

questions.stem:
A patient's chronic TMD pain persists despite conservative care.
Who would usually start low-dose tricyclic medication?
questions.why: Low-dose tricyclics are prescribed medically, not by the dentist routinely.

questions.stem:
You examine a patient who says she grinds her teeth.
Which signs suggest bruxism?
options: Attrition facets, fractured restorations and cusps, masseteric hypertrophy, a scalloped tongue and linea alba
questions.answerText: Attrition, fractures, masseteric hypertrophy, scalloped tongue, linea alba.
questions.why: These are the classic signs of bruxism.

questions.stem:
A known bruxist needs new posterior crowns.
How should the new work be protected?
options: A hard night-time splint, with metal or monolithic zirconia occlusal surfaces
questions.answerText: A hard night splint with metal or monolithic zirconia.
questions.why: Layered porcelain chips under parafunction.

questions.stem:
Multiple posterior crowns are planned.
What should precede them?
options: Examination on mounted casts to find interferences, the slide and the guidance
questions.why: It identifies interferences, the slide and guidance before multiple restorations.

questions.stem:
A patient needs restorations on most teeth with a planned OVD increase, and has an unstable ICP.
Which approach is appropriate?
options: Restore one tooth at a time without a plan
questions.why: An unstable ICP or OVD change needs a reproducible reference.

questions.stem:
A colleague plans occlusal equilibration.
When is it justified?
options: Only to remove specific interferences for restorative reasons
questions.why: Equilibration is irreversible.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old has typical masticatory myalgia with no red flags.
Is routine imaging needed?
options: No; imaging is targeted to specific questions such as bone pathology or an alternative diagnosis
questions.why: Imaging is targeted to a specific clinical question.

questions.stem:
A closed lock of 4 months has not improved with self-care, a splint and exercises.
What is appropriate?
questions.why: A closed lock not responding to conservative care is a referral scenario.

questions.stem:
A heavy bruxist with sound canines is having new posterior crowns.
Why is canine guidance favoured?
options: Canine guidance discludes the posterior teeth, reducing lateral load on the new crowns
questions.why: Canine guidance takes lateral load off the posterior restorations.

questions.stem:
A patient with myofascial pain and high stress asks what else may help.
Which adjuncts are appropriate?
questions.why: Physiotherapy, exercises, CBT and stress management address the biopsychosocial components.

questions.stem:
A patient with acute TMJ arthralgia asks about pain relief.
What is appropriate?
options: Simple analgesia, such as short-term NSAIDs
Steroid injections at the first visit
questions.why: Short-term NSAIDs suit acute arthralgia.

questions.stem:
A patient has an acute left disc displacement without reduction.
Which way does the mandible deviate on opening?
questions.why: The locked condyle cannot translate, so the jaw swings towards it.

questions.stem:
A student draws the outline of all possible incisal-point movements in the sagittal plane.
What is it called?
questions.why: It describes the border movements of the incisal point.

questions.stem:
A colleague prescribes a "Michigan splint".
What is it?
options: A full-coverage hard maxillary stabilisation splint
questions.why: That is a Michigan splint.

questions.stem:
You are examining a new TMD patient.
What should be documented?
options: Only the shade of the teeth
Pain location, movement limitation, joint noises, locking and functional impact
questions.why: These support a DC/TMD diagnosis.

questions.stem:
A patient's upper canine has reduced periodontal support, so it cannot take all lateral load alone.
Which guidance is preferable when restoring?
options: Group function, sharing the working-side load
questions.why: It shares lateral load when a canine cannot take it alone.

questions.stem:
A patient has a stable, comfortable ICP and needs a single onlay.
Which approach is correct?
questions.why: A stable, comfortable ICP is kept for single restorations.

questions.stem:
A patient denies grinding but has a marked ridge on the buccal mucosa and indentations along the tongue.
What do these signs suggest?
