options: Clenching or bruxism (linea alba and a scalloped tongue)
questions.why: Linea alba and a scalloped tongue are soft-tissue signs of clenching.

questions.stem:
A patient referred for NHS crowns has active caries, poor plaque control and bleeding gums.
What do the NHS prosthodontic entry criteria require first?
options: A stable oral environment: good hygiene, managed caries risk, treated caries and stable periodontal disease
questions.why: A stable oral environment. Good hygiene, managed caries risk, treated caries and stable periodontal disease come before NHS prosthodontics.

questions.stem:
You plan care for a patient with pain, caries, periodontitis and missing teeth.
What is the correct order of phases?
questions.why: Urgent, stabilisation, reassessment, definitive, maintenance.

questions.stem:
A patient is entering the stabilisation phase.
Which care belongs here?
options: Hygiene and diet advice, caries removal with temporisation, periodontal steps 1–2, extraction of hopeless teeth and interim prostheses
questions.answerText: Hygiene, caries control, periodontal steps 1–2, hopeless extractions, interim prostheses.
questions.why: Hygiene, caries control, periodontal steps 1–2, hopeless extractions, interim prostheses. Smoking cessation and medical risk control belong here too.

questions.stem:
At reassessment, a patient's plaque and bleeding scores have halved since stabilisation began.
What does this suggest?
questions.why: An engaging patient. About a 50% improvement in plaque and bleeding scores shows motivation.

questions.stem:
A patient has completed stabilisation and reassessment.
What does the definitive phase include?
options: Endodontics, periodontal surgery if needed, then fixed and removable prosthodontics
questions.why: Endodontics, periodontal surgery, then prosthodontics.

questions.stem:
Treatment is complete for a patient with a history of periodontitis and new bridgework.
How is the maintenance recall set?
options: Matched to risk, with supportive periodontal care and prosthesis review
questions.why: Risk-matched recall. Include supportive periodontal care and prosthesis review.

questions.stem:
A 32-year-old has rapidly progressing palatal erosion of the upper anteriors.
What is the first step?
options: Identify and remove the cause (diet diary, history of reflux or eating disorders), and refer to the GMP for intrinsic causes
questions.why: Identify and remove the cause. Use a diet diary and history; refer intrinsic causes to the GMP.

questions.stem:
A patient with dietary erosion asks for advice.
Which advice is appropriate?
options: Sip acidic drinks through the day
Confine acids to mealtimes, use a straw, avoid brushing straight after acid, and use high-fluoride toothpaste
questions.answerText: Acids at mealtimes, straw, delay brushing, high fluoride.
questions.why: Acids at mealtimes, straw, delay brushing, high fluoride.

questions.stem:
You decide to monitor a patient's tooth wear.
Which tools help?
options: Photographs, study casts, silicone indices and BEWE or Smith and Knight scores
questions.answerText: Photographs, casts, silicone indices, BEWE or Smith and Knight.
questions.why: Photographs, casts, silicone indices, BEWE or Smith and Knight.

questions.stem:
A patient with moderate erosion is being monitored.
When should restoration be considered?
options: At the first sign of wear
For pain or sensitivity, aesthetic or functional concern, structural compromise or pulpal risk, or documented progression despite prevention
questions.answerText: Symptoms, concern, structural or pulpal risk, or progression.
questions.why: Symptoms, concern, structural or pulpal risk, or progression. Wear alone is not an indication.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old with localised anterior wear needs restoration.
What is the first-line restorative approach?
options: Direct resin composite: additive, adhesive and repairable
questions.why: Direct composite. It is additive, adhesive, repairable and reversible.

questions.stem:
A colleague proposes conventional crowns as the first option for anterior wear.
Where do crowns sit in the restorative ladder?
options: Last, because they remove the most tooth
questions.why: Last. Crowns remove the most tooth.

questions.stem:
A student asks how the Dahl concept began.
What did Dahl use in 1975?
options: A removable cobalt–chromium anterior bite platform
questions.answerText: A removable Co-Cr anterior bite platform.
questions.why: A removable Co-Cr anterior bite platform. Today the principle uses direct composite at an increased OVD.

questions.stem:
Composite is placed on worn upper anteriors at an increased OVD.
How do the posterior contacts re-establish?
options: Intrusion of the anterior teeth and over-eruption of the posterior teeth, with some mandibular repositioning
Extrusion of the anterior teeth only
questions.why: Anterior intrusion and posterior over-eruption. There is also some mandibular repositioning.

questions.stem:
A patient asks how long the back teeth will be apart after Dahl composites.
What is typical?
questions.why: About 4–6 months, occasionally up to 18.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old has wear localised to the upper anteriors with no space to restore them, but the posterior teeth are unworn.
Which approach suits this?
options: Full-mouth crowns at an increased OVD
questions.why: Dahl. It suits localised anterior wear where dentoalveolar compensation has removed the space.

questions.stem:
A patient with localised anterior wear has implant crowns replacing 36 and 46.
Why may the Dahl approach fail?
options: Composite cannot be used near implants
Implants cannot erupt to re-establish posterior contact
questions.why: Implants cannot erupt. Implants or ankylosed posterior teeth stop contacts re-establishing.

questions.stem:
You consider the Dahl approach for a patient with localised anterior wear.
Which is a relative contraindication?
questions.why: Bisphosphonates. Drugs affecting bone turnover are a relative contraindication, with active periodontal disease, TMD, an anterior open bite tendency and poor compliance.

questions.stem:
You place Dahl composites today.
What should the patient be warned about?
options: Temporary speech change, tenderness and eating difficulty, with posterior contact taking months
questions.answerText: Temporary speech change, tenderness, eating difficulty and months to contact.
questions.why: Temporary speech change, tenderness, eating difficulty and months to contact.

questions.stem:
A patient has generalised severe wear and needs an OVD increase on most teeth.
How is this planned?
options: Direct composite on all teeth in one visit without testing
A diagnostic wax-up and a provisional trial at the new OVD; extensive reorganised rehabilitation is generally Level 3
questions.answerText: Wax-up and a provisional trial at the new OVD.
questions.why: Wax-up and a provisional trial at the new OVD. Extensive reorganisation is generally Level 3.

questions.stem:
You list ways of creating space for restorations.
Which method should be avoided?
options: Elective root canal treatment to gain space
questions.why: Elective root canal treatment. It sacrifices pulp vitality just to gain space.

questions.stem:
Surgical crown lengthening is proposed to gain height on worn upper incisors.
What is correct?
options: It is Level 3, and risks root exposure and an unfavourable crown–root ratio
questions.why: Level 3, with risks. Crown lengthening can expose roots and worsen the crown–root ratio.

questions.stem:
A colleague assumes a patient's OVD is reduced because the teeth are worn.
Why is this unsafe?
options: Worn teeth always mean reduced OVD
Dentoalveolar compensation often maintains OVD, so it should not be inferred from wear alone
questions.why: Compensation often maintains OVD. Do not infer reduced OVD from worn teeth alone.

questions.stem:
A patient with active, untreated reflux has severe palatal erosion.
Why should crowns not be planned yet?
options: The cause must be stabilised and the remaining tissue reviewed first
questions.why: Stabilise the cause first. Then review the remaining tissue.

questions.stem:
A patient has erosion, a bruxism habit and toothbrush abrasion.
How should the wear be approached?
options: Recognise that mixed mechanisms are common and address all relevant risk factors
questions.why: Mixed mechanisms are common. Address every relevant risk factor.

questions.stem:
You are deciding which teeth to keep in a failing dentition.
What gives a tooth strategic value?
options: Its abutment potential, occlusal stops and role in canine guidance
questions.answerText: Abutment potential, occlusal stops and canine guidance.
questions.why: Abutment potential, occlusal stops and canine guidance.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old has sound premolars and anteriors, and compromised lower molars needing complex treatment.
What approach is reasonable?
options: A shortened dental arch, avoiding heroic treatment of the molars when function is adequate
questions.why: Shortened dental arch. Avoid heroic molar treatment when function is adequate.

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old will gradually lose several teeth of poor prognosis over the next few years.
How should the transition to edentulism be managed?
options: Transitional acrylic RPDs to which teeth can be added, with overdenture abutments where possible
questions.answerText: Transitional acrylic RPDs and overdenture abutments.
questions.why: Transitional acrylic RPDs and overdenture abutments. Avoid sudden total clearance.

questions.stem:
A root is to be retained under a complete denture.
What must be true of it?
options: It must be root-filled or asymptomatic and free of caries
It must be above the ridge by 5 mm
questions.why: Root-filled or asymptomatic, and caries-free. Retained roots preserve bone and proprioception.

questions.stem:
A bridge is planned between 14 and 16. 16 has a guarded prognosis.
What is the principle?
options: Splint 16 with the bridge to strengthen it
Teeth of doubtful prognosis should not be bridge abutments
questions.answerText: Doubtful teeth are not bridge abutments.
questions.why: Doubtful teeth are not bridge abutments. Design RPDs so teeth can be added instead.

questions.stem:
A patient finishing periodontal therapy wants a bridge.
When is the periodontium stable enough?
options: PPD 4 mm or less with no bleeding at those sites
questions.answerText: PPD 4 mm or less with no bleeding.
questions.why: PPD 4 mm or less with no bleeding.

questions.stem:
You check readiness for definitive prosthodontics in primary care.
What are indicative full-mouth targets?
questions.why: Plaque under 20%, bleeding under 30%. Level 2–3 settings use stricter targets (bleeding under 10%).

questions.stem:
You restore a patient with a history of periodontitis.
Which features protect the periodontium?
options: Supragingival margins, correct contour, and cleansable embrasures and pontics
questions.answerText: Supragingival margins, correct contour, cleansable design.
questions.why: Supragingival margins, correct contour, cleansable design.

questions.stem:
A partial denture is needed for periodontally involved abutments.
Which design is appropriate?
options: Tooth-supported Co-Cr with rests, an open design away from the gingivae, guide planes and minimal clasp torque
questions.answerText: Tooth-supported Co-Cr, open design, minimal torque.
questions.why: Tooth-supported Co-Cr, open design, minimal torque.

questions.stem:
A patient's lower incisors are mobile, and the mobility now makes biting uncomfortable.
When is splinting indicated, and which type is preferred?
options: When increasing mobility interferes with function or comfort; adhesive splints
questions.answerText: When mobility affects function or comfort; adhesive splints.
questions.why: When mobility affects function or comfort; adhesive splints.

questions.stem:
A lower first molar with a Grade III furcation is proposed as a bridge abutment.
What is correct?
options: Root resection is routine Level 2 care
Furcation-involved molars are poor abutments; root resection belongs in specialist care
questions.answerText: Poor abutments; root resection is specialist.
questions.why: Poor abutments; root resection is specialist.

questions.stem:
Two patients have problems around implants: one has bleeding without bone loss; the other has bone loss.
Which is correct?
options: Peri-implant mucositis (reversible, no bone loss) is Level 2; peri-implantitis (bone loss) is Level 3
questions.why: Mucositis Level 2; peri-implantitis Level 3.

questions.stem:
A heavily broken-down lower premolar is to be crowned and needs root canal treatment.
What should be decided before the root canal treatment?
options: Restorability: sound coronal tissue, ferrule potential and periodontal support
questions.why: Restorability. Decide on sound tissue, ferrule potential and periodontal support before root canal treatment.

questions.stem:
A patient asks about the long-term risk to vital teeth prepared as conventional bridge abutments.
About how many become non-vital?
questions.why: About 10–15%. This is higher than for single crowns.

questions.stem:
A strategic upper canine has a combined endodontic–periodontal lesion and is the key abutment of a planned bridge.
At which level is this managed?
questions.why: Level 3. Combined endodontic–periodontal–prosthodontic problems on strategic teeth are specialist care.

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old has lost 46. There is no drifting and she is not bothered by the space.
What are the disadvantages of leaving it?
options: Appearance, drifting and over-eruption, which are often minimal
questions.answerText: Appearance, drift and over-eruption, often minimal.
questions.why: Appearance, drift and over-eruption, often minimal.

questions.stem:
A patient asks about an implant to replace 21.
Which disadvantages of implants should be discussed?
options: Surgery, cost, time, bone requirements, peri-implant disease and limited NHS access
questions.answerText: Surgery, cost, time, bone, peri-implant disease, NHS access.
questions.why: Surgery, cost, time, bone, peri-implant disease, NHS access.

questions.stem:
A patient needs routine conforming fixed and removable restorations with healthy tissues.
At what NHS complexity level is this?
questions.why: Level 1.

questions.stem:
You classify care at Level 2.
Which falls within Level 2?
options: Replacing and temporising multiple fixed units
questions.answerText: Replacing and temporising multiple fixed units.
questions.why: Replacing and temporising multiple fixed units. That is a moderately difficult technical need (Level 2).

questions.stem:
A 20-year-old with hypodontia needs multiple replacements.
At which level is this care?
options: Level 3, along with cleft, amelogenesis imperfecta and head and neck cancer rehabilitation
questions.why: Level 3. It covers developmental conditions and head and neck cancer rehabilitation.

questions.stem:
A patient's severe gag reflex has prevented every attempt at a denture.
At which level does care sit?
questions.why: Level 3. Severe gagging is Level 3; minor gagging is Level 2.

questions.stem:
A patient has undiagnosed facial pain and wants new crowns to cure it.
At which level is this managed?
questions.why: Level 3. Undiagnosed pain is complex care.

questions.stem:
A 15-year-old's permanent upper central incisor was avulsed 10 minutes ago and is clean.
What is the immediate action?
options: Replant it promptly if appropriate, and arrange urgent care
questions.why: Replant promptly if appropriate. Follow current IADT guidance and arrange urgent care.

questions.stem:
A 4-year-old's primary upper central incisor has been avulsed.
What is correct?
options: Store it in milk and replant later
Never replant an avulsed primary tooth
questions.why: Never replant a primary tooth. It risks damage to the permanent successor.

questions.stem:
An avulsed permanent tooth cannot be replanted at the scene.
What should be done?
options: Store it in an appropriate medium and arrange urgent expert care
questions.answerText: Appropriate storage medium and urgent care.
questions.why: Appropriate storage medium and urgent care.

questions.stem:
A replanted tooth is under review.
Which long-term complications are monitored?
options: Pulpal necrosis, inflammatory or replacement resorption, ankylosis, colour change and root fracture healing
questions.answerText: Necrosis, resorption, ankylosis, colour change, fracture healing.
questions.why: Necrosis, resorption, ankylosis, colour change, fracture healing.

questions.stem:
A 13-year-old lost 21 in an accident and asks for an implant.
What is correct?
options: An implant is the only option
A fixed implant is generally deferred until growth is complete
questions.why: Defer until growth is complete. Implants do not erupt with a growing jaw.

questions.stem:
The 13-year-old in the previous question needs a replacement until growth finishes.
Which interim options preserve future choices?
options: A resin-bonded bridge, a removable partial denture or orthodontic space management
questions.answerText: RBB, RPD or orthodontic space management.
questions.why: RBB, RPD or orthodontic space management. These keep future options open.

questions.stem:
A replanted incisor in a 12-year-old has become progressively infra-occluded.
What is the likely cause?
questions.why: Ankylosis. An ankylosed tooth cannot erupt with growth and becomes infra-occluded.

questions.stem:
An upper central incisor has a crown–root fracture extending below the gingiva.
What determines restorability?
options: The fracture position, root length, periodontal support and ferrule potential
questions.answerText: Fracture position, root length, support and ferrule.
questions.why: Fracture position, root length, support and ferrule.

questions.stem:
A 10-year-old has complex trauma to several incisors.
How should care be planned?
questions.why: Multidisciplinary advice.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old with bulimia has palatal erosion and wants veneers.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Liaise with the GMP, prevent and monitor, and delay definitive restoration until the condition is stable
questions.why: Liaise, prevent, delay definitive work.

questions.stem:
A bruxist has flat, shiny facets and recently fractured cusps.
Which preventive measure is appropriate?
questions.why: A night-time hard splint.

questions.stem:
An adult with active erosion and dentine sensitivity asks which toothpaste to use.
What is appropriate?
questions.why: 5000 ppm fluoride toothpaste.

questions.stem:
Direct composite has failed repeatedly on worn upper anteriors.
What are the next options before conventional crowns?
options: Indirect composite, or gold or ceramic onlays and palatal veneers
questions.answerText: Indirect composite, gold or ceramic onlays and palatal veneers.
questions.why: Indirect composite, gold or ceramic onlays and palatal veneers. These come before conventional crowns.

questions.stem:
A patient with mild, stable erosion and no symptoms was told by another dentist she needs crowns on all teeth.
What is the most appropriate advice?
questions.why: Prevention and monitoring. Mild, stable, symptomless wear needs no restoration.

questions.stem:
Dahl composites have just been placed on 13 to 23.
What is the immediate occlusal situation?
options: The posterior teeth are out of contact
The canines are out of contact
questions.why: Posterior teeth out of contact. That is the intended starting point.

questions.stem:
Conventional bridge preparation is planned on vital abutments.
What should be done before preparation?
options: Elective root canal treatment of both
Assess pulp status pre-operatively and record it
questions.why: Assess and record pulp status. Prepared abutments carry a long-term necrosis risk.

questions.stem:
You plan the transition to complete dentures in a 70-year-old with a failing dentition.
Which teeth are most worth keeping as overdenture abutments?
options: Canines, with their long roots and strategic position
questions.why: Canines. Long roots and a strategic position make them ideal overdenture abutments.

questions.stem:
A patient with several failing teeth asks for them all to be removed at once.
What is generally preferred?
options: Dental implants on the same day
A planned, staged transition, avoiding sudden total clearance where possible
questions.why: A planned, staged transition.

questions.stem:
An upper lateral incisor has had root canal treatment through a small access with little other tissue loss.
What restoration is appropriate?
questions.why: Conservative composite. Anterior root-filled teeth with little tissue loss need no crown.

questions.stem:
A lingual plate is proposed to splint mobile lower incisors.
When is this appropriate?
options: Only if the patient's oral hygiene allows
questions.why: Only if hygiene allows. A plate covers the gingival margins.

questions.stem:
A patient's full-mouth plaque score is 45% and bleeding score 50%. She wants a bridge now.
What is appropriate?
options: Improve hygiene and disease control first; she is not yet ready for definitive work
questions.why: Disease control first. Her scores are far above the targets for definitive work.

questions.stem:
A patient with treated periodontitis has completed prosthodontic care.
What does the maintenance phase include?
options: Supportive periodontal care, with prosthesis review at a risk-based recall
questions.answerText: Supportive periodontal care with prosthesis review.
questions.why: Supportive periodontal care with prosthesis review.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old missing 12 is offered orthodontic space closure.
What is the main disadvantage of this option?
questions.why: Time, appliances and Level 3 planning.

questions.stem:
A general dentist working at Level 2 is asked to place an implant for 36.
What is within the Level 2 scope?
options: Providing and maintaining simple implant-retained prostheses and diagnosing peri-implant disease; assessment, planning and placement are Level 3
questions.answerText: Simple implant prostheses and diagnosing peri-implant disease.
questions.why: Simple implant prostheses and diagnosing peri-implant disease. Assessment, planning and placement are Level 3.

questions.stem:
A student defines osseointegration.
Which definition (Brånemark) is correct?
options: A fibrous attachment between bone and implant
A periodontal ligament around the implant
Cementation of the implant into bone
A direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the surface of a load-bearing implant, with no intervening soft tissue
questions.answerText: Direct bone–implant connection with no soft tissue.
questions.why: Direct bone–implant connection with no soft tissue. That is Brånemark's definition.

questions.stem:
An implant feels firm at placement.
How do primary and secondary stability differ?
options: Primary is mechanical (at placement); secondary is biological (bone remodelling over weeks)
Primary is biological; secondary is mechanical
Secondary stability is achieved at placement
questions.why: Primary mechanical; secondary biological.

questions.stem:
A colleague notices implant stability values dropped a few weeks after placement.
When does the "stability dip" occur?
questions.why: About 2–4 weeks. Primary stability falls before secondary stability builds.

questions.stem:
An implant is planned next to a natural tooth.
What minimum distance from implant to tooth is advised?

Two adjacent implants are planned for 35 and 36.
What minimum distance between them is advised?
questions.why: 3 mm.

questions.stem:
An implant is planned in the posterior mandible.
What safety margin above the inferior alveolar canal is advised?
questions.why: 2 mm.

questions.stem:
A CBCT shows a thin buccal plate at a planned implant site.
How much buccal bone is usually wanted around an implant?
questions.why: At least 1.5–2 mm. Thin buccal bone risks recession and resorption.

questions.stem:
A temporary crown is placed on an implant 3 days after surgery.
Which ITI loading protocol is this?
questions.why: Immediate (within 1 week).

questions.stem:
An implant is restored 6 weeks after placement.
Which ITI loading protocol is this?
questions.why: Early (1 week to 2 months). Conventional loading is after 2 months.

questions.stem:
A patient's older implant crown keeps loosening.
Which implant–abutment connection is associated with more screw loosening?
questions.why: External hex. This historic design has more screw loosening.

questions.stem:
A colleague prefers a particular implant connection for its seal and stability.
Which connection offers these?
questions.why: Conical (Morse taper). It gives a better seal and stability.

questions.stem:
An abutment narrower than the implant platform is used.
What is this called, and what may it achieve?
options: Platform switching; it may reduce crestal bone loss
questions.why: Platform switching. It may reduce crestal bone loss.

questions.stem:
A patient asks whether an implant is suitable for her.
Which history most increases the risk of peri-implantitis?
options: A history of periodontitis, especially with smoking
questions.why: History of periodontitis with smoking. Other risks: poorly controlled diabetes, poor plaque control, no maintenance, radiotherapy, IV antiresorptives and bruxism.

questions.stem:
A 75-year-old edentulous patient struggles with a loose lower denture.
What is the minimum standard of care for the edentulous mandible?
options: Four implants with a fixed bridge
questions.why: Two-implant overdenture.

questions.stem:
Unsplinted ball or locator attachments are chosen for a two-implant mandibular overdenture.
What are their characteristics?
options: Easier hygiene and maintenance, less restorative space needed; inserts wear and need replacing
They need the most vertical space
questions.answerText: Easier hygiene, less space; inserts wear.
questions.why: Easier hygiene, less space; inserts wear.

questions.stem:
Implants for an overdenture are markedly divergent.
Which attachment system suits them?
options: A bar, which splints the implants and gives more retention but needs more vertical space and hygiene effort
questions.why: A bar. It splints divergent implants but needs more vertical space and hygiene effort.

questions.stem:
An edentulous patient wants an implant overdenture in the maxilla.
What is usual?
options: Usually 4 or more implants; a palateless design is possible
questions.why: Usually 4 or more; palateless possible.

questions.stem:
A single implant crown on 36 is planned and the patient wants it to be retrievable.
Which retention type is preferred?
options: Screw-retained: retrievable, with no subgingival cement
questions.why: Screw-retained. It is retrievable with no subgingival cement.

questions.stem:
A cement-retained implant crown has bleeding and suppuration around it a year after fitting.
What is a common cause?
questions.why: Residual cement. Excess subgingival cement is a recognised cause of peri-implant disease.

questions.stem:
A full-arch fixed implant bridge is planned.
Which statement is correct?
options: It is Level 3; passive fit is essential and distal cantilevers are kept short
questions.why: Level 3; passive fit; short cantilevers.

questions.stem:
A patient with a two-implant mandibular overdenture complains it is loose after 18 months.
What is the commonest cause?
options: Wear of the attachment inserts, needing replacement
questions.why: Insert wear. Loss of retention is the commonest overdenture complication.

questions.stem:
A single implant crown has been in place for 3 years.
What are its commonest complications?
options: Abutment screw loosening and ceramic chipping
questions.why: Screw loosening and ceramic chipping.

questions.stem:
You tighten the abutment screw of an implant crown.
How should the screw be torqued?
options: With a calibrated torque driver to the manufacturer's value
questions.why: A calibrated torque driver. Tighten to the manufacturer's value.

questions.stem:
A colleague plans a bridge joining a natural premolar to an implant.
Why should this be avoided?
options: Implants have no periodontal ligament, so differential mobility causes problems
questions.why: No periodontal ligament. Differential mobility makes rigid tooth–implant connection a problem.

questions.stem:
You review a patient with an implant crown.
What defines peri-implant health?
options: No erythema, bleeding or suppuration, and no bone loss beyond initial remodelling
questions.answerText: No erythema, bleeding or suppuration; no bone loss.
questions.why: No erythema, bleeding or suppuration; no bone loss.

questions.stem:
An implant shows bleeding on gentle probing, with no bone loss beyond initial remodelling.
What is the diagnosis and management level?
options: Peri-implant mucositis: reversible; Level 2 debridement, OHI and a prosthesis design check
questions.why: Mucositis; Level 2. It is reversible with debridement, OHI and a design check.

questions.stem:
No baseline radiograph exists for an implant with bleeding.
What findings indicate peri-implantitis?
options: Bone 3 mm or more apical to the implant platform, with PPD 6 mm or more and bleeding
questions.answerText: Bone 3 mm or more apical to the platform, PPD 6 mm or more with bleeding.
questions.why: Bone 3 mm or more apical to the platform, PPD 6 mm or more with bleeding. That is the 2017 World Workshop definition without baseline records.

questions.stem:
You fit a new implant-retained crown.
What should be recorded at fitting?
options: A baseline radiograph and probing depths
questions.why: Baseline radiograph and probing depths.

questions.stem:
A patient with an implant bar overdenture asks how to clean it.
Which maintenance is appropriate?
options: Interdental brushes and floss under the bar, professional debridement with instruments that will not scratch titanium, and annual review
questions.answerText: Interdental brushes, floss under the bar, non-scratch debridement, annual review.
questions.why: Interdental brushes, floss under the bar, non-scratch debridement, annual review.

questions.stem:
A hygienist is about to debride around a titanium implant abutment.
Which instruments should be used?
options: Instruments that will not scratch titanium (such as plastic, titanium or carbon-fibre tips)
questions.answerText: Instruments that will not scratch titanium.
questions.why: Instruments that will not scratch titanium.

questions.stem:
A patient asks whether an implant crown will "feel" like a natural tooth.
What is correct?
options: It has no periodontal ligament or physiological movement; feedback comes from osseoperception only
It moves more than a tooth
questions.why: Osseoperception only. There is no periodontal ligament or physiological movement.

questions.stem:
An implant is still in place after 10 years but has 5 mm of bone loss and recurrent suppuration.
How should its outcome be described?
options: It has survived, but is not a success
A failure because it is present
questions.why: Survived, not a success.

questions.stem:
A patient asks for an implant to replace 25.
What should the assessment start with?
options: The prosthesis: the missing-tooth problem, desired restoration, smile line, restorative space, occlusion, cleansability and the patient's priorities
questions.why: Prosthesis-first assessment.

questions.stem:
A Level 2 dentist is asked to perform a sinus lift.
What is appropriate?
options: Refer; sinus grafting and ridge augmentation are not routine Level 2 care
Proceed if the patient pays privately
questions.why: Refer. Sinus grafting and augmentation are not Level 2.

questions.stem:
A colleague plans to scan a full arch digitally for a cross-arch bridge.
Which statement about intraoral scanners is correct?
options: They are most accurate over full arches
They are excellent for short spans; accuracy falls over full arches through stitching errors
They record mucodisplaced edentulous tissue well
questions.answerText: Short spans best; stitching errors over full arches.
questions.why: Short spans best; stitching errors over full arches.

questions.stem:
You consider an intraoral scan for an edentulous upper arch.
What are the limitations of intraoral scanning?
options: Mobile edentulous mucosa, which cannot be mucodisplaced or border-moulded
questions.why: All of the above.

questions.stem:
A laboratory asks for a scan in STL format.
What does an STL file contain?
options: Surface geometry as triangles, in an open format without colour
questions.answerText: Surface triangles, open format, no colour.
questions.why: Surface triangles, open format, no colour.

questions.stem:
A clinician wants a digital model that shows gingival colour for shade communication.
Which file formats can carry colour and texture?
questions.why: PLY or OBJ. These carry colour and texture.

questions.stem:
A surgical guide is planned for an implant at 36.
Which data are merged?
options: A panoramic radiograph and an alginate cast
questions.why: DICOM merged with STL.

questions.stem:
A manufacturer quotes the trueness and precision of its scanner.
What do these terms mean?
options: Trueness is speed; precision is colour
Trueness is repeatability; precision is closeness to the reference
Trueness is closeness to the reference; precision is repeatability
questions.answerText: Trueness is closeness to the reference; precision is repeatability.
questions.why: Trueness is closeness to the reference; precision is repeatability.

questions.stem:
A laboratory mills a crown from a pre-sintered zirconia block.
What are the features of subtractive manufacture?
options: Dense, homogeneous material, but fine detail is limited by bur size
It is used only for wax
questions.answerText: Dense and homogeneous; limited by bur size.
questions.why: Dense and homogeneous; limited by bur size.

questions.stem:
A laboratory 3D-prints a model and a Co-Cr framework.
Which processes are additive?
options: Stereolithography (SLA), digital light processing (DLP) and selective laser melting (for metals)
questions.answerText: SLA, DLP and selective laser melting.
questions.why: SLA, DLP and selective laser melting.

questions.stem:
A practice buys a 3D printer.
What are its typical prosthodontic uses?
options: Models, surgical guides, trays, splints and temporary crowns
questions.why: Models, guides, trays, splints, temporaries.

questions.stem:
A patient asks about digital complete dentures.
What are their advantages and limitations?
options: Fewer visits, stored records and low-monomer milled bases with good fit; limited recording of functional borders and complex jaw relations
They always fit better than conventional dentures in all cases
questions.answerText: Fewer visits, stored records, low-monomer bases; limited functional borders.
questions.why: Fewer visits, stored records, low-monomer bases; limited functional borders.

questions.stem:
A patient's smile has been designed digitally.
What is still useful before treatment?
options: A physical mock-up from a wax-up for the patient's approval
questions.why: A physical mock-up. It remains useful for approval and consent.

questions.stem:
A clinician wants to record a patient's dynamic occlusion digitally.
Which technology does this?
questions.why: Jaw motion tracking.

questions.stem:
A practice designs crowns digitally.
How should the records be managed?
options: Save source files securely and document revisions
questions.why: Secure storage and documented revisions.

questions.stem:
A printed provisional crown is weaker than expected.
What affects the properties of printed restorations?
options: Post-curing and using a material indicated for the purpose
questions.why: Post-curing and material indication.

questions.stem:
A multi-implant full-arch prosthesis needs a passive fit.
What is appropriate?
options: An intraoral scan alone without verification
A validated technique, with a verification jig or conventional splinted impression where indicated
questions.why: Validated technique with verification. Passive fit on multiple implants is a known digital limitation.

questions.stem:
An implant crown on 46 has loosened three times.
What should be checked?
options: Screw torque, occlusal loading (including bruxism) and the connection
questions.why: Torque, occlusal load and connection.

questions.stem:
A patient has a two-implant mandibular overdenture opposing an upper complete denture.
What complication of the upper denture is common?
questions.why: Fracture of the upper denture. It is a recognised complication opposite implants.

questions.stem:
A bruxist has a new implant crown.
What is appropriate?
options: A protective night guard, as bruxism raises the risk of complications
questions.why: A protective night guard. Bruxism raises complication risk.

questions.stem:
A patient had radiotherapy to the mandible and wants implants there.
What is correct?
options: Implants in irradiated bone have the same success
They are contraindicated in all cases
questions.why: Higher failure; Level 3.

questions.stem:
A patient with bone metastases on high-dose IV zoledronic acid asks for implants.
What is appropriate?
options: Implants only after careful risk assessment and consent; they are generally avoided because of MRONJ risk
Stop the drug and place implants
questions.why: Careful risk assessment; generally avoided. MRONJ risk is high with IV antiresorptives.

questions.stem:
A patient with an HbA1c of 85 mmol/mol wants implants.
What is appropriate?
options: Recognise the raised risk and optimise glycaemic control first
questions.why: Optimise glycaemic control first.

questions.stem:
A Level 2 dentist manages peri-implant mucositis on a bar overdenture.
What does management include?
options: Mechanical debridement, OHI and a check of the prosthesis design for cleansability
questions.answerText: Debridement, OHI and a cleansability check.
questions.why: Debridement, OHI and a cleansability check.

questions.stem:
An implant has suppuration, a 7 mm pocket and radiographic bone loss.
What is appropriate?
options: Debride and review in a year
questions.why: Refer as peri-implantitis.

questions.stem:
A patient's locator-retained overdenture has lost its retention.
What is the usual first step?
questions.why: Replace the matrix.

questions.stem:
A clinician plans aesthetic rehabilitation using a facial scan and a virtual articulator.
What do these add?
options: They integrate facial references into the digital plan
They remove the need for records
questions.why: Facial references in the plan. They support, not replace, examination and consent.

questions.stem:
A crown on 46 has come off for the third time. The preparation looks short and tapered.
What is the correct approach?
options: Recement with a stronger cement and review
Check for caries and assess the preparation; recement only if sound and retentive, otherwise improve retention or redesign
questions.why: Find the cause first. Repeated decementation points to resistance form; an identical replacement will fail the same way.

questions.stem:
A patient with a 4-year-old fixed-fixed bridge reports a bad taste. One retainer is loose, but the bridge is still held by the other.
What is appropriate?
options: Remove the bridge, treat the caries and redesign
Recement through a hole in the retainer
questions.why: Remove, treat caries, redesign. Differential movement loosened one retainer while the other held.

questions.stem:
A small chip has come off the porcelain of a metal–ceramic crown, without exposing metal.
What is appropriate?
options: Use zinc phosphate to fill it
Polish it, or repair with composite (HF and silane on the ceramic)
questions.why: Polish or repair with composite. Use HF and silane on ceramic, or MDP on any exposed metal.

questions.stem:
Porcelain has repeatedly fractured from the same metal–ceramic crown. It was more than 2 mm thick and unsupported.
What is the definitive solution?
options: Replace and redesign with proper metal support, or a metal or zirconia occlusal surface
questions.why: Replace and redesign. Unsupported porcelain over 2 mm will chip again; give metal support or a metal or zirconia occlusal surface.

questions.stem:
A patient has sensitivity to cold a week after a crown was cemented on a vital tooth.
What is the first management?
options: Check the occlusion, desensitise and monitor sensibility
questions.why: Check occlusion, desensitise, monitor. Most early sensitivity settles.

questions.stem:
A crowned upper premolar has become non-vital with a periapical lesion; the crown is otherwise sound.
What is appropriate?
options: Root canal treatment through the crown, then seal the access (or replace the crown)
questions.answerText: Root canal treatment through the crown.
questions.why: Root canal treatment through the crown. Seal the access, or replace the crown if needed.

questions.stem:
A post-crowned premolar has a vertical root fracture with no ferrule.
What is the usual outcome?
options: Extraction; prevention depends on ferrule and post design
questions.why: Usually extraction. Prevention depends on ferrule and post design.

questions.stem:
Bleeding and swelling develop around one newly fitted crown.
What should be suspected first?
options: Residual excess cement, until proven otherwise
questions.why: Residual cement. Suspect it until proven otherwise.

questions.stem:
A patient complains of food packing between a new crown on 36 and 37.
What is the likely cause and remedy?
options: An open or weak contact; adjust or replace the restoration
questions.why: An open or weak contact. Adjust or replace the restoration.

questions.stem:
A single-wing resin-bonded bridge has debonded. The wing is intact and there is no caries.
What is appropriate?
options: Clean, re-sandblast and rebond under rubber dam with MDP cement, check the occlusion, and redesign if it debonds repeatedly
questions.answerText: Clean, sandblast and rebond with MDP.
questions.why: Clean, sandblast and rebond with MDP. An intact debonded RBB with no caries is rebonded, not remade.

questions.stem:
You audit failures of conventional bridges in your practice.
What are the leading causes of failure in the literature?
questions.why: Caries and loss of retention.

questions.stem:
You consent a patient for crowns on vital teeth.
Which common biological complication should be mentioned?
options: The later need for endodontic treatment
questions.why: Later need for endodontics. It is a common biological complication of crowned vital teeth.

questions.stem:
A Co-Cr framework will not seat at try-in. Disclosing medium shows widespread contacts, with no single interference.
What is the most likely cause and action?
options: A distorted impression or cast; re-impression and remake
Too much retention; open the clasps
questions.why: Distorted impression or cast. Widespread misfit means re-impression and remake.

questions.stem:
A patient's RPD clasp has become loose.
What is a common cause?
options: Distortion from the patient removing the denture by the clasp
questions.answerText: Distortion by removal on the clasp.
questions.why: Distortion by removal on the clasp. Work hardening, a wrong undercut and wear are other causes.

questions.stem:
A Co-Cr clasp fractures at the shoulder after several adjustments.
What is the cause?
options: Fatigue, aggravated by repeated adjustment of low-ductility Co-Cr or casting porosity
questions.why: Fatigue. Repeated adjustment of low-ductility Co-Cr, or casting porosity, makes it worse.

questions.stem:
An RPD abutment has become painful and mobile.
Which causes should be considered?
options: Occlusal overload, an unseated rest, free-end saddle rotation or a clasp active at rest
questions.answerText: Overload, unseated rest, saddle rotation or active clasp.
questions.why: Overload, unseated rest, saddle rotation or active clasp.

questions.stem:
A lower free-end saddle sinks and the indirect retainer lifts when pressed.
What is the remedy?
questions.why: Reline the saddle.

questions.stem:
A patient with an RPD has new caries on the abutments.
What is the likely cause?
options: Plaque retention at clasps and minor connectors, and high sugar intake
questions.answerText: Plaque at clasps and minor connectors, and sugar.
questions.why: Plaque at clasps and minor connectors, and sugar.

questions.stem:
An edentulous patient asks how often to have her dentures checked.
What is the recommendation?
options: At least annually, for mucosal examination, fit and occlusal wear
questions.why: At least annually. Check the mucosa, fit and occlusal wear.

questions.stem:
A patient's dentures are loose, but the appearance, OVD and occlusion are good.
What is the appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Reline or rebase. Remake only when OVD, appearance or occlusion are also wrong.

questions.stem:
A denture has fractured in two.
What principles apply to the repair?
options: Reassemble the pieces roughly and add acrylic
Reassemble the fracture accurately before pouring a cast; note that self-cure repairs are weaker, and investigate the cause of repeated fractures
Make a new denture each time
questions.why: Accurate reassembly; investigate repeated fractures. Self-cure repairs are weaker.

questions.stem:
A patient asks how to clean her acrylic complete dentures.
What is the correct advice?
options: Brush with a soft brush and soap or non-abrasive cleanser over a basin of water, soak overnight, and leave them out at night
questions.answerText: Soft brush and non-abrasive cleanser over water, overnight soak, night removal.
questions.why: Soft brush and non-abrasive cleanser over water, overnight soak, night removal.

questions.stem:
Newly processed complete dentures are too tall at fitting, though the wax try-in was correct.
Which laboratory error is likely?
options: Raised OVD from flash during processing
questions.why: Raised OVD from flash. It is a processing error.

questions.stem:
A practice wants fewer laboratory errors.
What are the best preventive measures?
options: Clear written prescriptions, inspection of impressions and casts at each stage, photographs and shade information, and agreed delivery times
questions.answerText: Clear prescriptions, quality control, photographs, agreed times.
questions.why: Clear prescriptions, quality control, photographs, agreed times.

questions.stem:
A paper reports 95% survival of a prosthesis at 10 years.
What does "survival" mean, and how does it differ from success?
options: Survival means still in place; success means in place and free of complications
questions.answerText: Survival is in place; success is complication-free.
questions.why: Survival is in place; success is complication-free. Ask which one a paper reports.

questions.stem:
A patient asks how long a conventional bridge lasts.
What is the approximate benchmark survival?
questions.why: About 89% at 10 years.

questions.stem:
A patient asks about the longevity of a single metal–ceramic crown.
What is the approximate benchmark?
questions.why: About 95% at 5 years.

questions.stem:
A patient asks how long a modern resin-bonded bridge lasts.
What is the approximate benchmark?
options: About 80–90% at 5–10 years, with cantilevers performing well
questions.why: About 80–90% at 5–10 years. Cantilever designs perform well.

questions.stem:
A practice plans maintenance appointments for its patients.
Which prosthesis needs frequent maintenance?
questions.why: Implant overdenture attachments.

questions.stem:
A lower Co-Cr RPD has fractured for the third time at the same place.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Tell the patient to eat softer food
Diagnose the cause (thickness, support, occlusal forces) and change the design
questions.answerText: Diagnose the cause and change the design.
questions.why: Diagnose the cause and change the design. Treat failure as feedback to the plan.

questions.stem:
A patient signed a consent form for a bridge, but the risks were never discussed and she felt pressured.
What makes consent valid?
options: It is informed, voluntary, given by a person with capacity, specific to the treatment, documented, and can be withdrawn
questions.answerText: Informed, voluntary, capacitous, specific, documented, withdrawable.
questions.why: Informed, voluntary, capacitous, specific, documented, withdrawable. Consent is a process, not a signature.

questions.stem:
You are consenting a professional violinist for a lower molar extraction near the lingual nerve.
Which case set the standard for disclosure of risks?
options: Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015): material risks to a reasonable patient, or to this patient, and reasonable alternatives
questions.why: Montgomery (2015). It requires disclosure of material risks and reasonable alternatives, and replaced Bolam for disclosure.

questions.stem:
A clinician's crown preparation technique is challenged in a negligence claim.
Which test applies to the standard of treatment?
options: Bolam, qualified by Bolitho (opinion must withstand logical analysis)
questions.why: Bolam qualified by Bolitho. They still apply to diagnosis and treatment.

questions.stem:
A patient alleges negligence after a crown.
What must be proved?
options: Duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and resulting harm
Only that the patient is unhappy
questions.why: Duty, breach, causation, harm.

questions.stem:
An associate's error injures a patient. The practice owner is also sued.
What principle allows this?
options: Vicarious liability: an employer is liable for employees' acts in the course of employment
questions.why: Vicarious liability.

questions.stem:
A patient with capacity declines a recommended bridge and chooses no replacement.
Which Mental Capacity Act principle applies?
options: Decide in the clinician's best interests
An unwise decision does not mean the person lacks capacity
questions.answerText: An unwise decision is not incapacity.
questions.why: An unwise decision is not incapacity.

questions.stem:
You need to assess an 80-year-old's capacity to consent to extractions.
What is the two-stage test?
options: An impairment of mind or brain; then whether the person can understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate the decision
questions.answerText: Impairment, then understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate.
questions.why: Impairment, then understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate.

questions.stem:
A patient with fluctuating dementia consented last week but seems confused today.
Which principle about capacity applies?
questions.why: Decision-specific and time-specific. Reassess on the day.

questions.stem:
A 17-year-old wants an RBB and her parent disagrees.
What is the legal position?
options: 16–17-year-olds are presumed to have capacity to consent (Family Law Reform Act 1969)
questions.why: Presumed capacity at 16–17.

questions.stem:
A 14-year-old requests treatment without her parents knowing.
When may she consent?
questions.why: Gillick competence.

questions.stem:
A Scottish dentist treats an adult lacking capacity.
Which legislation applies?
questions.why: Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000.

questions.stem:
You use a decision aid with a patient choosing between a bridge and an implant.
What does NICE NG197 (shared decision-making) recommend discussing?
options: Benefits, risks, alternatives and doing nothing (BRAN)
questions.why: BRAN. Discuss benefits, risks, alternatives and doing nothing.

questions.stem:
A student lists the GDC's nine principles.
Which is NOT one of them?
options: Raise concerns if patients are at risk
Have a clear and effective complaints procedure
questions.why: Maximising income. It is not a GDC principle.

questions.stem:
A dentist is planning CPD for the next cycle.
What are the enhanced CPD requirements?
options: At least 100 verifiable hours per 5-year cycle, at least 10 hours in every 2-year period, with a personal development plan
questions.answerText: 100 hours in 5 years, at least 10 in every 2, with a PDP.
questions.why: 100 hours in 5 years, at least 10 in every 2, with a PDP.

questions.stem:
A newly qualified dentist asks about indemnity.
What is correct?
questions.why: Indemnity is mandatory.

questions.stem:
A dentist extracts a tooth and discovers it was the wrong one.
Who has a professional duty of candour?
questions.why: All registrants.

questions.stem:
After an error, a dentist apologises to the patient.
What is the legal status of an apology?
options: It must be in writing only
An apology is not an admission of liability
questions.answerText: An apology is not an admission of liability.
questions.why: An apology is not an admission of liability.

questions.stem:
A CQC-registered practice has a notifiable safety incident.
Which duty applies to the provider?
questions.why: The statutory duty of candour. It applies to CQC-registered providers for notifiable incidents.

questions.stem:
A patient develops a serious adverse reaction to a prescribed antibiotic.
How should it be reported?
options: Through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme
questions.why: MHRA Yellow Card.

questions.stem:
A batch of defective impression trays causes repeated distortions.
Where are medical device incidents reported?
questions.why: MHRA.

questions.stem:
A nurse suffers a serious injury from a workplace accident.
Under which regulations, and to whom, is it reported?
options: The Equality Act, to the court
questions.why: RIDDOR to the HSE.

questions.stem:
A healthy lower molar is extracted instead of its carious neighbour.
How is this classified?
questions.why: A never event.

questions.stem:
An NHS patient complains about her dentures.
What is the acknowledgement timescale and time limit for complaints?
options: Acknowledge within 1 month; no time limit
Acknowledge within 3 working days; complaints normally within 12 months of the event or of becoming aware
questions.why: Acknowledge within 3 working days; 12 months.

questions.stem:
A complaint is not resolved locally.
Where does it escalate?
options: NHS: the GDC; private: the CQC
NHS: the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman; private: the Dental Complaints Service
questions.why: PHSO (NHS) or Dental Complaints Service (private).

questions.stem:
A nurse raises concerns about unsafe practice by her employer.
Which law protects her?
questions.why: Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998.

questions.stem:
A dentist realises an entry in yesterday's notes is wrong.
How should it be corrected?
options: Add a dated, signed note of the correction, leaving the original visible
Ask the nurse to change it
questions.why: A dated, signed correction. Never alter the original.

questions.stem:
A practice is clearing old records.
How long must adult and child records be kept (NHS England guidance)?
options: Adults at least 11 years after last treatment; children until age 25 or 11 years after last treatment, whichever is longer
questions.answerText: Adults 11 years; children to 25 or 11 years, whichever is longer.
questions.why: Adults 11 years; children to 25 or 11 years, whichever is longer.

questions.stem:
A patient requests a copy of her records.
What does UK GDPR require?
options: A response within one month, normally free of charge
A response within 6 months with a fee
questions.why: One month, normally free.

questions.stem:
Police ask for a patient's records without a court order or consent, in a minor matter.
When may confidentiality be breached?
options: With consent, when required by law (such as a court order), or in the public interest to prevent serious harm, sharing the minimum necessary
questions.why: Consent, law, or public interest. Share the minimum necessary.

questions.stem:
A practice reviews how it shares patient information.
Which principles govern confidential information sharing?
questions.why: Caldicott principles.

questions.stem:
A new practice installs intraoral X-ray sets.
What does IRR17 require of the employer?
options: Registering with the HSE, appointing a radiation protection adviser and supervisor, and setting local rules and a controlled area
questions.answerText: HSE registration, RPA, RPS, local rules, controlled area.
questions.why: HSE registration, RPA, RPS, local rules, controlled area.

questions.stem:
You set up the controlled area for an intraoral X-ray set.
What is the typical extent?
options: Within about 1.5 m of the tube and patient, and within the primary beam until it is attenuated
questions.answerText: About 1.5 m, and the primary beam.
questions.why: About 1.5 m, and the primary beam.

questions.stem:
You review who does what under IR(ME)R 2017.
Who are the duty holders?
questions.why: Employer, referrer, practitioner, operator.

questions.stem:
An audit shows radiographs taken with round collimation and no film holders.
Which optimisation measures should be introduced?
options: Rectangular collimation, film holders, the fastest suitable receptor, appropriate exposure settings, and image-quality audit
questions.answerText: Rectangular collimation, holders, fast receptor, QA audit.
questions.why: Rectangular collimation, holders, fast receptor, QA audit.

questions.stem:
You check the steam steriliser's display.
What is the standard sterilisation cycle?
questions.why: 134–137°C for at least 3 minutes.

questions.stem:
A practice will sterilise wrapped handpieces and hollow instruments.
Which steriliser is needed?
questions.why: A type B vacuum steriliser. It is needed for wrapped and hollow instruments.

questions.stem:
You review the practice's instrument cleaning.
What is best practice under HTM 01-05?
questions.why: A washer-disinfector.

questions.stem:
A nurse asks which steriliser tests are done daily.
What is correct?
options: An automatic control test, plus a steam penetration test for vacuum sterilisers
questions.answerText: Automatic control test, plus steam penetration for vacuum.
questions.why: Automatic control test, plus steam penetration for vacuum.

questions.stem:
Impressions and try-ins move between the surgery and the laboratory.
What does HTM 01-05 require?
options: Rinse and disinfect them in both directions, and label them as disinfected
questions.why: Disinfect both ways and label.

questions.stem:
You review dental unit waterline management.
What flushing is recommended?
options: Only at the end of the day
About 2 minutes at the start of the day and 20–30 seconds between patients, with a biocide
questions.answerText: 2 minutes at the start, 20–30 seconds between patients.
questions.why: 2 minutes at the start, 20–30 seconds between patients.

questions.stem:
A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used syringe.
What is the immediate management?
options: Encourage bleeding, wash with soap and water without scrubbing, cover, report, and contact occupational health urgently (HIV PEP ideally within 1 hour)
Ignore it if the patient seems healthy
Wait until the end of the day
questions.answerText: Bleed, wash, cover, report, occupational health urgently.
questions.why: Bleed, wash, cover, report, occupational health urgently. HIV PEP ideally within 1 hour, up to 72 hours.

questions.stem:
A newly employed dentist will perform exposure-prone procedures.
What is required?
options: Hepatitis B vaccination with a documented response
questions.answerText: Hepatitis B vaccination with documented response.
questions.why: Hepatitis B vaccination with documented response.

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old has unexplained facial bruising and multiple untreated carious teeth.
What is the dentist's role?
options: Recognise, record and refer; do not investigate yourself
questions.why: Recognise, record, refer. Do not investigate yourself.

questions.stem:
A 15-year-old discloses female genital mutilation.
What must a regulated professional in England and Wales do?
options: Report the known case to the police
questions.why: Report to the police. It is mandatory for known FGM in under-18s in England and Wales.

questions.stem:
A wheelchair user cannot reach your upstairs surgery.
What does the Equality Act 2010 require?
options: Reasonable adjustments for a person with a protected characteristic (disability)
questions.why: Reasonable adjustments. Disability is one of nine protected characteristics.

questions.stem:
A practice manager lists the pillars of clinical governance.
Which list is correct?
options: Clinical effectiveness and audit, risk management, education and training, patient involvement, information management, staff management and research
questions.why: The seven pillars.

questions.stem:
A dentist checks her RPD records against a published standard.
What is this activity?
options: Audit, measuring practice against a standard
questions.why: Audit. Audit measures against a standard; research creates new knowledge.

questions.stem:
An audit found poor recording of RPD designs, and changes have been made.
What closes the audit loop?
questions.why: Re-audit.

questions.stem:
A practice uses small, repeated cycles to test a new recall system.
What is this quality-improvement method?
questions.why: PDSA cycles.

questions.stem:
You are appraising evidence for a new bonding protocol.
Which evidence is at the top of the hierarchy?
options: A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
questions.answerText: A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs.
questions.why: A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs.

questions.stem:
A guideline rates the evidence for a recommendation as "low certainty".
Which system grades certainty of evidence?
questions.why: GRADE.

questions.stem:
A new caries test correctly identifies 90% of carious surfaces.
What does this figure describe?
questions.why: Sensitivity.

questions.stem:
The same test is used in a population with very low caries prevalence.
What happens to its positive predictive value?
options: It falls, because PPV depends on prevalence
questions.why: PPV falls with low prevalence.

questions.stem:
A treatment reduces failure from 30% to 20%.
What is the number needed to treat?
questions.why: 10. The absolute risk reduction is 10%, so NNT = 1 ÷ 0.10.

questions.stem:
A trial reports a risk ratio of 0.85 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.70 to 1.04.
What does this mean?
options: The result is not statistically significant, because the interval crosses 1
questions.why: Not significant. The interval crosses 1.

questions.stem:
A dentist moves from England to Wales.
Which bodies regulate services in each of the four UK nations?
options: CQC (England), Healthcare Improvement Scotland, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, RQIA (Northern Ireland)
questions.why: CQC, HIS, HIW, RQIA. The GDC is the professional regulator.

questions.stem:
A dentist applies to provide Level 2 prosthodontics.
What is required?
options: A formal link with a consultant-led managed clinical network, a minimum caseload, outcome recording (PROMs and PREMs), audit and complication reporting
questions.answerText: Network link, caseload, PROMs and PREMs, audit, complication reporting.
questions.why: Network link, caseload, PROMs and PREMs, audit, complication reporting.

questions.stem:
You must tell a patient that her failing teeth cannot be saved.
Which framework structures breaking bad news?
options: SPIKES: setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, emotions, strategy and summary
questions.why: SPIKES.

questions.stem:
A patient speaks little English and her 12-year-old son offers to interpret.
What is appropriate?
questions.why: A professional interpreter. Never use family members or children.

questions.stem:
An NHS patient in England starts a course involving a bridge.
What supports informed consent and reduces complaints?
options: A written treatment plan and estimate (FP17DC)
questions.why: A written plan and estimate (FP17DC).

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old has an upper complete denture and a lower Kennedy Class I RPD. 33 is broken down to the gingival margin but its root is sound. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and has taken alendronic acid for 7 years.
What is the most appropriate management of 33?
options: Stop apixaban for 3 days and extract it
Extract it under antibiotic cover after a 3-month drug holiday
Root-treat and retain the root as an overdenture abutment, if feasible, rather than extracting
Leave it untreated under the denture
Crown it to act as a clasped abutment
questions.answerText: Retain the root as an overdenture abutment.
questions.why: Retain the root as an overdenture abutment. Over 5 years of oral bisphosphonate raises MRONJ risk, so root retention beats extraction; apixaban is not stopped.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old has palatal erosion of the upper incisors and reflux symptoms. There is no space to restore the teeth, and she asks for porcelain veneers.
What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Liaise with her GMP about the reflux, give preventive advice, and monitor before any restoration
Prepare the teeth for veneers now
questions.why: Manage the cause and monitor. Stabilise reflux erosion before any irreversible veneers.

questions.stem:
An 83-year-old care-home resident with moderate dementia has lost both dentures. Staff report that she cannot eat solid food.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Do nothing, as dementia contraindicates dentures
Copy dentures from the lost originals
Assess capacity, act in her best interests with carer involvement, and provide simple conventional dentures with labelling
questions.answerText: Capacity, best interests, simple dentures, labelling.
questions.why: Capacity, best interests, simple dentures, labelling. Copying is impossible because the dentures are lost.

questions.stem:
A patient with a known latex allergy develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension minutes after an impression was taken by a nurse wearing latex gloves.
What is the immediate management?
options: Remove the allergen, call for help, and give adrenaline 1:1000, 500 micrograms IM
questions.answerText: Remove the allergen; adrenaline 500 micrograms IM.
questions.why: Remove the allergen; adrenaline 500 micrograms IM. Anaphylaxis needs IM adrenaline first.

questions.stem:
A cement-retained implant crown on 21 was fitted 6 months ago. There is bleeding on probing at a 4 mm pocket, and the radiograph shows a small radiopaque fleck at the margin with no bone loss.
What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Peri-implant mucositis from residual cement: remove the cement, debride, give OHI and review (Level 2)
Occlusal overload; adjust the opposing tooth
questions.why: Mucositis from residual cement; Level 2. Remove the cement and debride; there is no bone loss.

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old had radiotherapy to the mandible 3 years ago. A lower molar under his RPD has become non-restorable.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Extract it in primary care with antibiotics
Refer for specialist assessment because of the lifelong osteoradionecrosis risk; consider endodontic retention if possible
Leave it and reline the RPD
Place an implant at the same visit
questions.why: Specialist referral. Osteoradionecrosis risk is lifelong; avoid extraction in the field where possible.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old has palatal erosion, parotid enlargement and calluses on her knuckles. She asks for crowns and does not want her parents to know.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Approach with empathy, seek her consent to liaise with her GMP, and focus on prevention and monitoring before restoration
questions.why: Empathy, consented liaison, prevention first. She is an adult, so her confidentiality is respected.

questions.stem:
A 77-year-old with an acrylic upper denture has diffuse palatal erythema. She takes warfarin and simvastatin and wears the denture day and night.
What is the most appropriate management?
options: Denture hygiene, night removal, soaking, correcting the fit, and nystatin if it persists
questions.answerText: Hygiene, night removal, fit; nystatin if needed.
questions.why: Hygiene, night removal, fit; nystatin if needed. Azoles interact with warfarin and simvastatin.

questions.stem:
A resin-bonded bridge replacing 21 has debonded three times. The patient is a bruxist with a deep overbite and heavy contact on the wing.
What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Rebond again with the same design
Review the occlusion and design, and discuss alternatives such as a conventional bridge, an implant or an RPD
questions.answerText: Review the occlusion and design; discuss alternatives.
questions.why: Review the occlusion and design; discuss alternatives. Repeated debonding in a bruxist with heavy contact means the design must change.

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old has generalised severe wear, dentine exposure on most teeth and a planned OVD increase of 4 mm.
What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Crowns on all teeth at the current OVD
Dahl composites on the posterior teeth only
A diagnostic wax-up and provisional trial at the new OVD, with referral for Level 3 planning
questions.why: Wax-up, provisional trial, Level 3. Generalised wear with an OVD increase is reorganised rehabilitation.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old with treated, stable periodontitis and high caries risk needs a lower Kennedy Class II RPD. The lingual sulcus is 9 mm deep.
Which design is most appropriate?
options: An acrylic mucosa-borne plate covering the gingivae
Co-Cr with a lingual plate and distal rests
Co-Cr, tooth-supported, with a mesial rest and RPI on the terminal abutment, a lingual bar, an open design and maximum saddle extension
questions.answerText: Tooth-supported Co-Cr with RPI, lingual bar and open design.
questions.why: Tooth-supported Co-Cr with RPI, lingual bar and open design. A 9 mm sulcus allows a bar; high caries risk favours minimal coverage.

questions.stem:
A new upper complete denture drops on wide opening, and the patient gags. The posterior border is thick, and the distobuccal flange is long.
What is the most appropriate correction?
options: Add adhesive and increase the OVD
Trim the distobuccal flange and thin the posterior border, preserving the post-dam seal
questions.answerText: Trim the distobuccal flange and thin the posterior border.
questions.why: Trim the distobuccal flange and thin the posterior border. Keep the post-dam seal.

questions.stem:
A 14-year-old's replanted upper central incisor is now infra-occluded and ankylosed. He is still growing.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Monitor and seek multidisciplinary specialist advice; defer any implant until growth is complete
Crown the tooth to level it
Extract it and leave the space
Orthodontic extrusion of the ankylosed tooth
questions.answerText: Monitor with multidisciplinary advice; defer implants.
questions.why: Monitor with multidisciplinary advice; defer implants. Ankylosed teeth cannot be extruded orthodontically.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old on IV zoledronic acid for myeloma wants implants to stabilise her lower complete denture.
What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop the zoledronic acid and place implants
A well-fitting conventional denture with relief over bony prominences; implants are generally avoided because of high MRONJ risk
questions.why: A well-fitting conventional denture. High-dose IV antiresorptives carry high MRONJ risk, so implants are generally avoided.

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old with an HbA1c of 80 mmol/mol, generalised Stage III periodontitis and missing 46 wants a bridge.
What is the most appropriate sequence?
options: Periodontal therapy and referral to the GMP for diabetic control first; reassess before any definitive bridge
questions.answerText: Periodontal therapy and diabetic control first.
questions.why: Periodontal therapy and diabetic control first. Definitive work waits for stability.

questions.stem:
A heavy bruxist had root canal treatment on 46 two weeks ago. The tooth has an MOD cavity with thin cusps and a temporary restoration.
What is the most appropriate restoration?
options: Prompt cuspal coverage (onlay or crown) in metal or monolithic zirconia, plus a night guard
Leave the temporary for a year
A post and amalgam core only
questions.answerText: Prompt cuspal coverage, monolithic material, night guard.
questions.why: Prompt cuspal coverage, monolithic material, night guard.

questions.stem:
You realise after the patient has left that you extracted 15 instead of 14.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Contact her, explain, apologise, offer a remedy, report it as a never event and document everything
Ask a colleague to see her next time
questions.answerText: Candour, apology, remedy, never-event report, documentation.
questions.why: Candour, apology, remedy, never-event report, documentation.

questions.stem:
An NHS patient writes to complain about the cost and fit of her new denture.
What is the first required step?
options: Acknowledge it within 3 working days and investigate locally
Refer it to the Ombudsman at once
questions.why: Acknowledge within 3 working days.

questions.stem:
A patient with an implanted cardiac defibrillator and a high smile line needs a crown on 11 with a slightly subgingival margin.
What retraction method and margin position are appropriate?
options: Electrosurgery and a deep margin at the bone crest
Adrenaline cord and a 3 mm subgingival margin
No retraction and a supragingival margin regardless of aesthetics
Plain or aluminium chloride cord, with the margin just subgingival and about 3 mm from the bone crest
questions.answerText: Cord retraction, margin about 3 mm from the crest.
questions.why: Cord retraction, margin about 3 mm from the crest. Avoid electrosurgery with an ICD; respect the supracrestal attachment.

questions.stem:
An upper RPD is needed for anterior and posterior saddles. The patient has a large torus and refuses surgery.
Which major connector is most appropriate?
options: Narrow mid-palatal bar over the torus
questions.why: Anteroposterior strap.

questions.stem:
An 85-year-old attending for a denture reline has fingertip bruising on both arms. Her carer answers all questions for her.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Report directly to the police without discussion
Record your findings and refer through the practice safeguarding lead to adult social care
questions.answerText: Record and refer via the safeguarding lead.
questions.why: Record and refer via the safeguarding lead. Do not investigate yourself.

questions.stem:
A 20-year-old with hypodontia (missing 12, 22, 35 and 45) wants fixed replacements.
What is the most appropriate pathway?
options: Interim RBBs or an RPD, with referral for multidisciplinary Level 3 care
questions.why: Interim prostheses and Level 3 referral. Hypodontia is complex multidisciplinary care.

questions.stem:
During try-in, a crown slips from your fingers to the back of the patient's mouth. He is coughing forcefully and can speak.
What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Encourage coughing; if the crown is not retrieved, arrange urgent chest imaging to exclude inhalation
questions.answerText: Encourage coughing; image if not retrieved.
questions.why: Encourage coughing; image if not retrieved. Back blows are only for ineffective coughing.

questions.stem:
An implant supporting a crown on 36 shows suppuration, a 7 mm pocket and 4 mm of radiographic bone loss since the baseline radiograph.
What is the most appropriate action?
options: Debride and review in a year
questions.why: Peri-implantitis: refer.

questions.stem:
A patient with masticatory myalgia insists on "having her bite adjusted" before her crowns are made.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Explain that reversible care comes first (self-care and a stabilisation splint), and do not equilibrate to treat TMD
Prepare the crowns at a new OVD
questions.answerText: Reversible care first; no equilibration for TMD.
questions.why: Reversible care first; no equilibration for TMD.

questions.stem:
A 79-year-old with a severely resorbed mandible has burning and numbness of the lower lip whenever she wears her new lower denture. The symptoms resolve when it is out.
What is the most likely cause and action?
options: Pressure on the mental nerve; relieve the fitting surface over the foramen
questions.why: Mental nerve pressure. Symptoms that resolve when the denture is removed point to pressure; relieve the fitting surface.

questions.stem:
A patient with lower canine overdenture abutments has new root caries on both.
What is the most appropriate preventive measure?
options: Fluoride gel in the fitting surface of the denture, with meticulous hygiene and a diet review
Wear the denture day and night
questions.answerText: Fluoride gel in the denture, hygiene, diet.
questions.why: Fluoride gel in the denture, hygiene, diet.

questions.stem:
A patient has a two-implant lower overdenture opposing an upper complete denture. The upper anterior ridge has become flabby.
What is the most appropriate approach to a new upper denture?
options: A compressive putty impression and heavy anterior contacts
A selective-pressure (windowed) impression, with balanced occlusion avoiding heavy anterior contact
Excision of the flabby ridge first, routinely
questions.answerText: Selective pressure, balanced occlusion, light anterior contact.
questions.why: Selective pressure, balanced occlusion, light anterior contact. This limits combination-syndrome-type loading.

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old with Sjögren's syndrome has a Co-Cr RPD and multiple new root caries lesions.
What is the most appropriate integrated plan?
options: High-fluoride toothpaste, a neutral saliva substitute, an open RPD design and a short recall
questions.answerText: High fluoride, neutral substitute, open design, short recall.
questions.why: High fluoride, neutral substitute, open design, short recall.

questions.stem:
A trial reports that a new denture adhesive reduces denture failure from 40% to 30%.
What is the number needed to treat?
questions.why: 10. The absolute risk reduction is 10%, so NNT = 1 ÷ 0.10.

questions.stem:
A colleague requests CBCT at every annual implant review "to be safe".
What is correct?
options: Each exposure must be justified individually; a periapical radiograph against baseline usually answers the clinical question
questions.why: Individual justification.

questions.stem:
A patient asks the practice to delete all her records because she is moving abroad.
What is the correct response?
options: Explain that records must be retained (adults at least 11 years after last treatment), and offer copies
questions.why: Retain the records; offer copies.

questions.stem:
A 17-year-old with capacity wants a resin-bonded bridge. Her mother refuses.
What is the correct position?
options: The 17-year-old is presumed to have capacity and can consent
questions.why: Presumed capacity at 17.

questions.stem:
An 81-year-old with dementia whose capacity fluctuates needs a painful, infected tooth removed. On the day, she cannot weigh the information.
What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Proceed because she agreed last month
Act in her best interests, consulting those close to her and choosing the least restrictive option, unless she regains capacity
Wait for a court order in every case
questions.why: Best interests, least restrictive option.

questions.stem:
A crown arrives from a new laboratory with no statement of manufacture.
What should you do?
options: Accept it if it fits well
Ask the patient to sign a waiver
Request the statement and confirm the laboratory is MHRA-registered before fitting
questions.answerText: Statement of manufacture and MHRA registration.
questions.why: Statement of manufacture and MHRA registration.

questions.stem:
You take an impression for a patient with known hepatitis B.
